why_correct: Ray Bradbury sets the story on Venus, where it rains without stopping for seven years and the sun breaks through for only one hour. That single hour is what the whole story turns on, so the planet is one where the sun appears very rarely.

why_wrong.0: It does rain almost daily on that planet, but this misses what makes the story remarkable. The rain is the background; the point is the sun that almost never comes. Choose the option that names the rare thing, not the ordinary one.
why_wrong.2: The opposite of the story. The children have waited seven years for one hour of sunlight, and most of them cannot even remember what the sun looks like.
why_wrong.3: The planet is not dark. It is grey, wet and endlessly rainy, which is not the same as darkness. Bradbury describes a washed-out, colourless world under constant rain.

why_correct: Margot arrived from Earth only five years earlier, so she alone remembers the sun and can describe it. That memory is what sets her apart from children who have known nothing but rain, and it is why they resent her.

why_wrong.0: Margot is the frail one, not the strong one. Bradbury describes her as pale and washed out, and she is physically no match for the children who push her into the closet.
why_wrong.2: There is a teacher in the story, but Margot is a nine-year-old classmate, the same age as the others.
why_wrong.3: No character in the story is a scientist. Margot's knowledge of the sun comes from having lived on Earth, not from any study.

why_correct: The children cannot bear that Margot remembers something they have lost and can describe it in a way they cannot match. That jealousy, sharpened by irritation at her poem and her certainty, is what makes them shut her in the closet.

why_wrong.0: Hatred is too simple, and the ending proves it. When the sun goes and they remember her, they are ashamed. Children who genuinely hated her would not feel that.
why_wrong.2: Margot never refuses to study. Her withdrawal is from the games and the other children, not from lessons.
why_wrong.3: She breaks no rule. If anything, the rule-breakers are the children, who lock a classmate away while the teacher is out of the room.

why_correct: The moment the rain returns, the children remember Margot still shut in the closet. Bradbury has them stand frozen and unable to look at each other, which is the picture of guilt and shame, and he ends the story there rather than showing what they say to her.

why_wrong.0: Their anger was spent before the sun came out. What the hour outdoors leaves behind is not anger but the sick realisation of what they did to her.
why_wrong.2: They are excited and careless while the sun is out, and that is exactly the point. The question asks about after it appeared, when the joy has drained away and the memory of Margot returns.
why_wrong.3: They are deeply affected. Bradbury shows them moving slowly, not meeting each other's eyes, which is the whole force of the ending.

why_correct: Emily Bronte opens the poem with the mist lying mild upon the hill and rising from the valley below, a quiet upward drift that sets the still, gentle mood of the whole poem.

why_wrong.0: The poem's landscape is inland moor country, hills and a valley. There is no sea in it.
why_wrong.2: A desert is dry, and mist needs moisture. The poem's world is damp, green and cool, the opposite of desert country.
why_wrong.3: Nothing in the poem is urban. Bronte writes only of hill, valley, mist and sky, with no city anywhere in view.

why_correct: Every choice Bronte makes is a quiet one. The mist is mild, the movement is slow, and the poem watches rather than acts. Together these create a peaceful, calm mood, with a touch of gentle sadness underneath.

why_wrong.1: Nothing in the poem is loud or energetic. There is no noise and no hurry, only soft drifting mist. Judge mood by the words a poet chooses, and here every word is a gentle one.
why_wrong.2: Mist can be made to feel frightening, but Bronte does not do that. Her very first word is mild, which steers the reader away from fear.
why_wrong.3: There is no anger and no one to be angry with. The poem has no conflict in it at all.

why_correct: The poem is a picture of the natural world: mist, hill, valley, cloud and sky. Bronte's subject is the quiet beauty of that landscape and the feeling it stirs, not any human event.

why_wrong.0: There is no industry in the poem. No machines, no work, no smoke, only open country.
why_wrong.2: There is no war and no conflict of any kind. The poem is still and untroubled throughout.
why_wrong.3: City life is precisely what the poem leaves out. Bronte writes about hills and valleys, far from any town.

why_correct: Tom wakes, decides he does not want to go to school, and hunts through his body for an ailment worth staying home for. The pretence comes first and the symptom is found afterwards, which shows avoiding school was the aim all along.

why_wrong.0: Medicine is the last thing Tom wants. When Aunt Polly produces the painkiller, his scheme starts to go badly wrong for him.
why_wrong.2: Tom is not trying to see a doctor. Aunt Polly is the one who decides on treatment, and Tom regrets provoking it.
why_wrong.3: He is trying to get out of a day, not to arrange a meeting. And he does meet friends, but only on his way to school after the plan collapses.

why_correct: Tom searches for a complaint and remembers a loose tooth. Toothache becomes the illness he settles on, and the loose tooth is what drives the rest of the episode, so it is his main problem.

why_wrong.0: Tom does try out other symptoms while searching, but a headache is not the one he settles on, and it is not what Aunt Polly ends up treating.
why_wrong.2: Tom's first attempt is a supposedly mortifying toe, not an ear. Look for the complaint the story actually follows through, which is the tooth.
why_wrong.3: There is no fever. A fever would have been easy for Aunt Polly to check, which is part of why Tom's chosen ailment has to be one only he can feel.

why_correct: Aunt Polly sees through Tom quickly. She works out that the complaint is being enlarged for effect and deals with it briskly by pulling the tooth, which ends both the tooth and the performance.

why_wrong.0: If she had believed he was seriously ill, she would have kept him home, which is the outcome Tom wanted and did not get.
why_wrong.2: Nothing so grave is involved. Aunt Polly's remedy is a thread and a firm tug, dealt with at home in a moment.
why_wrong.3: Not quite. The tooth really was loose and really did hurt, and that is what makes Tom's trick clever. He exaggerates a real complaint rather than inventing one, which is harder to disprove.

why_correct: The gap in his teeth lets Tom spit in a brand-new way, and that novelty makes him the centre of attention among the other boys. He walks away proud, having gained far more than the day off he originally wanted.

why_wrong.0: The opposite happens. Rather than hiding the gap, Tom shows it off and enjoys the audience it earns him.
why_wrong.2: His anger, such as it was, ended with the tooth. What follows is pure enjoyment.
why_wrong.3: The fear came before the extraction, not after. Once it is over, the gap becomes something to display.

why_correct: The young seagull's wings are perfectly sound. What holds him on the ledge is the certainty that he will fall, while his brothers and sister have already flown. His problem is confidence, which is why the story is about overcoming fear rather than about learning a skill.

why_wrong.0: Swimming is not the issue. In fact once he is airborne his family lands him on the sea and he floats, which shows the sea was never the danger he imagined.
why_wrong.2: He is not injured. He runs about the ledge and flaps his wings quite normally; only the drop stops him.
why_wrong.3: He is hungry, not sick, and hunger is what eventually pushes him off the ledge rather than keeping him on it.

why_correct: Two things come together. He is starving after a day alone on the ledge, and his mother hovers near him with a piece of fish just out of reach. Hunger plus that pull from his family is what finally makes him dive off.

why_wrong.0: The wind holds him up once he is in the air, but it does not push him off. He dives towards the fish himself, which matters because the story is about him making the choice.
why_wrong.2: He is not escaping anything. His family is not a threat, and the ledge is safe. He leaves it because he is drawn forward, not driven away.
why_wrong.3: There is no danger and no predator. The story's tension is entirely inside the young seagull.

why_correct: The seagull does not stop being afraid and then fly. He flies, and the fear falls away in the doing of it. That is the story's lesson: confidence is the result of acting, not something you must find beforehand.

why_wrong.0: Too absolute, and not what happens. The seagull's fear is natural and no one shames him for it. He acts in spite of it, which is not the same as avoiding it.
why_wrong.2: The story is about a bird learning to do what birds are made for. Reading it as an argument against flying turns the ending upside down.
why_wrong.3: His family is central. They coax him, they refuse to feed him on the ledge, and they are around him the moment he lands on the sea.

why_correct: In the passive, the tense stays the same as the active. Taught is simple past, so the passive needs was plus the past participle: The lesson was taught by the teacher. Object becomes subject, the doer moves behind by.

why_wrong.0: Correct passive shape, wrong tense. Is taught is present, but the active sentence says taught, which is past. Changing the voice must never change the tense.
why_wrong.2: This has no auxiliary verb at all. Without was, the lesson taught by the teacher is only a phrase, not a complete sentence.
why_wrong.3: Has taught is active perfect, not passive. The passive perfect would be has been taught, and in any case the original is simple past, not perfect.

why_correct: Jupiter is by far the largest planet in the Solar System. It is about eleven times the diameter of Earth, and its mass is greater than that of all the other planets put together.

why_wrong.0: Earth is only the fifth largest planet, and the largest of the four small rocky ones. The giants are all further out from the Sun.
why_wrong.1: Mars is smaller than Earth, roughly half its diameter. It looms large in our imagination because it is close and well studied, not because it is big.
why_wrong.3: Saturn is the second largest, and a good guess. But Jupiter is bigger. Saturn only looks larger in photographs because of its rings, which are far wider than the planet itself.

why_correct: Mahatma Gandhi is called the Father of the Nation for leading the freedom movement along the path of non-violence and satyagraha. The title was famously given to him by Subhas Chandra Bose in a 1944 radio address.

why_wrong.0: Nehru was independent India's first Prime Minister, and he is remembered as the architect of modern India, but the title Father of the Nation belongs to Gandhi.
why_wrong.2: Bose led the Indian National Army and is called Netaji. It was in fact Bose who addressed Gandhi as Father of the Nation, so he gave the title rather than held it.
why_wrong.3: Sardar Patel is the Iron Man of India, remembered for uniting the princely states into one country after independence.

why_correct: Kolkata is the capital of West Bengal and the seat of its government, its legislative assembly and the Calcutta High Court. It was also the capital of British India until 1911.

why_wrong.0: Siliguri is an important city in north Bengal and the gateway to the northeast, but it is not the state capital.
why_wrong.1: Durgapur is a major industrial and steel town in Paschim Bardhaman district, not the seat of government.
why_wrong.3: Howrah sits directly across the Hooghly from Kolkata and is joined to it by the Howrah Bridge, but it is a separate city and not the capital.

why_correct: Nitrogen makes up about 78 per cent of the Earth's atmosphere by volume, well over twice as much as everything else combined. It is unreactive, which is why it simply accumulates rather than being used up.

why_wrong.0: Oxygen is second, at about 21 per cent. It matters most to us because we breathe it, but importance and abundance are not the same thing.
why_wrong.1: Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04 per cent of the air. Tiny as that is, it drives the greenhouse effect and feeds photosynthesis.
why_wrong.3: Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe, but barely present in our atmosphere. It is so light that Earth's gravity cannot hold on to it.

why_correct: Rabindranath Tagore wrote Jana Gana Mana in Bengali in 1911, and it was adopted as India's national anthem by the Constituent Assembly on 24 January 1950.

why_wrong.0: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote Vande Mataram, which is the national song, not the national anthem. India has both, and this is the pair most often confused.
why_wrong.2: Kazi Nazrul Islam is the rebel poet, Bidrohi Kobi, and the national poet of Bangladesh. Note that Tagore also wrote Bangladesh's anthem, Amar Sonar Bangla.
why_wrong.3: Sarojini Naidu was a poet and freedom fighter known as the Nightingale of India, and the first woman governor of an Indian state, but she did not write the anthem.

why_correct: There are seven continents: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia. Asia is the largest and Australia the smallest.

why_wrong.0: Five is the count used in some models that merge the Americas and leave out Antarctica, as on the Olympic rings. The standard geographical answer is seven.
why_wrong.1: Six comes from combining North and South America into one, or Europe and Asia into Eurasia. Both are used in some countries, but not in the Indian syllabus.
why_wrong.3: There is no eighth continent in standard geography. Zealandia, the mostly submerged landmass around New Zealand, is sometimes proposed but is not accepted for exams.

why_correct: The Royal Bengal Tiger has been India's national animal since 1973, when it replaced the lion at the launch of Project Tiger.

why_wrong.0: The lion was the national animal until 1973, and the Asiatic lion of Gir remains a protected national treasure. But the title now belongs to the tiger.
why_wrong.1: The elephant is India's national heritage animal, declared in 2010. A separate honour, and a common mix-up with this question.
why_wrong.3: The peacock is the national bird, not the national animal. Read such questions carefully: bird, animal, flower and tree are all separate titles.

why_correct: The United Nations headquarters stands on the bank of the East River in New York City, on land that is international territory. The General Assembly and the Security Council meet there.

why_wrong.0: Geneva hosts the UN Office at Geneva and many agencies such as the WHO, so it is a major UN centre, but the headquarters is in New York.
why_wrong.1: Paris is the headquarters of UNESCO, a UN agency, which is what makes this a tempting answer.
why_wrong.2: London hosts the International Maritime Organization but is not the UN's headquarters. Take care: the UN's Charter was signed in San Francisco, in the United States, not in Europe.

why_correct: The Godavari is called Dakshina Ganga, the Ganga of the South. It is the longest river in peninsular India, rising at Trimbakeshwar in Maharashtra and flowing east to the Bay of Bengal.

why_wrong.0: The Krishna is a major peninsular river rising at Mahabaleshwar, but it is shorter than the Godavari and does not carry that title.
why_wrong.1: The Kaveri is called Dakshina Bhagirathi, or the Ganga of the South in Tamil tradition. Close, and a fair mistake, but for this exam the Dakshina Ganga is the Godavari.
why_wrong.3: The Narmada flows west, not east, and empties into the Arabian Sea. It is one of the few major Indian rivers to do so.

why_correct: Dr Rajendra Prasad became independent India's first President on 26 January 1950, when the Constitution came into force. He is still the only person to have served two full terms in the office.

why_wrong.1: Dr S. Radhakrishnan was the first Vice-President and then the second President. The teacher and philosopher whose birthday India keeps as Teachers' Day, but the second in this office, not the first.
why_wrong.2: Nehru was the first Prime Minister, not the first President. Prime Minister leads the government, President is head of state, and the two must not be swapped.
why_wrong.3: Dr Zakir Husain was the third President, and the first Muslim to hold the office. He died in office in 1969.

why_correct: The Ottoman Empire, ruled from Turkey, was called the Sick Man of Europe in the nineteenth century because it was steadily losing territory and strength while the great powers waited to divide what was left. The phrase is usually credited to Tsar Nicholas I of Russia.

why_wrong.0: England in this period was at the height of its power, with the largest empire in the world. It was one of the powers watching the sick man, not the sick man itself.
why_wrong.2: Russia was the country that coined the phrase and hoped to gain from Ottoman decline, particularly access to the Black Sea straits.
why_wrong.3: France was weakened after Napoleon's fall but recovered through the nineteenth century and remained a major power. The label was never applied to it.

why_correct: The February Revolution of 1848 overthrew King Louis Philippe and established the Second Republic in France. It set off a wave of risings across Europe, which is why 1848 is called the Year of Revolutions.

why_wrong.0: 1830 is the July Revolution, which removed Charles X and put Louis Philippe on the throne. The same country, an earlier revolution, and the most common confusion in this chapter.
why_wrong.2: Nothing revolutionary happened in France in 1859. That year belongs to Italian unification, when France fought Austria alongside Piedmont.
why_wrong.3: By 1890 France had been a republic for twenty years, since the fall of Napoleon III in 1870.

why_correct: The Congress of Vienna worked to three principles: legitimacy, restoring the old ruling houses; compensation, repaying the victors with territory; and balance of power, keeping any one state from dominating Europe again as Napoleon had.

why_wrong.1: Four is one too many. The settlement rested on legitimacy, compensation and balance of power, and nothing further was adopted as a founding principle.
why_wrong.2: Five overstates it. The Quadruple Alliance and the Concert of Europe were arrangements that followed from the Congress, not extra principles agreed at it.
why_wrong.3: Six is well beyond what the Congress agreed. The three principles were deliberately few, because they had to be acceptable to rival powers.

why_correct: Tsar Alexander I represented Russia at Vienna and attended in person, unusually for a monarch. He also promoted the Holy Alliance that followed the Congress.

why_wrong.0: Nicholas I became Tsar in 1825, ten years after the Congress. He is the one remembered for the Sick Man of Europe remark, not for Vienna.
why_wrong.1: Castlereagh represented Britain at the Congress, not Russia.
why_wrong.3: Talleyrand represented France, the defeated power, and used the principle of legitimacy so skilfully that France was admitted to the settlement almost as an equal.

why_correct: The Congress met in Vienna, the capital of Austria, from 1814 to 1815. It was hosted and dominated by the Austrian chancellor Metternich, which is why the years that followed are called the Age of Metternich.

why_wrong.0: France was the defeated power. It was represented by Talleyrand, but the settlement was made in the victors' territory, not on French soil.
why_wrong.2: Prussia was one of the four great powers at the table, but the Congress was not held there.
why_wrong.3: Russia sent Tsar Alexander I to Vienna. The conference took place in Austria.

why_correct: Giuseppe Mazzini founded Young Italy in Marseilles in 1831, a secret society for young patriots working towards a unified Italian republic. He is remembered as the soul of Italian unification.

why_wrong.1: Garibaldi is the sword of unification, the soldier who led the Thousand Red Shirts to Sicily. He was inspired by Mazzini but did not found Young Italy.
why_wrong.2: Cesare Cantu was an Italian historian and writer, not the founder of a revolutionary society.
why_wrong.3: Carlo Troya was an Italian historian and briefly a minister in Naples. Like Cantu, a name from the period rather than the answer here.

why_correct: James Hargreaves invented the Spinning Jenny in 1764. It let one worker spin several threads at once, and it is one of the machines that began the Industrial Revolution in the cotton industry.

why_wrong.0: Samuel Crompton invented the Spinning Mule in 1779, which combined the Jenny with Arkwright's water frame. Later, and a different machine.
why_wrong.1: John Kay invented the Flying Shuttle in 1733. That sped up weaving so much that spinners could not keep pace, which is the shortage the Spinning Jenny was made to solve.
why_wrong.2: James Watt improved the steam engine. His work powered the factories, but he did not invent a spinning machine.

why_correct: Digging began under Egypt, where the canal lies, with the Suez Canal Company set up under a concession from the Egyptian viceroy Said Pasha. Work started in 1859 and the canal opened in 1869.

why_wrong.1: Russia had no part in the Suez project. Its own canal ambitions lay elsewhere, and it was more concerned with the Ottoman straits.
why_wrong.2: The French engineer Ferdinand de Lesseps designed the canal and French investors funded much of it, which makes this a fair guess. But the digging was begun in and by Egypt, on Egyptian soil.
why_wrong.3: Britain opposed the canal at first and only bought into it in 1875, when Egypt sold its shares. It came late to a project already built.

why_correct: Robert Owen is called the Father of British Socialism. A mill owner at New Lanark in Scotland, he cut working hours, banned child labour in his mills and built schools, showing that industry could be run humanely.

why_wrong.0: Louis Blanc was a French socialist, remembered for the national workshops of 1848 and the right to work.
why_wrong.2: Proudhon was French and famous for the phrase property is theft. Often studied alongside Owen, but not British.
why_wrong.3: Charles Fourier was another French socialist, who proposed cooperative communities called phalanxes. Note that three of the four options here are French, so the word British in the question is the clue.

why_correct: Both Opium Wars were fought between Britain and China. The first, from 1839 to 1842, ended with the Treaty of Nanking and the cession of Hong Kong; the second, from 1856 to 1860, opened China further to foreign trade.

why_wrong.0: France and Holland were rivals in Europe and Asia, but the Opium Wars were fought in China over the opium trade.
why_wrong.1: France did join Britain in the Second Opium War, so France and China is partly true of the second war. It is wrong for the first, and the question asks about both.
why_wrong.3: China and Japan fought the Sino-Japanese War of 1894 to 1895, a different conflict thirty years later.

why_correct: Ivan IV, known as Ivan the Terrible, was crowned in 1547 as the first ruler to take the title Tsar of All Russia. The word Tsar comes from Caesar and was a claim to imperial authority.

why_wrong.0: Nicholas I ruled from 1825 to 1855, nearly three centuries after the title was first taken.
why_wrong.1: Alexander II ruled from 1855 and is remembered for emancipating the serfs in 1861, not for adopting the title.
why_wrong.3: Alexander III ruled from 1881. Look for the earliest ruler in such questions, and Ivan IV in the sixteenth century is by far the earliest here.

why_correct: Peter the Great, who ruled from 1682 to 1725, is called the Father of Modern Russia. He westernised the army, the navy, dress and administration, and built St Petersburg as Russia's window on Europe.

why_wrong.0: Nicholas I was a conservative who worked to hold back change, which is close to the opposite of modernising.
why_wrong.1: Ivan IV was the first Tsar, and that is his claim to fame. Being first is not the same as modernising.
why_wrong.2: Mikhail Romanov founded the Romanov dynasty in 1613. He began the family that Peter belonged to, but the reforms were Peter's.

why_correct: The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was formally created on 30 December 1922, when Russia, Ukraine, Belorussia and the Transcaucasian republic joined into one union state.

why_wrong.0: 1921 is the year the civil war effectively ended and Lenin launched the New Economic Policy. Groundwork for the union, but not the union itself.
why_wrong.2: 1924 is the year Lenin died and the first Soviet constitution was adopted. The USSR already existed by then.
why_wrong.3: By 1926 Stalin was consolidating power. Nothing about the union's formation happened that year.

why_correct: Herbert Clark Hoover was President when the Wall Street Crash came in October 1929, and he held office through the worst years of the Depression until March 1933.

why_wrong.0: Franklin D. Roosevelt followed Hoover in 1933 and answered the Depression with the New Deal. He is the president of the recovery, not of the crash, and this is the classic trap in this question.
why_wrong.1: Woodrow Wilson was president through the First World War and left office in 1921, well before the crash.
why_wrong.3: Abraham Lincoln was president during the Civil War in the 1860s, some seventy years earlier.

why_correct: Mein Kampf, meaning My Struggle, was written by Hitler while imprisoned after the failed Munich Putsch and published in 1925. It sets out his ideology and his plans, which makes it a key source for the period.

why_wrong.1: War and Peace is Tolstoy's novel about Russia and the Napoleonic wars. Russian fiction, not German autobiography.
why_wrong.2: Fathers and Sons is a novel by the Russian writer Turgenev, about the clash between generations.
why_wrong.3: Resurrection is another Tolstoy novel. Three of the four options are nineteenth-century Russian novels, so the odd one out is the answer.

why_correct: The axis is the imaginary line through the centre of the Earth about which it rotates, and its two ends are the North Pole and the South Pole. It is tilted at 23 and a half degrees from the vertical, which is what gives us the seasons.

why_wrong.0: Both the Equator and the Tropic of Cancer are circles running round the Earth, not points. An axis has to join two points.
why_wrong.2: The Arctic and Antarctic Circles are also lines of latitude, and both lie well away from the poles that the axis actually passes through.
why_wrong.3: The Prime Meridian and the Equator are both great circles on the surface. They cross each other in the Gulf of Guinea, but neither is an end of the axis.

why_correct: The Equator runs east to west round the middle of the Earth, so it separates everything above it from everything below it: the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere.

why_wrong.0: The Eastern and Western Hemispheres are divided by the Prime Meridian and the 180 degree line, which run north to south. Swapping these two is the most common error in this chapter.
why_wrong.2: The Land and Water Hemispheres are a separate idea, centred near France and near New Zealand. They have nothing to do with the Equator.
why_wrong.3: The heat zones are marked out by the Tropics and the Polar Circles, and there are five of them, not two.

why_correct: The Equator is the starting line from which all latitude is measured, so its own latitude is 0 degrees. It is also the longest line of latitude and the only one that is a great circle.

why_wrong.0: 90 degrees is the latitude of the poles, the highest value latitude can reach.
why_wrong.1: 23 and a half degrees is the Tropic of Cancer in the north and the Tropic of Capricorn in the south.
why_wrong.3: 66 and a half degrees marks the Arctic Circle and the Antarctic Circle.

why_correct: The Prime Meridian, 0 degrees longitude, passes through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich in London. It was fixed there by international agreement in 1884 and is the base for Greenwich Mean Time.

why_wrong.0: Paris had its own prime meridian and argued for it at the 1884 conference, but Greenwich was chosen because most shipping already used it.
why_wrong.1: India's own Standard Meridian is 82 and a half degrees east, which passes near Mirzapur, not through New Delhi.
why_wrong.3: Kolkata lies at about 88 degrees east. No meridian of special international standing runs through it.

why_correct: Longitudes are measured east and west of the Prime Meridian, from 0 up to 180 degrees in each direction. They run pole to pole and are also called meridians.

why_wrong.0: North and south of the Equator is how latitude is measured. This is the pair to keep straight: latitude north and south, longitude east and west.
why_wrong.2: All lines of longitude meet at both poles, so the poles cannot be used as a starting point to measure from.
why_wrong.3: Longitudes are counted along the Equator, but they are measured from the Prime Meridian. The question asks about the reference line, not the path.

why_correct: India's Standard Meridian is 82 and a half degrees east, passing near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh. It is exactly 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich, which gives Indian Standard Time.

why_wrong.0: 75 degrees east passes through western India but is not the standard meridian. Note that a standard meridian is usually chosen as a multiple of 7 and a half degrees, so that the time difference comes out in neat half hours.
why_wrong.1: 90 degrees east lies to the east of India's standard meridian, closer to Bangladesh, and is the standard meridian for that country.
why_wrong.3: 70 degrees east passes near the far western edge of India, well away from the centre a standard meridian should represent.

why_correct: Endogenic forces come from inside the Earth. Endo means within, and these are the forces of earthquakes, volcanoes, folding and faulting that build up the major landforms.

why_wrong.0: Exogenic forces are the opposite: they act from outside, through rivers, wind, glaciers and rain, and they wear landforms down rather than build them.
why_wrong.2: Gravity is a force, and it drives landslides and river flow, but it acts from outside the crust and is grouped with the exogenic forces.
why_wrong.3: Atmospheric forces such as wind and rain act on the surface, which again makes them exogenic.

why_correct: The Himalayas are fold mountains, raised when the Indian plate collided with the Eurasian plate and the sediments of the Tethys Sea were crumpled upward. They are young fold mountains and are still rising.

why_wrong.0: Block mountains are formed by faulting, when a block of land is pushed up or its neighbours drop away. The Vosges and the Black Forest are examples.
why_wrong.1: Residual mountains are old mountains worn down by erosion, such as the Aravallis. The Himalayas are the opposite: young, sharp and still growing.
why_wrong.3: Volcanic mountains are built from erupted lava, like Fujiyama or Kilimanjaro. The Himalayas have no volcanic origin.

why_correct: Erosion is the wearing away of the surface by moving agents such as rivers, wind, glaciers and waves, which loosen material and carry it off. The carrying away is what distinguishes it.

why_wrong.0: Deposition is the laying down of material at the end of the journey. It builds land up rather than wearing it away.
why_wrong.1: Weathering breaks rock down where it stands, without moving it. Weathering plus transport is erosion, so the difference is movement.
why_wrong.3: Sedimentation is a form of deposition, the settling of sediment carried by water or wind.

why_correct: A rift valley forms when the land between two parallel faults sinks, leaving a steep-sided trough. The East African Rift Valley and the Narmada valley in India are examples.

why_wrong.0: Folding bends rock layers upward and downward and builds mountains such as the Himalayas. It does not drop a block of land.
why_wrong.2: Volcanism builds cones and plateaus from erupted material rather than opening a valley by subsidence.
why_wrong.3: Weathering breaks down rock in place and works far too slowly and too shallowly to create a feature on this scale.

why_correct: A plateau is an elevated area with a broad flat top and at least one steep side, so it is commonly called a tableland. The Deccan Plateau is the familiar Indian example.

why_wrong.0: Highland is a loose word for any high ground, including mountains. It is not the specific name for a flat-topped upland.
why_wrong.2: Lowlands are low, level areas such as plains, which is the opposite of a plateau's elevation.
why_wrong.3: A valley is a low area between higher ground, cut by a river or a glacier.

why_correct: Sand dunes are built by wind, which lifts loose sand and drops it where its speed falls. They are typical of deserts such as the Thar, where there is dry loose sand and little vegetation to hold it.

why_wrong.0: Rivers deposit deltas, floodplains and levees. Their sediment is laid down in water, not heaped into wind-shaped ridges.
why_wrong.1: Glaciers deposit moraines and drumlins, made of unsorted rock and clay rather than fine sand.
why_wrong.3: Sea waves build beaches, spits and bars along the coast. Coastal dunes exist, but the wind shapes them even there, not the waves.

why_correct: A delta is formed by river deposition. Where a river meets the sea its speed drops sharply, so the silt it carries settles and builds up land at the mouth. The Sundarbans delta of the Ganga and Brahmaputra is the largest in the world.

why_wrong.1: Wind erosion carves features such as mushroom rocks. Erosion removes material, while a delta is made of material added.
why_wrong.2: Glaciers deposit moraines in cold, high regions. Deltas form at river mouths, usually at sea level.
why_wrong.3: Earthquakes can alter a coastline suddenly, but a delta is built slowly, over centuries, by silt.

why_correct: Moraines are the ridges of rock, gravel and clay that a glacier carries and then dumps as it melts. They are named by where they lie: lateral, medial, terminal and ground moraines.

why_wrong.0: Dunes are heaped by wind in dry regions, not by ice.
why_wrong.2: Deltas are built by rivers at their mouths.
why_wrong.3: Meanders are the loops a river makes across a flat plain. They are a river feature and are formed by erosion and deposition together, not by ice.

why_correct: Weathering is the breakdown of rock in situ, meaning in its own place, by temperature change, water, chemicals or the action of plants and animals. Nothing is carried away, and that is what separates it from erosion.

why_wrong.0: Transportation is the carrying of broken material by water, wind or ice. It is the step that follows weathering, and joining the two gives erosion.
why_wrong.2: Deposition is the dropping of sediment at the end of transport, the last stage rather than the first.
why_wrong.3: Glacier movement is one agent of erosion. Weathering is a process, not the movement of any one agent.

why_correct: Metabolism, the sum of all the chemical reactions inside a body, is the one thing every living organism does without exception. Nothing alive can stop metabolising and remain alive.

why_wrong.0: Locomotion is movement from place to place, and plants and fixed animals such as corals and sponges do not do it. Living things all show movement of some kind, but not locomotion.
why_wrong.2: Reproduction is universal for species but not for individuals. A mule or a worker bee never reproduces, and it is unquestionably alive.
why_wrong.3: Photosynthesis belongs only to green plants, algae and some bacteria. Every animal is alive without it.

why_correct: The kidneys are the main excretory organs. They filter the blood and remove urea, excess salts and water as urine, and they also regulate the body's water and salt balance.

why_wrong.0: The heart pumps blood. It is central to circulation but removes no waste itself.
why_wrong.1: The lungs do excrete, giving out carbon dioxide and some water vapour, so this is a reasonable answer. But the main excretory organ, handling nitrogenous waste, is the kidney.
why_wrong.3: The liver converts toxic ammonia into urea, so it prepares the waste. The kidney is what actually removes it from the body.

why_correct: A tissue is a group of similar cells doing one particular job together, such as muscle tissue or nerve tissue. The order of organisation runs cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism.

why_wrong.0: An organ is made of several different tissues working together, like the heart with muscle, nerve and connective tissue. The question specifies similar cells, which is one step lower.
why_wrong.1: An organ system is a group of organs, such as the digestive system, so it is two levels above tissue.
why_wrong.3: An organism is the whole living individual, the top of the ladder.

why_correct: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use chlorophyll to trap sunlight and convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose, storing solar energy as chemical energy in that glucose.

why_wrong.0: Respiration does the reverse: it releases the energy stored in glucose rather than capturing it. The two processes are opposites and are the pair most often swapped.
why_wrong.2: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves. It moves water, not energy.
why_wrong.3: Digestion breaks large food molecules into smaller ones. Plants make their own food, so they do not need it.

why_correct: Transpiration is the loss of water as vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata of the leaves. The pull it creates is what draws water up from the roots.

why_wrong.0: Osmosis is the movement of water across a semi-permeable membrane, which is how roots take water in. Liquid water moving in, not vapour moving out.
why_wrong.2: Guttation is the loss of liquid water droplets from the leaf margins through hydathodes, usually at night. Water is lost, but as liquid, not vapour.
why_wrong.3: Imbibition is the absorption of water by solids such as dry seeds, which makes them swell.

why_correct: The energy released when glucose is broken down is stored in ATP, adenosine triphosphate, which is called the energy currency of the cell because every energy-requiring process spends it.

why_wrong.0: DNA carries genetic information. It is a store of instructions, not of usable energy.
why_wrong.1: NADP is a carrier of hydrogen and electrons, and it is important in photosynthesis. It shuttles reducing power rather than being the cell's energy currency.
why_wrong.3: RNA carries genetic messages from DNA to the ribosome and helps build proteins.

why_graced: This question has been graced: every candidate receives the mark, whatever they wrote and even if they left it blank. The stem carries a double negative. "Not a non-renewable resource" means simply "a renewable resource", and three of the four options are renewable: solar energy, wind energy and forest timber. The setter meant to ask which one is non-renewable, and coal and petroleum was the intended answer, but that is not the question that was printed. No change of key can repair a defect that lies in the stem, so the question was withdrawn from scoring.

why_wrong.0: Solar energy is renewable, so as the question was actually printed this is a correct answer. It is listed here only because the whole question was withdrawn, not because there is anything wrong with the reasoning.
why_wrong.1: Wind energy is likewise renewable, and is in fact driven by solar heating of the atmosphere. Again correct as printed.
why_wrong.2: Coal and petroleum are the fossil fuels, formed from buried organic matter over millions of years and consumed far faster than they form, so they are the non-renewable pair. This is what the setter had in mind, but the double negative makes it the one option that does not answer the printed stem.
why_wrong.3: Forest timber is renewable so long as felling is matched by replanting, which is why sustainable forestry is possible at all. Correct as printed.

why_correct: Decomposers, mainly bacteria and fungi, break dead plants and animals down into simple nutrients that return to the soil for producers to use again. They are what closes the nutrient cycle.

why_wrong.0: Producers are green plants, which make food from sunlight. They take up the nutrients decomposers release rather than releasing them.
why_wrong.2: Primary consumers are herbivores. They eat living plants, not dead matter.
why_wrong.3: Apex predators sit at the top of the food chain and hunt live prey. When they die they too become food for the decomposers.

why_correct: Stomata are the tiny pores on the leaf surface, each bounded by two guard cells that open and close it. They allow gas exchange for photosynthesis and are the main route for transpiration.

why_wrong.0: Lenticels are pores too, but they are found in the bark of woody stems, not on leaves.
why_wrong.2: Pits are thin areas in the wall between two plant cells, inside the plant rather than on its surface.
why_wrong.3: Hydathodes are openings at the leaf margin that release liquid water in guttation. Real leaf openings, but not the ones meant here, and they release water rather than exchanging gas.

why_correct: Anaerobic respiration takes place without oxygen. It yields far less energy than the aerobic kind and produces alcohol and carbon dioxide in yeast, or lactic acid in our muscles when they are short of oxygen.

why_wrong.0: Aerobic respiration is exactly the opposite: it requires oxygen and releases much more energy per glucose molecule.
why_wrong.2: External respiration is the exchange of gases between the lungs and the blood, which is breathing rather than cellular respiration.
why_wrong.3: Photorespiration is a wasteful process in plants in which oxygen is taken up instead of carbon dioxide. It needs oxygen, so it cannot be the answer.

why_correct: Quinine is an alkaloid, and alkaloids contain nitrogen, so it counts as a nitrogenous waste product of plants. It is obtained from cinchona bark and is used against malaria.

why_wrong.1: Resins are plant waste, but they are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen with no nitrogen in them.
why_wrong.2: Gums are carbohydrate in nature and again contain no nitrogen. The test in this question is not whether it is waste but whether it holds nitrogen.
why_wrong.3: Latex is the milky fluid of plants such as rubber and papaya. It is a waste product, but not a nitrogenous one.

why_correct: Polio is caused by the poliovirus and is prevented by vaccination, both the oral drops and the injected vaccine. India's pulse polio campaign made the country polio-free in 2014.

why_wrong.0: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a protozoan carried by the Anopheles mosquito. Not a virus, and there is no routine vaccine for it in India.
why_wrong.1: Tuberculosis is preventable by the BCG vaccine, so it meets half the question. But it is caused by a bacterium, not a virus, and the question asks for both.
why_wrong.3: Cholera is caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, spread through contaminated water. Again bacterial, not viral.

why_correct: Haemoglobin is the red pigment in our red blood cells. It contains iron, which gives it the colour, and it carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues.

why_wrong.0: Haemocyanin is a respiratory pigment too, but it contains copper and is blue. It is found in molluscs and arthropods, not in humans.
why_wrong.2: Chlorophyll is the green pigment of plants that traps sunlight.
why_wrong.3: Leucoplasts are colourless plastids in plant cells that store starch, oil or protein. Plant structures, and colourless at that.

why_correct: BCG protects against tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. In India it is given at birth and is part of the universal immunisation programme.

why_wrong.0: Cholera has its own oral vaccine and is caused by a different bacterium altogether.
why_wrong.1: Typhoid is prevented by the typhoid vaccine, against Salmonella typhi. A different bacterium and a different vaccine.
why_wrong.3: Tetanus is prevented by the tetanus toxoid, usually given in the DPT combination. The clue is in the name: Bacillus Calmette-Guerin is the strain used against TB.

why_correct: Water is abiotic, meaning non-living. The abiotic components of an ecosystem are its physical and chemical surroundings: water, air, soil, light and temperature.

why_wrong.0: Plants are living, and as producers they are a biotic component.
why_wrong.1: Microbes are living organisms and act as decomposers, so they are biotic. Being invisible does not make something non-living.
why_wrong.3: Humans are living organisms and are biotic consumers within the ecosystem.

why_correct: In the brown ring test for a nitrate, freshly prepared iron(II) sulphate solution is added to the sample and concentrated sulphuric acid is poured carefully down the side of the tube. The acid liberates nitric acid, which the iron(II) reduces to nitric oxide, NO. That NO is what binds to another iron(II) ion to form the nitrosyl complex [Fe(H2O)5NO]2+, and it is that complex which appears as the brown ring at the junction of the two layers.

why_wrong.0: Sulphur dioxide is the gas of the sulphite and bisulphite tests: it turns acidified potassium dichromate green and decolourises potassium permanganate. It plays no part in the ring test, and it forms no coloured complex with iron(II).
why_wrong.1: Nitrogen dioxide is the tempting answer, because brown fumes of NO2 are what you see when a nitrate is heated or when copper reacts with concentrated nitric acid, and the ring itself is brown. But in the ring test the reduction stops at NO, and it is NO, not NO2, that co-ordinates to iron(II). This was the printed key and it has been corrected.
why_wrong.2: Water is not a gas under the conditions of the test, and in any case concentrated sulphuric acid is present precisely to remove water. Nothing about steam would produce a coloured ring.

why_correct: A neutral sodium atom has 11 electrons. The plus sign means it has lost one, so Na+ has 10 electrons. That gives it the stable configuration of neon, which is why sodium forms this ion so readily.

why_wrong.1: 11 is the number of electrons in a neutral sodium atom, and also its atomic number. The charge on the ion is what tells you an electron has gone.
why_wrong.2: 9 would mean sodium had lost two electrons. Its charge is written as a single plus, so only one is lost.
why_wrong.3: 12 would mean sodium had gained an electron. Metals lose electrons to form positive ions; they do not gain them.

why_correct: Surface tension is force per unit length, so its SI unit is the newton per metre. It can equally be written as joule per square metre, since it is also energy per unit area.

why_wrong.0: Joule per metre is force, not surface tension, because a joule is a newton metre. Dividing by a metre simply gives newtons back.
why_wrong.2: Newton per centimetre has the right kind of quantity but the wrong unit of length. SI units use the metre.
why_wrong.3: Joule per centimetre is wrong twice over: energy per length rather than force per length, and centimetres rather than metres.

why_correct: Both have atomic number 17, so both are chlorine, but their mass numbers are 35 and 37. Same number of protons, different numbers of neutrons, which is exactly the definition of isotopes.

why_wrong.1: Isobars have the same mass number but different atomic numbers. Here the mass numbers differ and the atomic numbers match, so it is the other way round.
why_wrong.2: Isothermic means at the same temperature. That is a term from heat, and it does not describe a relation between atoms.
why_wrong.3: There is a clear relation here, so none of these cannot be right. Check the two numbers separately: the lower one is the atomic number and the upper one the mass number.

why_correct: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a material medium to travel through. A vacuum has no particles to vibrate, so no sound can pass and its velocity there is zero.

why_wrong.1: 1.5 metres per second is far too slow for sound anywhere. Sound travels at about 340 metres per second in air and about 1500 in water, and the figure here looks like that water value with the wrong unit.
why_wrong.2: 25 metres per second is a walking-pace figure, not a wave speed, and in any case sound cannot travel in a vacuum at all.
why_wrong.3: Infinity is what light might tempt you to guess, since light does cross a vacuum. But light is electromagnetic and needs no medium, while sound is mechanical and does.

why_correct: An echo is a sound heard again after it reflects off a distant surface. The reflected sound must reach the ear at least a tenth of a second after the original, so the reflecting surface has to be about 17 metres away or more.

why_wrong.0: Vibration is what produces sound in the first place, at the source. It is the cause of sound, not a result of reflection.
why_wrong.1: Oscillation is the same idea as vibration, a to-and-fro motion, and again it describes how sound is made.
why_wrong.3: Compression is a region of a sound wave where the particles are crowded together. It is a part of the wave itself, not an effect of reflecting it.

why_graced: This question has been graced: every candidate receives the mark, whatever they wrote and even if they left it blank. All four options are genuine colloids. Blood is a colloidal suspension of proteins and cells in plasma, cheese is a gel, milk is an emulsion of liquid fat in water and paint is a sol of solid pigment in a liquid. Milk is the textbook example and was the intended answer, but no candidate could fairly be told that the other three are wrong, so the question was withdrawn from scoring.

why_wrong.0: Blood is a colloid: the plasma proteins are dispersed in water at colloidal size, which is why blood shows the Tyndall effect and why it cannot be separated by ordinary filtration. Correct as printed.
why_wrong.1: Cheese is a colloid of the gel type, a liquid dispersed in a solid. Correct as printed.
why_wrong.2: Milk is an emulsion, tiny droplets of liquid fat dispersed in water and kept apart by casein acting as the emulsifying agent. This is the answer the setter intended and the one the textbook gives.
why_wrong.3: Paint is a sol, solid pigment particles dispersed in a liquid medium. Correct as printed.

why_correct: Power is the rate of doing work, so its SI unit is the watt, which is one joule per second. It is named after James Watt.

why_wrong.0: The ohm is the unit of electrical resistance.
why_wrong.1: Kilometre per hour is a unit of speed, and it is not an SI unit either. The SI unit of speed is the metre per second.
why_wrong.2: The newton is the unit of force. Force times distance gives work in joules, and work divided by time gives power in watts, so the newton is two steps away.

why_correct: Rutherford fired alpha particles, which are helium nuclei carrying a double positive charge, at a thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, but a very few bounced back, and that led him to the idea of a small dense positive nucleus.

why_wrong.0: Beta rays are fast electrons. Being negative and very light, they would have been deflected by the foil's own electrons and could not have shown the nucleus.
why_wrong.2: Gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation with no charge, so they would not be deflected by charge at all. The whole experiment depended on the projectile being charged and heavy.
why_wrong.3: Only one type was used. The experiment is known as the alpha-particle scattering experiment for that reason.

why_correct: Methyl orange is an acid-base indicator, red in acid and yellow in alkali, so the colour change marks the point of neutralisation. It is the standard indicator for a strong acid against a weak base.

why_wrong.0: Methylene blue is a dye and a redox indicator, not an acid-base one, so it does not signal neutralisation.
why_wrong.1: Bromine is a reactive element used as a test for unsaturation in organic chemistry. It is a reagent, not an indicator.
why_wrong.3: Sodium is a metal. It reacts violently with water and would take part in the reaction rather than report on it.

why_correct: Chlorine has atomic number 17, so its electrons fill as 2, 8, 7. That leaves 7 in the outermost shell, one short of eight, which is why chlorine so readily gains an electron to form the chloride ion.

why_wrong.0: 2 is the number in chlorine's innermost shell, the K shell, not the outermost.
why_wrong.2: 3 is the outer-shell count for aluminium, which has 13 electrons arranged 2, 8, 3.
why_wrong.3: 1 is the outer-shell count for hydrogen or for the alkali metals such as sodium.

why_correct: Permanent hardness is caused by the sulphates and chlorides of calcium and magnesium, and calcium sulphate is the standard example. It cannot be removed by boiling, which is what makes it permanent.

why_wrong.0: Copper sulphate is not a normal constituent of natural water and is not a cause of hardness. Hardness comes from calcium and magnesium salts.
why_wrong.1: Sodium hydrogen sulphate contains sodium, and sodium salts do not cause hardness. Sodium compounds are in fact used to soften water.
why_wrong.3: Sulphuric acid would make water acidic, not hard. Note that temporary hardness is caused by the bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium and is removed by boiling; permanent hardness is the sulphates and chlorides.

why_correct: Petroleum is a mixture of liquids with different boiling points, so it is separated by fractional distillation in a tall column. Each fraction, including kerosene, diesel and wax, condenses at its own level.

why_wrong.0: Evaporation separates a dissolved solid from a liquid, such as salt from water. It cannot separate one liquid from another.
why_wrong.1: Decomposition breaks a compound into different substances. These fractions are already present in petroleum and only need separating, not breaking down.
why_wrong.3: Simple distillation separates a liquid from a non-volatile solid, or two liquids with widely separated boiling points. Petroleum's many fractions have close boiling points, so the fractionating column is needed.

why_correct: Newton's second law gives force as mass times acceleration, F equals ma. Its unit, the newton, is defined from this as the force that gives a mass of one kilogram an acceleration of one metre per second squared.

why_wrong.1: F equals Wmg is not a formula at all. W usually stands for weight, and weight is already mg, so this multiplies the same quantity twice over.
why_wrong.2: F equals mst mixes mass with distance and time in a way that gives the wrong dimensions entirely.
why_wrong.3: mgh is the formula for gravitational potential energy, measured in joules, not for force.

why_correct: A dibasic acid gives two hydrogen ions per molecule on ionising. Sulphuric acid, H2SO4, releases two, which makes it dibasic. Basicity counts the replaceable hydrogens, not the total hydrogen atoms.

why_wrong.0: Sodium sulphate is a salt, not an acid. It is what remains after sulphuric acid has been neutralised.
why_wrong.1: Zinc sulphate is also a salt, formed when zinc reacts with sulphuric acid.
why_wrong.2: Ammonium hydroxide is a base, not an acid. It gives hydroxide ions rather than hydrogen ions, so it is the opposite of what the question asks for.

why_correct: Euclid's ladder runs downward: the boundaries of a solid are surfaces, the boundaries of a surface are curves or lines, and the boundaries of a line are points. Each step down loses one dimension, and a solid is three-dimensional, so its boundary is the two-dimensional surface.

why_wrong.1: Curves bound surfaces, not solids. They are one step further down the ladder.
why_wrong.2: Lines also bound surfaces. Think of the edges of a page: they bound the flat sheet, not a block.
why_wrong.3: Points bound lines, and they are at the very bottom of the ladder, two steps below what a solid needs.

why_graced: This question has been graced: every candidate receives the mark, whatever they wrote and even if they left it blank. The textbook statement is that if C lies between A and B such that AC equals BC, then AC is half of AB. The condition AC equals BC has dropped out of the printed stem, and without it C is merely somewhere between A and B, not necessarily at the midpoint. Between does not mean midway, so no fixed relation between AC and AB follows and none of the four options can be derived from what was printed.

why_wrong.0: AC equals AB would mean C has reached B itself, which contradicts C lying between A and B.
why_wrong.1: AC equals half of AB is the intended answer, and it is true when C is the midpoint. That is exactly the condition the printed stem forgot to state, so as the question stands you cannot conclude it.
why_wrong.2: AB equals half of AC is impossible whatever C does. AC is a part of AB, so AC can never exceed AB, let alone be twice as long.
why_wrong.3: AC equals one third of AB is true for one particular position of C and false for every other, exactly like the half, so it has no better claim than option B.

why_correct: The square root of 2 cannot be written as a fraction of two integers, so it is irrational. The other three are perfect squares, and the square root of a perfect square is always a whole number.

why_wrong.1: The square root of 4 is 2, a whole number, and every whole number is rational because it can be written as 2 over 1.
why_wrong.2: The square root of 9 is 3, again a whole number and therefore rational.
why_wrong.3: The square root of 16 is 4, rational for the same reason. The test is not whether there is a root sign but whether the number under it is a perfect square.

why_correct: Work outwards from the inside. The cube root of x squared is x to the power two thirds. Taking the fourth root of that divides the power by four again, and two thirds divided by four is one sixth. So the value is x to the power one sixth, the sixth root of x. A quicker route is to multiply the three indices at once: two, divided by three, divided by four.

why_wrong.0: x on its own is x to the power one, which is what is left if the two root signs are ignored and only the square is cancelled. Every root sign divides the power, so the answer has to come out far smaller than x itself.
why_wrong.1: x to the power one half is the square root of x. There is no square root in this question at all: the signs are a cube root inside a fourth root, and the square is on the x, not on the root.
why_wrong.2: x to the power one third is the cube root of x. This uses the inner cube root but loses one of the other two steps along the way, so the working has been stopped early. Both roots and the square must all be applied.

why_correct: Use the identity a cubed minus b cubed equals the cube of the difference plus three times the difference, when ab is 1. So x cubed minus 1 over x cubed equals the cube of root 3 plus 3 times root 3, which is 3 root 3 plus 3 root 3, giving 6 root 3.

why_wrong.1: 3 root 3 is the cube of root 3 on its own. It is the first half of the identity, and it forgets the 3 times the difference term that must be added.
why_wrong.2: 3 comes from squaring root 3. That would be the answer to a question about x squared, not x cubed, and this identity has a plus 2 or minus 2 in it rather than a cube.
why_wrong.3: Root 3 is simply the value given in the question. The cube must be worked out, not copied across.

why_correct: The distance of a point from the x axis is the size of its y coordinate, because you measure straight up or down to reach the axis. For the point 2 comma 3 that distance is 3 units.

why_wrong.0: 2 is the x coordinate, which gives the distance from the y axis, not the x axis. This is the single most common slip in the topic: distance from the x axis uses y, and distance from the y axis uses x.
why_wrong.1: 5 units is the sum of the two coordinates, and it has no geometric meaning here. The distance from the origin would be the square root of 13.
why_wrong.3: There is a definite answer, so none of these cannot be right.

why_correct: Complementary angles add to 90 degrees. If the angle is x, its complement is 90 minus x, and the angle is 14 more, so x equals 90 minus x plus 14. That gives 2x equals 104 and x equals 52 degrees, whose complement is 38.

why_wrong.0: 38 degrees is the complement, the smaller of the pair. The two are right, but the question asks for the angle that is larger by 14, which is 52.
why_wrong.2: 50 degrees is close, but its complement is 40 and the difference is 10, not 14. Always check the pair adds to 90 and differs by the amount given.
why_wrong.3: There is a definite answer, so none of these is wrong here.

why_correct: Only statement two is true. All three angles equal to 60 gives a sum of 180, which is exactly what a triangle's angles must add to, and that is the equilateral triangle.

why_wrong.1: Two obtuse angles would each be more than 90, so the two alone would exceed 180 before the third angle is counted. A triangle can have at most one obtuse angle.
why_wrong.2: If all three angles were more than 60, the sum would be more than 180, which is impossible. This is the same reasoning as statement two, only with the inequality made strict.
why_wrong.3: Statements one and three are both impossible, so all three cannot be true. Test each against the angle sum of 180 rather than judging them by feel.

why_correct: The longest straight object that fits in a box lies along its space diagonal, which is the square root of the sum of the squares of the three edges. That is the square root of 64 plus 36 plus 4, or the square root of 104, which simplifies to 2 root 26.

why_wrong.0: 2 root 13 is the square root of 52, which is half of 104. This comes from dividing somewhere it should not be divided.
why_wrong.1: 2 root 14 is the square root of 56, which uses only two of the three edges: 64 minus 8 or a similar slip. All three dimensions must be squared and added.
why_wrong.3: 10 root 2 is the square root of 200, which is what you get by adding the edges first and then squaring. Squaring must come before adding.

why_correct: A face of a cube is a square, so a perimeter of 40 means each side is 40 divided by 4, that is 10 cm. The volume is the side cubed, 10 times 10 times 10, which is 1000 cubic centimetres.

why_wrong.0: 1600 is the square of 40, which treats the perimeter as though it were the side. Divide by 4 first.
why_wrong.2: 800 is the total surface area, 6 times 10 squared minus something, or another area-shaped slip. Volume needs the side cubed.
why_wrong.3: 160 is 40 times 4, which multiplies where the perimeter should have been divided.

why_correct: For a sphere of radius 1 the volume is four thirds pi and the surface area is 4 pi. Dividing gives one third, so the ratio is 1 to 3. In general the ratio is r to 3, which is worth remembering.

why_wrong.0: 4 to 3 is the fraction in the volume formula on its own, with the surface area not divided in at all.
why_wrong.1: 3 to 4 is that same fraction turned upside down, and it still ignores the surface area.
why_wrong.3: 3 to 1 is the correct ratio the wrong way round, that is surface area to volume. Keep the order the question asks for: volume first, then surface area.

why_correct: Same height means the sphere's diameter equals the cube's edge, so if the edge is a the radius is a over 2. The sphere's volume is pi a cubed over 6 and the cube's is a cubed, so the ratio is pi to 6. Taking pi as 22 over 7 gives 22 to 42, which is 11 to 21.

why_wrong.0: 3 to 4 comes from the four thirds in the volume formula and leaves out both the radius being half the edge and the value of pi.
why_wrong.1: 21 to 11 is the correct ratio reversed, which is the cube to the sphere. The sphere sits inside the cube, so its share must be the smaller one.
why_wrong.2: 4 to 3 is again just the fraction from the formula, and it wrongly makes the sphere larger than the cube that contains it.

why_correct: Euclid's second axiom says that if equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal. Here z is added to both sides of x plus y equals 10, so the two sides stay equal.

why_wrong.0: The first axiom says things which are equal to the same thing are equal to one another. That compares three quantities; it does not add anything.
why_wrong.2: The third axiom is about subtraction: if equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal. Here z is added, not taken away.
why_wrong.3: The fourth axiom says things which coincide with one another are equal. That is a geometric statement about figures lying on each other, not an arithmetic one.

why_correct: In a triangle, sides opposite equal angles are equal. Angle R equals angle P, and the side opposite angle R is PQ while the side opposite angle P is QR. So PQ equals QR, which is 4 cm.

why_wrong.0: 2 cm matches neither given side. Nothing in the question halves a length.
why_wrong.1: 2.5 cm is half of PR. Halving belongs to medians and midpoints, and the question is about equal angles, not midpoints.
why_wrong.3: 5 cm is PR, the side opposite angle Q, and angle Q is the one not mentioned. The trick is to find the side opposite each equal angle rather than reaching for the length that is written down.

why_correct: The third side is 42 minus 18 minus 10, that is 14 cm, and the semi-perimeter s is 21. Heron's formula gives the area as the square root of 21 times 3 times 11 times 7, which is the square root of 4851, and since 4851 is 441 times 11, the area is 21 root 11 square centimetres.

why_wrong.0: 20 root 11 would need 4400 under the root. The number outside comes out of 441, which is 21 squared, so it must be 21.
why_wrong.1: 19 root 11 has the right surd but the wrong coefficient. Check by squaring: 4851 divided by 11 is 441, and the square root of 441 is 21.
why_wrong.2: 22 root 11 is the near miss you get by using 22 rather than 21 somewhere, most often by taking the perimeter's half wrongly. The semi-perimeter here is exactly 21.

why_correct: In Ted Hughes's poem the oak trees are alive and speaking. They hold a trial, they grieve for their felled kin, and they demand a promise from the boy, so they stand for nature itself and its living spirit.

why_wrong.0: Human greed is what threatens the trees, not what the trees are. The greed belongs to the people who cut them down.
why_wrong.2: The poem sets itself against industrial growth rather than symbolising it. Growth here is the slow growth of a wood.
why_wrong.3: The oaks do behave strangely, holding a court in the boy's dream, but Hughes means them as real trees given voice, not as creatures out of myth.

why_correct: The oaks make the boy swear that for every tree felled he will plant two. So the promise is active: protect the trees that stand and plant new ones.

why_wrong.0: There is no journey in the poem. The boy walks into a wood and comes out changed, and nothing is said of travelling further.
why_wrong.1: Stopping the cutting is only half of it, and it is the passive half. The oaks ask for two trees planted for every one lost, so mere abstention would not satisfy them.
why_wrong.3: Farming is never mentioned. The promise concerns forest trees, not crops.

why_correct: The poem's argument is that human beings belong to the natural world and owe it a duty, which is why the boy walks out of the wood with a tree's heart in his chest. That is environmental responsibility.

why_wrong.0: There is no war in the poem. The trial the oaks hold is a moral reckoning, not a battle.
why_wrong.2: Nothing in the poem happens at sea. The whole of it takes place in a wood.
why_wrong.3: Family is in the title, My Own True Family, but Hughes uses the word to mean the trees. He widens family to include the natural world, which is the point rather than the subject.

why_correct: The kite carries a message that reaches long-lost relatives, and the letter that comes back reunites the family. The runaway kite of the title is what restores people to one another.

why_wrong.0: There is no competition in the story and no prize. The kite is flown for pleasure, and its importance is accidental.
why_wrong.2: No school event is involved. The story is a family one throughout.
why_wrong.3: Nothing is dug up or searched for. What is found is a person, not treasure.

why_correct: Claude and Philippa live on an island, and their isolation is what makes the story work. It is because they are cut off that a kite carried away on the wind can reach someone they could not otherwise have found.

why_wrong.0: There is a sea in the story and boats in it, but the children live on land.
why_wrong.2: No mountain appears. The setting is coastal, with the wind off the water that carries the kite.
why_wrong.3: A farm would be inland and ordinary. The island setting is what makes the kite's journey remarkable.

why_correct: The story is about a family separated and then joined again by chance. Every turn of it, the kite, the message and the letter, works towards bringing relatives together, so family bonding is its subject.

why_wrong.0: Nobody competes with anybody. There is no contest in the story at all.
why_wrong.2: Kite flying here is a children's pastime, not a sport, and the story stops caring about the kite the moment the message is found.
why_wrong.3: No one grows rich or successful. The reward at the end is a relative, not a fortune.

why_correct: Masefield's poem opens with I must go down to the seas again, and the whole poem is that longing repeated. The poet feels an irresistible pull towards a voyage.

why_wrong.0: The city is what the poet wants to leave. It is never named, but everything he asks for is the opposite of it.
why_wrong.2: No mountains appear. His images are all of ship, sail, wind and wave.
why_wrong.3: Careful here. The desire is for the voyage itself and for the freedom of it. The poem ends with a quiet sleep and a long trick over, which is a rest at the end of the journey rather than a wish to sail for ever.

why_correct: Before instruments, sailors navigated by the stars. A star to steer her by is therefore an image of guidance and sure direction, one of the plain necessities the poet lists alongside a tall ship and a wheel.

why_wrong.0: Confusion is the opposite of what a guiding star means. It is the thing that removes confusion.
why_wrong.2: Danger is present in the sea itself, but a star is a comfort against it, not a threat.
why_wrong.3: The star shines in the darkness rather than standing for it. It is precisely what makes the dark navigable.

why_correct: The poem's rhythm rolls like the sea, and its images are of wind, spray, flung spume and the vagrant gypsy life. Together they make a mood that is excited and adventurous, a call to go rather than a lament.

why_wrong.1: The poem is anything but dull. Its energy is in the beat of the lines, which is one good way to judge a poem's mood.
why_wrong.2: There is no fear in it. The poet knows the sea is wild and wants it anyway.
why_wrong.3: There is no anger and nothing to be angry at. The only tension is the pull between the poet and the shore.

why_correct: Built is simple past, so the passive must be was plus the past participle: The house was built by them. The object becomes the subject and the doer follows by.

why_wrong.1: Is built is the present passive, but the active sentence is in the past. Changing the voice must never change the tense.
why_wrong.2: Has built is active, not passive. The passive perfect would be has been built, and the original is simple past in any case.
why_wrong.3: There is no auxiliary verb at all here, so this is a phrase rather than a sentence. Every passive needs a form of be.

why_correct: In indirect speech after a past reporting verb, will becomes would and tomorrow becomes the next day. Both the tense and the time word shift back, giving He said that he would go the next day.

why_wrong.0: The tense has not shifted. After he said, will must become would.
why_wrong.2: Goes is the simple present, which is the wrong tense twice over. The original is future, so the reported form must be would go.
why_wrong.3: Went is simple past, but the original speaks of the future. And tomorrow still needs to become the next day.

why_correct: Since is used with a point in time, the moment something began. Monday is a point, so she has been ill since Monday.

why_wrong.1: For is used with a length of time, as in for three days. Monday names a moment, not a stretch, and this is the pair to keep straight: since for a point, for for a period.
why_wrong.2: From also marks a starting point, but it needs a matching to or till, and it does not sit with the present perfect the way since does.
why_wrong.3: By means not later than a deadline, which is a different idea altogether and does not fit an illness that is still going on.

why_correct: The definite article the is used before something unique, and there is only one Earth. The same rule covers the Sun, the Moon and the sky.

why_wrong.0: A is indefinite and means any one of many. It cannot go before something there is only one of.
why_wrong.1: An is the same indefinite article, used before a vowel sound, and it fails for the same reason.
why_wrong.3: Leaving out the article is right for some proper nouns, such as India, but Earth in this sense takes the.

why_correct: An adjective describes a noun. Beautiful tells us what the garden is like, so it is the adjective in the sentence.

why_wrong.0: Garden is a noun, and it is the thing being described rather than the describing word.
why_wrong.1: Attracted is the verb, the action of the sentence.
why_wrong.3: Visitors is a noun too, the object of the verb. A quick test: an adjective can usually take very in front of it, and only beautiful passes.

why_correct: This is the second conditional, used for something imagined or contrary to fact, and it takes were for every subject. If I were you is the fixed form, and the main clause would accept confirms it.

why_wrong.0: Am is the ordinary present, which belongs to a real condition such as If I am late, I will call. Here the main clause has would, so the condition is imaginary.
why_wrong.1: Was is the everyday past of I, and it is heard in speech, but the unreal conditional takes the subjunctive were.
why_wrong.3: Be on its own has no tense and cannot follow I in a conditional clause.

why_correct: Mars is called the Red Planet because its surface is covered in iron oxide dust, which is rust, and that gives it a reddish colour visible even from Earth.

why_wrong.0: Venus is the hottest planet and appears white or yellowish through its thick clouds of sulphuric acid.
why_wrong.2: Jupiter is the largest planet and shows bands of cream and brown with the Great Red Spot, which is a storm rather than the planet's colour.
why_wrong.3: Saturn is the ringed planet, pale gold in appearance.

why_correct: Dr B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly and is called the Father of the Indian Constitution. He was also independent India's first Law Minister.

why_wrong.0: Gandhi is the Father of the Nation. He was not a member of the Constituent Assembly, and the two titles are commonly swapped.
why_wrong.1: Nehru was the first Prime Minister and moved the Objectives Resolution, which became the basis of the Preamble, but he did not chair the drafting.
why_wrong.3: Sardar Patel chaired important committees on fundamental rights and minorities, and he is remembered for integrating the princely states.

why_correct: Canberra is the capital of Australia. It was purpose-built as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne, which both wanted the honour, and became the seat of government in 1927.

why_wrong.0: Sydney is Australia's largest city and its best known, which is exactly why it is the usual wrong answer. Largest is not the same as capital.
why_wrong.1: Melbourne was in fact the seat of government from 1901 until Canberra was ready, but it is not the capital now.
why_wrong.3: Perth is the capital of Western Australia, a state capital rather than the national one.

why_correct: Nitrogen makes up about 78 per cent of the atmosphere by volume. It is chemically unreactive, so it stays in the air rather than being consumed.

why_wrong.0: Oxygen is second at about 21 per cent. We notice it most because we breathe it, but it is not the most abundant.
why_wrong.1: Carbon dioxide is about 0.04 per cent. Small in quantity, large in effect, since it drives the greenhouse effect.
why_wrong.3: Hydrogen is the commonest element in the universe but is almost absent from our air, because it is too light for Earth's gravity to hold.

why_correct: The United Nations headquarters is in New York City, on the bank of the East River. The site is international territory, and the General Assembly and Security Council meet there.

why_wrong.0: Geneva houses the UN Office at Geneva and agencies such as the WHO, which makes it a major UN city but not the headquarters.
why_wrong.1: Paris is the headquarters of UNESCO, a specialised agency of the UN.
why_wrong.2: London hosts the International Maritime Organization. Useful check: the UN was founded at San Francisco in 1945, in the United States.

why_correct: Rabindranath Tagore wrote Jana Gana Mana in Bengali in 1911, and the Constituent Assembly adopted it as the national anthem on 24 January 1950.

why_wrong.0: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote Vande Mataram, the national song. India has both a national anthem and a national song, and this is the pair most often confused.
why_wrong.2: Sarojini Naidu was a poet and freedom fighter called the Nightingale of India, and the first woman to be governor of an Indian state.
why_wrong.3: Subhas Chandra Bose led the Indian National Army. It was his troops who adopted a version of Jana Gana Mana as an anthem, but Tagore wrote it.

why_correct: The Ganga is the longest river in India, running about 2,525 kilometres from Gangotri to the Bay of Bengal. Its basin is also the largest in the country.

why_wrong.0: The Yamuna is the Ganga's longest tributary, about 1,376 kilometres, so it is long but joins another river rather than being the longest itself.
why_wrong.1: The Godavari is the longest river of peninsular India, which is why it is called Dakshina Ganga, but it is shorter than the Ganga.
why_wrong.2: The Brahmaputra is longer overall, at about 2,900 kilometres, but most of that lies in Tibet and Bangladesh. Within India the Ganga is longer, and that is what the question asks.

why_correct: World Environment Day falls on 5 June each year. It was established by the United Nations in 1972, the year of the Stockholm Conference on the human environment.

why_wrong.0: 22 April is Earth Day, a separate observance and the one most often confused with this.
why_wrong.2: 8 March is International Women's Day.
why_wrong.3: 16 September is the International Day for the Preservation of the Ozone Layer, which marks the Montreal Protocol. Environmental, but a different day.

why_correct: Punjab means the land of five waters, from panj meaning five and ab meaning water. The five rivers are the Sutlej, Beas, Ravi, Chenab and Jhelum, all tributaries of the Indus.

why_wrong.0: Haryana was carved out of Punjab in 1966 and shares much of its culture, but the name and the five rivers belong to Punjab.
why_wrong.2: Rajasthan is India's driest large state and has only one major perennial river, the Chambal.
