why_wrong.3: Himachal Pradesh is where several of those rivers rise, which makes it a fair guess, but the name belongs to the plains they water.

why_correct: The ampere is the SI unit of electric current, and it is one of the seven base units. One ampere is a flow of one coulomb of charge per second.

why_wrong.0: The volt is the unit of potential difference, which drives the current rather than measuring it.
why_wrong.1: The ohm is the unit of resistance, which opposes the current. Ohm's law ties all three together: volts equal amperes times ohms.
why_wrong.3: The watt is the unit of power, and in electricity it is volts times amperes.

why_correct: Eighteen Fifty Seven was written by Surendra Nath Sen and published in 1957, the centenary year, at the request of the Government of India. It is the standard scholarly account of the revolt of 1857.

why_wrong.0: V. D. Savarkar wrote The Indian War of Independence 1857, which treats the revolt as a national war. The same event, a different book and a very different argument.
why_wrong.1: Susobhan Sarkar was a Marxist historian of Bengal, best known for Notes on the Bengal Renaissance.
why_wrong.2: R. C. Majumdar wrote The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857, which argues against calling it a war of independence. He and Sen are often confused because both wrote on 1857 in the centenary period.

why_correct: The Indian Association was founded in 1876, with Anand Mohan Basu as its first Secretary. It was the most important political body in Bengal before the Indian National Congress.

why_wrong.0: Krishna Mohan Banerjee was a scholar and reformer of the earlier Young Bengal generation, not an office bearer of the Association.
why_wrong.2: Surendranath Banerjee was the leading founder and the public voice of the Indian Association, which is why his name comes first to mind. Founder and first Secretary are different roles, and the Secretary was Anand Mohan Basu.
why_wrong.3: Sibnath Sastry was a Brahmo reformer and the historian of the Brahmo Samaj.

why_correct: The Jatiyo Mela, begun in 1867 by Nabagopal Mitra and the Tagores, was renamed the Hindu Mela in 1870. It was an early attempt to build national feeling through indigenous crafts, sport and song.

why_wrong.0: 1867 is the year the Mela was founded, under its original name. Founding and renaming are different events, and this is the trap in the question.
why_wrong.1: 1868 falls between the two events and marks neither.
why_wrong.2: 1869 is likewise a year in which nothing decisive happened to the Mela's name.

why_correct: Abanindranath Tagore painted Bharat Mata in 1905, during the Swadeshi movement against the partition of Bengal. He showed her as a calm ascetic figure with four hands, and the painting became an emblem of the nation.

why_wrong.0: Gaganendranath Tagore was Abanindranath's elder brother, a painter known for cubist experiments and political cartoons.
why_wrong.1: Rabindranath Tagore was their uncle. He wrote and also painted in later life, but Bharat Mata is not his.
why_wrong.2: Nandalal Basu was Abanindranath's pupil and later illustrated the Constitution of India. The teacher painted Bharat Mata, not the student.

why_correct: Digdarshan, the first monthly periodical in Bengali, appeared from Serampore in 1818 with John Clark Marshman as its editor.

why_wrong.0: James Augustus Hickey brought out the Bengal Gazette in 1780, the first newspaper in India, but it was in English.
why_wrong.1: William Carey was the Serampore missionary and printer, a central figure in Bengali printing, but not the editor of this journal.
why_wrong.3: Joshua Marshman was John Clark Marshman's father and another of the Serampore trio. Father and son are easily confused, and the editor here was the son.

why_correct: Sambad Prabhakar was started by Iswar Chandra Gupta in 1831 as a weekly and became a daily in 1839, making it the first Bengali daily newspaper. It became the training ground of a whole generation of Bengali writers, Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay and Dinabandhu Mitra among them.

why_wrong.0: Bengal Gazette, brought out by James Augustus Hicky in 1780, was the first printed newspaper in India, but it was in English, not Bengali, and it was a weekly.
why_wrong.1: Digdarshan, published from Serampore in 1818, was the first Bengali monthly magazine, and question 30 on this very paper says so. A monthly magazine cannot also be the first daily newspaper.
why_wrong.2: Samachar Darpan, also from Serampore in 1818, was the first Bengali weekly newspaper, and it is easy to confuse first weekly with first daily. This was the printed key and it has been corrected.

why_correct: Panchanan Karmakar is called the Gutenberg of Bengal. He cut the first Bengali movable metal types at Serampore, which is what made printing in Bengali possible at all.

why_wrong.0: Charles Wilkins was the Englishman who supervised the first Bengali types, and Karmakar was the craftsman who cut them. Both are named in the story, and the title belongs to the man who did the cutting.
why_wrong.1: James Augustus Hickey printed the first newspaper in India, in English, and had nothing to do with Bengali type.
why_wrong.3: John Andrews was an associate of Hickey's press, not a typecutter.

why_correct: The Indian Journal of Physics was published from 1926 by the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science, founded by Mahendralal Sarkar in 1876. C. V. Raman announced the Raman effect in that journal.

why_wrong.0: The Bengal Technical Institute grew out of the national education movement and became Jadavpur University. It taught engineering rather than publishing a physics journal.
why_wrong.1: Calcutta Science College, part of Calcutta University, was where Raman held his chair, so it is closely tied to the same story. The journal was the Association's.
why_wrong.3: The Bose Institute was founded by Jagadish Chandra Bose in 1917 for plant and physical research, and it published its own transactions.

why_correct: Prasannakumar Tagore first used the term National Education, well before the movement of 1905 gave it wide currency.

why_wrong.1: Sir Ashutosh Mukhopadhyay led Calcutta University and expanded Indian control of higher education, but he did not coin the phrase.
why_wrong.2: Rabindranath Tagore founded Santiniketan and wrote at length on education, so he is the natural guess. Founding a school and coining a term are different things.
why_wrong.3: Jagadish Chandra Bose was a scientist and the founder of the Bose Institute, not the author of this phrase.

why_correct: Rathindranath Tagore, Rabindranath's son, was the first Vice-Chancellor of Visva-Bharati when it became a university.

why_wrong.0: Indira Gandhi studied at Santiniketan and later served as the university's Chancellor as Prime Minister, but she was never its first Vice-Chancellor.
why_wrong.2: Rabindranath Tagore founded Visva-Bharati and was its Acharya, its guiding head. The obvious answer, and the reason the question is asked, but the Vice-Chancellorship went to his son.
why_wrong.3: Indira Devi Chaudhurani was Rabindranath's niece, a writer and musician who preserved his songs.

why_correct: Singaravelu Chettiar organised the first May Day in India, at Madras in 1923, where the red flag was used for the first time in the country. He was among the earliest Indian communists.

why_wrong.1: Chittaranjan Das was the Deshbandhu, a nationalist leader of Bengal and a founder of the Swaraj Party, but not the organiser of May Day.
why_wrong.2: Surendranath Sen is the historian of 1857 who appears elsewhere on this paper, not a labour leader.
why_wrong.3: Gandhi led the national movement and took up workers' causes at Ahmedabad, but May Day is a communist and trade union observance and was not his.

why_correct: Dewan Chamanlal was the first General Secretary of the All India Trade Union Congress when it was founded in 1920.

why_wrong.0: Chittaranjan Das presided over the AITUC in 1923, so he held high office in it, but the first General Secretary was Chamanlal.
why_wrong.2: Lala Lajpat Rai was the first President of the AITUC in 1920. President and General Secretary are different posts, and this is the pair the question is testing.
why_wrong.3: Balgangadhar Tilak was a leader of the extremist wing of the Congress and died in 1920, the year the AITUC was founded.

why_correct: The Madras Labour Union, founded in 1918 by B. P. Wadia, is regarded as the first proper trade union in India, because it had a formal organisation, members and funds.

why_wrong.0: The Workers' and Peasants' Party was a political party of the 1920s, not a trade union.
why_wrong.1: The Centre of Indian Trade Unions was formed in 1970, more than fifty years later.
why_wrong.3: The All India Trade Union Congress was founded in 1920 and is the oldest federation of unions. A federation is a body of unions, so the first single union came first, in 1918.

why_correct: The Eka or unity movement began in 1921 in the districts of Hardoi, Bahraich and Sitapur in Uttar Pradesh, where tenants swore to pay only the recorded rent and not to give forced labour.

why_wrong.1: Madhya Pradesh saw tribal movements of its own but not the Eka movement.
why_wrong.2: Bengal's peasant risings were the Tebhaga movement of 1946 and, earlier, the indigo revolt.
why_wrong.3: Bihar's peasant movement of this period was the Champaran satyagraha of 1917, led by Gandhi against indigo planters.

why_correct: Thirty-three communist and trade union leaders were arrested in the Meerut Conspiracy Case of 1929. The trial dragged on for four years and gave the accused a public platform, which won the movement wide sympathy.

why_wrong.0: 30 is close but short. The figure of 33 is the one recorded for this case.
why_wrong.1: 31 is likewise a near miss.
why_wrong.3: 38 overstates the number. The detail worth carrying away is that the trial began in 1929 and that the government's attempt to break the movement helped publicise it instead.

why_correct: The axis is the imaginary line through the centre of the Earth about which it rotates, and its two ends are the North Pole and the South Pole. It is tilted at 23 and a half degrees from the vertical, which is what gives us the seasons.

why_wrong.0: Both the Equator and the Tropic of Cancer are circles running round the Earth, not points. An axis has to join two points.
why_wrong.2: The Arctic and Antarctic Circles are also lines of latitude, and both lie well away from the poles that the axis actually passes through.
why_wrong.3: The Prime Meridian and the Equator are both great circles on the surface. They cross each other in the Gulf of Guinea, but neither is an end of the axis.

why_correct: The Equator runs east to west round the middle of the Earth, so it separates everything above it from everything below it: the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere.

why_wrong.0: The Eastern and Western Hemispheres are divided by the Prime Meridian and the 180 degree line, which run north to south. Swapping these two is the most common error in this chapter.
why_wrong.2: The Land and Water Hemispheres are a separate idea, centred near France and near New Zealand. They have nothing to do with the Equator.
why_wrong.3: The heat zones are marked out by the Tropics and the Polar Circles, and there are five of them, not two.

why_correct: The Equator is the starting line from which all latitude is measured, so its own latitude is 0 degrees. It is also the longest line of latitude and the only one that is a great circle.

why_wrong.0: 90 degrees is the latitude of the poles, the highest value latitude can reach.
why_wrong.1: 23 and a half degrees is the Tropic of Cancer in the north and the Tropic of Capricorn in the south.
why_wrong.3: 66 and a half degrees marks the Arctic Circle and the Antarctic Circle.

why_correct: The Prime Meridian, 0 degrees longitude, passes through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich in London. It was fixed there by international agreement in 1884 and is the base for Greenwich Mean Time.

why_wrong.0: Paris had its own prime meridian and argued for it at the 1884 conference, but Greenwich was chosen because most shipping already used it.
why_wrong.1: India's own Standard Meridian is 82 and a half degrees east, which passes near Mirzapur, not through New Delhi.
why_wrong.3: Kolkata lies at about 88 degrees east. No meridian of special international standing runs through it.

why_correct: Longitudes are measured east and west of the Prime Meridian, from 0 up to 180 degrees in each direction. They run pole to pole and are also called meridians.

why_wrong.0: North and south of the Equator is how latitude is measured. This is the pair to keep straight: latitude north and south, longitude east and west.
why_wrong.2: All lines of longitude meet at both poles, so the poles cannot be used as a starting point to measure from.
why_wrong.3: Longitudes are counted along the Equator, but they are measured from the Prime Meridian. The question asks about the reference line, not the path.

why_correct: India's Standard Meridian is 82 and a half degrees east, passing near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh. It is exactly 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich, which gives Indian Standard Time.

why_wrong.0: 75 degrees east passes through western India but is not the standard meridian. Note that a standard meridian is usually chosen as a multiple of 7 and a half degrees, so that the time difference comes out in neat half hours.
why_wrong.1: 90 degrees east lies to the east of India's standard meridian, closer to Bangladesh, and is the standard meridian for that country.
why_wrong.3: 70 degrees east passes near the far western edge of India, well away from the centre a standard meridian should represent.

why_correct: Endogenic forces come from inside the Earth. Endo means within, and these are the forces of earthquakes, volcanoes, folding and faulting that build up the major landforms.

why_wrong.0: Exogenic forces are the opposite: they act from outside, through rivers, wind, glaciers and rain, and they wear landforms down rather than build them.
why_wrong.2: Gravity is a force, and it drives landslides and river flow, but it acts from outside the crust and is grouped with the exogenic forces.
why_wrong.3: Atmospheric forces such as wind and rain act on the surface, which again makes them exogenic.

why_correct: The Himalayas are fold mountains, raised when the Indian plate collided with the Eurasian plate and the sediments of the Tethys Sea were crumpled upward. They are young fold mountains and are still rising.

why_wrong.0: Block mountains are formed by faulting, when a block of land is pushed up or its neighbours drop away. The Vosges and the Black Forest are examples.
why_wrong.1: Residual mountains are old mountains worn down by erosion, such as the Aravallis. The Himalayas are the opposite: young, sharp and still growing.
why_wrong.3: Volcanic mountains are built from erupted lava, like Fujiyama or Kilimanjaro. The Himalayas have no volcanic origin.

why_correct: Erosion is the wearing away of the surface by moving agents such as rivers, wind, glaciers and waves, which loosen material and carry it off. The carrying away is what distinguishes it.

why_wrong.0: Deposition is the laying down of material at the end of the journey. It builds land up rather than wearing it away.
why_wrong.1: Weathering breaks rock down where it stands, without moving it. Weathering plus transport is erosion, so the difference is movement.
why_wrong.3: Sedimentation is a form of deposition, the settling of sediment carried by water or wind.

why_correct: A rift valley forms when the land between two parallel faults sinks, leaving a steep-sided trough. The East African Rift Valley and the Narmada valley in India are examples.

why_wrong.0: Folding bends rock layers upward and downward and builds mountains such as the Himalayas. It does not drop a block of land.
why_wrong.2: Volcanism builds cones and plateaus from erupted material rather than opening a valley by subsidence.
why_wrong.3: Weathering breaks down rock in place and works far too slowly and too shallowly to create a feature on this scale.

why_correct: A plateau is an elevated area with a broad flat top and at least one steep side, so it is commonly called a tableland. The Deccan Plateau is the familiar Indian example.

why_wrong.0: Highland is a loose word for any high ground, including mountains. It is not the specific name for a flat-topped upland.
why_wrong.2: Lowlands are low, level areas such as plains, which is the opposite of a plateau's elevation.
why_wrong.3: A valley is a low area between higher ground, cut by a river or a glacier.

why_correct: Sand dunes are built by wind, which lifts loose sand and drops it where its speed falls. They are typical of deserts such as the Thar, where there is dry loose sand and little vegetation to hold it.

why_wrong.0: Rivers deposit deltas, floodplains and levees. Their sediment is laid down in water, not heaped into wind-shaped ridges.
why_wrong.1: Glaciers deposit moraines and drumlins, made of unsorted rock and clay rather than fine sand.
why_wrong.3: Sea waves build beaches, spits and bars along the coast. Coastal dunes exist, but the wind shapes them even there, not the waves.

why_correct: A delta is formed by river deposition. Where a river meets the sea its speed drops sharply, so the silt it carries settles and builds up land at the mouth. The Sundarbans delta of the Ganga and Brahmaputra is the largest in the world.

why_wrong.1: Wind erosion carves features such as mushroom rocks. Erosion removes material, while a delta is made of material added.
why_wrong.2: Glaciers deposit moraines in cold, high regions. Deltas form at river mouths, usually at sea level.
why_wrong.3: Earthquakes can alter a coastline suddenly, but a delta is built slowly, over centuries, by silt.

why_correct: Moraines are the ridges of rock, gravel and clay that a glacier carries and then dumps as it melts. They are named by where they lie: lateral, medial, terminal and ground moraines.

why_wrong.0: Dunes are heaped by wind in dry regions, not by ice.
why_wrong.2: Deltas are built by rivers at their mouths.
why_wrong.3: Meanders are the loops a river makes across a flat plain. They are a river feature and are formed by erosion and deposition together, not by ice.

why_correct: Weathering is the breakdown of rock in situ, meaning in its own place, by temperature change, water, chemicals or the action of plants and animals. Nothing is carried away, and that is what separates it from erosion.

why_wrong.0: Transportation is the carrying of broken material by water, wind or ice. It is the step that follows weathering, and joining the two gives erosion.
why_wrong.2: Deposition is the dropping of sediment at the end of transport, the last stage rather than the first.
why_wrong.3: Glacier movement is one agent of erosion. Weathering is a process, not the movement of any one agent.

why_correct: After fertilisation the ovary ripens into the fruit, which encloses and protects the seeds. The rule to hold on to is that the ovary becomes the fruit and the ovule becomes the seed.

why_wrong.0: The seed develops from the ovule, not the ovary. The two changes happen together, which is why they are so easily swapped.
why_wrong.2: The ovule is what was there before fertilisation. It is the starting point, not the product.
why_wrong.3: The embryo forms from the fertilised egg inside the ovule, and it sits within the seed. It is one level smaller than what the question asks for.

why_correct: The stamen is the male reproductive part of a flower. It has two parts, the anther, which makes pollen, and the filament that holds it up.

why_wrong.0: The pistil, also called the carpel, is the female part, made of stigma, style and ovary. This is the pair the question is really testing.
why_wrong.2: Sepals are the small green leaf-like parts that protect the bud before it opens. They are not reproductive at all.
why_wrong.3: Petals are the coloured parts that attract insects for pollination. They help reproduction happen but take no part in it themselves.

why_correct: The neuron is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system. Each one has a cell body, dendrites that receive signals and an axon that carries them away.

why_wrong.0: The nephron is the unit of the kidney, not the nervous system. The two names sound alike, which is exactly why they are offered together.
why_wrong.2: Alveoli are the tiny air sacs of the lungs where gases are exchanged.
why_wrong.3: The axon is a part of a neuron, the fibre that carries the impulse away from the cell body. A part of the unit is not the unit itself.

why_correct: Forests and oceans are the main natural carbon sinks. Trees absorb carbon dioxide in photosynthesis and lock it into wood, while the oceans dissolve it and their plankton take it up.

why_wrong.0: Factories are a source of carbon dioxide, releasing it into the air. A sink absorbs; a source emits.
why_wrong.1: Deserts have very little plant life and so absorb very little carbon dioxide.
why_wrong.3: The atmosphere is where the carbon dioxide collects, so it is the reservoir being filled rather than the sink drawing it down.

why_correct: Asthma is a disease of the lungs, in which the airways narrow and become inflamed, making breathing difficult. It is often triggered by dust, pollen or pollution.

why_wrong.0: Heart disease can also cause breathlessness, which is why this seems plausible, but asthma is a disorder of the airways themselves.
why_wrong.1: The liver has no part in breathing. Its diseases include hepatitis and cirrhosis.
why_wrong.3: The kidney is the excretory organ. Its failure affects the filtering of blood, not the passage of air.

why_correct: Ex-situ means off site, conserving a species away from its natural home. A botanical garden does exactly that, as do zoos, seed banks and gene banks.

why_wrong.0: A biosphere reserve protects a whole living landscape where the species already are, so it is in-situ.
why_wrong.2: A national park is also in-situ conservation, protecting habitat in place.
why_wrong.3: A sanctuary likewise protects animals within their own habitat. Three of the four options are in-situ, so the odd one out is the answer.

why_correct: Carbon dioxide is the main greenhouse gas driving global warming. Others such as methane trap more heat per molecule, but carbon dioxide is released in such quantity by burning fuels that its total effect is the largest.

why_wrong.0: Nitrogen makes up most of the atmosphere but is not a greenhouse gas. Being abundant and being warming are quite separate things.
why_wrong.1: Oxygen is essential for life and for burning, but it does not trap heat.
why_wrong.3: Argon is an inert gas making up about one per cent of the air and plays no part in the greenhouse effect.

why_correct: Thalassemia is an inherited disorder in which the globin chains of haemoglobin are not made properly, so the red cells cannot carry oxygen well and the patient becomes anaemic.

why_wrong.0: Insulin is the hormone whose lack causes diabetes. A protein, but the wrong disease.
why_wrong.2: Melanin is the pigment of skin and hair. Its absence causes albinism, another genetic condition, which makes it a tempting distractor.
why_wrong.3: Keratin is the protein of hair, nails and the outer skin.

why_correct: DNA contains adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine. Uracil replaces thymine in RNA, so it is the base absent from DNA.

why_wrong.0: Adenine is present in DNA and pairs with thymine.
why_wrong.2: Guanine is present in DNA and pairs with cytosine.
why_wrong.3: Cytosine is present in DNA. The one to remember is the swap: thymine in DNA, uracil in RNA.

why_correct: Meiosis is called reductional division because the chromosome number is halved, from diploid to haploid. That halving is what keeps the chromosome number constant from one generation to the next when gametes fuse.

why_wrong.0: Mitosis is equational division: the daughter cells have the same chromosome number as the parent. It is the opposite of what meiosis does.
why_wrong.2: Binary fission is how bacteria and some protists divide, a much simpler process without spindle or chromosomes in this sense.
why_wrong.3: Amitosis is direct division without any spindle or visible chromosomes, seen in some simple cells.

why_correct: In Mendel's monohybrid cross the F2 generation shows three dominant to one recessive, a phenotypic ratio of 3 to 1. That result is what led Mendel to the law of segregation.

why_wrong.0: 1 to 2 to 1 is the genotypic ratio of the same cross, that is one pure dominant, two hybrids and one pure recessive. Genotype and phenotype ratios are the classic mix-up here, because the two hybrids look identical to the pure dominant.
why_wrong.2: 9 to 3 to 3 to 1 is the F2 phenotypic ratio of a dihybrid cross, which follows two characters at once.
why_wrong.3: 1 to 1 is the ratio of a test cross, where a hybrid is crossed with a pure recessive.

why_correct: Auxin causes phototropism. It gathers on the shaded side of a shoot, makes those cells lengthen more, and the unequal growth bends the shoot towards the light.

why_wrong.0: Gibberellin promotes stem elongation and seed germination, but it acts evenly rather than in response to the direction of light.
why_wrong.2: Cytokinin promotes cell division and delays the ageing of leaves.
why_wrong.3: Abscisic acid is the stress hormone. It closes stomata and enforces dormancy, so it slows growth rather than directing it.

why_correct: The medulla oblongata, at the base of the brain stem, controls the involuntary actions that keep us alive: heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure, swallowing, coughing and vomiting.

why_wrong.0: The cerebrum is the seat of thought, memory and voluntary action, which is the opposite of involuntary.
why_wrong.1: The cerebellum controls balance and the coordination of movement. Important and largely unconscious, but not the control of heartbeat and breathing.
why_wrong.3: The hypothalamus regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst and the pituitary gland. Also involuntary, but not these two functions.

why_correct: Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm, which follows the division of the nucleus and completes the making of two separate cells.

why_wrong.0: Karyokinesis is the division of the nucleus, the step that comes first. Karyo means nucleus and cyto means cell, and that is the way to tell the two apart.
why_wrong.1: Mitosis is the whole process of division in body cells, of which cytokinesis is the last stage.
why_wrong.3: Meiosis is the reductional division that makes gametes, again a whole process rather than this one step.

why_correct: In a cactus the leaves are reduced to spines, which cuts the surface area available for transpiration to almost nothing. The stem takes over photosynthesis and stores water, and the spines also deter animals.

why_wrong.0: Broad flat leaves would have a large surface and lose water fast. They suit wet, shady places, which is the opposite of a desert.
why_wrong.2: Air cavities in the stem are an adaptation of water plants such as the lotus, helping them float and get oxygen.
why_wrong.3: Shallow fibrous roots do occur in cacti to catch brief rain, but they gather water rather than conserve it. The question asks about conserving, so the spines are the answer.

why_correct: The molar mass of carbon dioxide is 12 plus 32, that is 44 grams. So 22 grams is half a mole, and since one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 litres at STP, half a mole occupies 11.2 litres.

why_wrong.0: 22.4 litres is the volume of one full mole. That would need 44 grams of carbon dioxide, not 22, so this answer skips the step of finding the number of moles.
why_wrong.2: 2.24 litres is the volume of one tenth of a mole. The decimal point has slipped.
why_wrong.3: 1.12 litres is one twentieth of a mole, again a factor-of-ten slip from the right answer.

why_correct: Water vapour is a greenhouse gas, and in fact the most abundant one. Like carbon dioxide and methane, its molecules absorb the infrared radiation the Earth gives off and re-radiate it back downwards.

why_wrong.0: Oxygen is not a greenhouse gas. Its molecule is made of two identical atoms and cannot absorb infrared in the way a greenhouse gas must.
why_wrong.1: Hydrogen is likewise a two-atom molecule of identical atoms and does not trap heat.
why_wrong.3: Nitrogen makes up most of the atmosphere but is not a greenhouse gas either, for the same reason. The pattern is worth noting: the greenhouse gases here have three or more atoms in the molecule.

why_correct: Bauxite, mainly hydrated aluminium oxide, is the ore of aluminium. It is purified by the Bayer process and then reduced by electrolysis, because aluminium is too reactive to be extracted by carbon.

why_wrong.0: Haematite is an ore of iron, Fe2O3, and the chief one worked in India.
why_wrong.2: Malachite is an ore of copper, a green basic carbonate.
why_wrong.3: Chalcocite is another copper ore, a sulphide. Two of the four options here are copper ores, so it is worth learning ores in groups by metal.

why_correct: Nessler's reagent is the standard test for ammonia. With ammonia or an ammonium salt it gives a brown precipitate, sometimes called Nessler's brown, and the test is sensitive enough to detect very small amounts.

why_wrong.0: Nitrogen dioxide is identified by its own reddish brown colour and its acidic, choking nature, not by Nessler's reagent.
why_wrong.1: Hydrogen sulphide is detected with lead acetate paper, which turns black, and by its smell of rotten eggs.
why_wrong.2: Hydrogen chloride gives dense white fumes with ammonia and turns moist blue litmus red. Note that HCl and NH3 are the classic pair, one acidic and one alkaline, so keep their tests apart.

why_correct: Iron is extracted by thermal reduction in the blast furnace, where carbon and carbon monoxide reduce the oxide ore to the metal. Moderately reactive metals are the ones extracted this way.

why_wrong.0: Silver is a low-reactivity metal found largely in the native state, so it needs no reduction of this kind.
why_wrong.1: Magnesium is highly reactive and is obtained by electrolysis of its molten chloride. Carbon cannot reduce it.
why_wrong.3: Gold is the least reactive of these and occurs free in nature. The rule to apply is that highly reactive metals need electrolysis, moderately reactive ones are reduced by carbon, and the least reactive are found native.

why_correct: Chloroform is CHCl3. Chlorinating it once more replaces its last hydrogen and gives carbon tetrachloride, so this is the one reaction of the four that does not yield chloroform. It consumes it instead.

why_wrong.0: Methane with chlorine in sunlight substitutes one hydrogen at a time, and chloroform appears as the third product in that chain.
why_wrong.1: Methyl chloride is the first product of that chain, and further chlorination carries it on towards chloroform.
why_wrong.2: Dichloromethane is the second product, and one more chlorination gives chloroform directly. Read the question carefully: it asks which does not yield chloroform.

why_correct: A liquid has no fixed shape of its own, so length and area mean nothing for it. Only its volume can expand, which gives one type of thermal expansion, called cubical or volume expansion.

why_wrong.0: Liquids certainly do expand on heating, which is exactly how a thermometer works.
why_wrong.1: 3 is the answer for solids, which have linear, superficial and cubical expansion because a solid holds a definite shape. That contrast is what the question is testing.
why_wrong.3: 2 would fit something with length and area but no volume, which describes nothing. Note that real and apparent expansion are two ways of measuring the same one expansion, not two types of it.

why_correct: In hypermetropia, or long sight, the image forms behind the retina. A convex lens converges the light before it enters the eye and brings the image forward onto the retina.

why_wrong.0: A plano lens has one flat surface, and the term alone does not say whether it converges or diverges. It is not a correction in itself.
why_wrong.2: A concave lens diverges light and corrects myopia, or short sight. This is the pair to keep straight: concave for short sight, convex for long sight.
why_wrong.3: Only one type corrects this defect, so all of these cannot be right.

why_correct: Potassium chloride is an ionic compound, and like dissolves like. Benzene is a non-polar solvent with no ability to pull the ions apart, so KCl is insoluble in it.

why_wrong.1: Glycerol is polar and carries hydroxyl groups, so it can dissolve ionic salts to some extent.
why_wrong.2: Water is the most polar of common solvents and dissolves KCl readily.
why_wrong.3: Alcohol is polar too, and although KCl dissolves in it only slightly, it is not insoluble. Benzene is the only genuinely non-polar option here.

why_correct: Urea is made industrially from carbon dioxide and ammonia at high pressure. The two combine to give ammonium carbamate, which then loses water to form urea.

why_wrong.0: Carbon dioxide and water give carbonic acid, not urea. Nitrogen has to come from somewhere, and neither of these supplies it.
why_wrong.2: NH4 written alone is not a substance. The ammonium ion cannot exist by itself; it needs an accompanying negative ion.
why_wrong.3: Ammonium chloride is a salt used in dry cells and as a flux. It is not the feedstock for urea, which uses ammonia gas directly.

why_correct: Going down group one, the outer electron sits in a larger shell and is better shielded, so it is easier to remove and ionisation energy falls. Order down the group is Li, Na, Rb, Cs, so increasing ionisation energy is Cs, Rb, Na, Li.

why_wrong.1: This puts lithium lowest, but lithium is the smallest of these atoms and holds its electron most tightly, so its ionisation energy is the highest.
why_wrong.2: The order here is jumbled and does not follow the group at all. Sort the elements by position first, then reverse for ionisation energy.
why_wrong.3: This has caesium highest, which is the wrong way round. Caesium's outer electron is furthest from the nucleus and the easiest of all to remove.

why_correct: The becquerel is the SI unit of radioactivity, defined as one disintegration per second. It is named after Henri Becquerel, who discovered radioactivity in 1896.

why_wrong.0: The joule is the unit of energy, not of the rate of decay.
why_wrong.1: Radium is an element, not a unit. The old unit named for a person here is the curie, named after Marie and Pierre Curie.
why_wrong.3: The rutherford is a real but obsolete unit of radioactivity, equal to a million disintegrations per second. It was never the SI unit.

why_correct: A ray striking a surface perpendicularly has an angle of incidence of zero, so it passes straight through without bending. The deviation is therefore zero degrees.

why_wrong.1: 90 degrees would mean the ray turned a right angle, which no glass slab does.
why_wrong.2: 180 degrees would mean the ray came straight back the way it came, which is total reversal, not refraction.
why_wrong.3: 30 degrees suggests some bending, but refraction only occurs when the ray meets the surface at an angle. At perpendicular incidence there is none.

why_correct: Ammonia is dried with quicklime, calcium oxide, because it is a basic drying agent and does not react with the alkaline gas. The rule is that a drying agent must not react with what it dries.

why_wrong.0: Calcium chloride reacts with ammonia to form an addition compound, so it would absorb the gas rather than merely dry it. This is the classic exception to remember, since calcium chloride dries almost everything else.
why_wrong.2: Sulphuric acid is acidic and would react with ammonia at once to give ammonium sulphate.
why_wrong.3: Phosphorus pentoxide is also acidic and would likewise react with ammonia instead of drying it.

why_correct: Thermal conductivity is the rate of heat flow per unit area per unit temperature gradient, so its SI unit is watt per metre per kelvin. It combines power, length and temperature.

why_wrong.0: Watt per metre leaves out the temperature altogether, and thermal conductivity is defined in terms of a temperature difference.
why_wrong.1: The calorie is not an SI unit of energy, and this expression is also missing the temperature term.
why_wrong.2: Multiplying by metre and kelvin instead of dividing turns the unit upside down. Build the unit from the definition and the divisions come out as negative powers.

why_correct: Every even integer can be written as 2n, so every odd integer is one more than an even one, that is 2n plus 1. Whatever integer n you choose, 2n plus 1 is always odd.

why_wrong.0: n alone can be anything, odd or even, so it does not guarantee an odd number.
why_wrong.1: n plus 1 has the same problem. If n is odd then n plus 1 is even, so this can be either.
why_wrong.3: 2n is the general form of an even integer, which is the opposite of what is wanted. Test any form by putting in n equal to 1 and 2 and seeing whether the result is always odd.

why_correct: A quadratic with given sum s and product p of roots is x squared minus sx plus p. That gives x squared minus root 2 x plus one third, and multiplying throughout by 3 clears the fraction to give 3x squared minus 3 root 2 x plus 1.

why_wrong.1: The sign of the middle term is wrong. The formula subtracts the sum of the roots, so a positive sum of root 2 gives a negative middle term.
why_wrong.2: Both the middle sign and the constant sign are wrong here. A positive product of one third must give a positive constant after multiplying by 3.
why_wrong.3: There is a correct option, so none of the above is not needed. Check any answer by dividing through by 3 and reading off the sum and product.

why_correct: Two lines are parallel when the ratios of the coefficients of x and y are equal, so 3 over 2 equals 2k over 5. Cross-multiplying gives 4k equals 15, so k is 15 over 4.

why_wrong.0: 4 over 15 is the answer turned upside down, which comes from cross-multiplying the wrong way. Substitute back to check: with k equal to 15 over 4, the coefficient of y is 15 over 2, and 3 over 2 does equal 15 over 2 divided by 5.
why_wrong.2: 4 over 5 does not satisfy the condition. It looks like the coefficients have been paired up incorrectly.
why_wrong.3: 5 over 4 is close in appearance but wrong. Note that for parallel lines only the x and y ratios must match, while the constant term ratio must differ.

why_correct: The discriminant is b squared minus 4ac, which here is 1 minus 32, that is minus 31. A negative discriminant means the roots are not real, so the equation has no real roots.

why_wrong.0: Roots of opposite signs would need a negative product, that is a negative value of c over a. Here both are positive, and in any case the roots are not real at all.
why_wrong.1: Both positive would need a positive sum of roots, which is minus b over a, but that is minus one half here.
why_wrong.2: Both negative is the closest guess, since the sum is negative and the product positive, but the discriminant settles it first. Always check the discriminant before asking about signs.

why_correct: The nth term is a plus n minus 1 times d. With a equal to 28, d equal to minus 4 and n equal to 7, that is 28 plus 6 times minus 4, which is 28 minus 24, giving 4.

why_wrong.1: 5 would come from using 28 minus 23, which does not match any correct step here.
why_wrong.2: 3 comes from multiplying by 7 rather than by n minus 1. The formula uses one less than the term number, which is the commonest slip in this topic.
why_wrong.3: 7 is simply the value of n copied across rather than the term calculated.

why_correct: In an arithmetic progression each term is the previous one plus the common difference. Starting at 10 and adding 10 each time gives 10, 20, 30, 40.

why_wrong.0: The differences here are 20, 20 and 10, which are not constant, so this is not an arithmetic progression at all.
why_wrong.2: These have a common difference of 5, not 10. The first term is right and the difference is wrong.
why_wrong.3: The differences here are 8, 2 and 10, which are all different. A quick test for any option is to subtract each term from the next and check that you get the same number every time.

why_correct: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles, so they cut it into four right triangles with legs of 8 and 6. The side is the hypotenuse, the square root of 64 plus 36, which is 10 cm.

why_wrong.0: 20 cm is the sum of the halves doubled, or a similar slip. The side must be shorter than the longer diagonal of 16, so 20 is impossible on sight.
why_wrong.1: 8 cm is half the longer diagonal, which is one leg of the right triangle rather than its hypotenuse.
why_wrong.3: 9 cm falls between the two legs, but the hypotenuse is always longer than either leg, so it must exceed 8.

why_correct: The midpoint is the average of the coordinates: x is 2 plus minus 2 over 2, and y is 4 plus minus 4 over 2. Both come to zero, so the midpoint is the origin.

why_wrong.0: This mixes the x of one point with the y of the other rather than averaging.
why_wrong.1: Same error the other way round. The midpoint formula adds the two x values and halves them, then does the same for y.
why_wrong.3: This is simply point B copied out. Notice that A and B are opposite each other through the origin, so the midpoint had to be the origin.

why_correct: By the section formula, the x coordinate of the dividing point is 6m minus 3n over m plus n, and this equals minus 1. That gives 6m minus 3n equal to minus m minus n, so 7m equals 2n and the ratio is 2 to 7. The y coordinate confirms it, since minus 16 plus 70 over 9 is 6.

why_wrong.0: 1 to 3 does not satisfy the section formula. Substituting it gives an x coordinate of 0.75, not minus 1.
why_wrong.1: 3 to 4 gives an x coordinate of about 1.7, which is well away from minus 1.
why_wrong.3: 2 to 5 is the nearest miss and gives an x coordinate of about 0.43. Always substitute your ratio back into both coordinates as a check.

why_correct: From the identity sin squared plus cos squared equals 1, sin X is the square root of 1 minus a squared over b squared. Putting that over a common denominator gives the square root of b squared minus a squared, all over b.

why_wrong.0: The square root has been dropped. Squaring gives b squared minus a squared over b squared, so the root must be taken before dividing by b.
why_wrong.1: b minus a over b comes from subtracting the sides rather than their squares. The identity works on squares, and the square root of a difference is not the difference of the square roots.
why_wrong.3: This makes the same mistake, taking the root of b minus a rather than of b squared minus a squared. A quick check with a 3, 4, 5 triangle settles it.

why_correct: Since tan of an angle times tan of its complement equals 1, the terms pair off: 1 with 89, 2 with 88, and so on, each pair giving 1. That leaves tan 45 in the middle, which is also 1, so the whole product is 1.

why_wrong.0: The product would be zero only if one factor were zero, and tan is zero only at 0 degrees, which is not in this list.
why_wrong.2: 2 would need the pairs to leave something over, but every term pairs off exactly and the leftover tan 45 is itself 1.
why_wrong.3: One half would need some factor less than 1 to remain unpaired. Look for the complementary pairing whenever a product runs from 1 degree up to 89.

why_correct: The height, the distance along the ground and the angle of elevation form a right triangle, so tan 60 equals height over 15. Since tan 60 is root 3, the height is 15 root 3 metres.

why_wrong.1: 10 root 3 would come from a distance of 10 metres. The 15 given in the question is the distance along the ground and must be the one multiplied.
why_wrong.2: 12 root 3 corresponds to a distance of 12 metres, which again is not what was given.
why_wrong.3: 20 root 3 would need a distance of 20 metres. Since the angle is 60 degrees, which is more than 45, the tower must be taller than 15 metres, and that alone rules some options in or out.

why_correct: A tangent meets a radius at 90 degrees, so the quadrilateral formed by the centre, the two points of contact and the outside point has two right angles. Its four angles total 360, so the angle between the tangents is 360 minus 90 minus 90 minus 110, which is 70 degrees.

why_wrong.0: 90 degrees would only occur if the angle between the radii were also 90. The two angles are supplementary, so they are equal only in that one case.
why_wrong.1: 50 degrees does not fit, since 110 plus 50 is 160 rather than 180. The shortcut worth remembering is that the two angles add to 180.
why_wrong.3: 40 degrees is the difference between 110 and 70, not the angle itself.

why_correct: The radius meets the tangent at a right angle, so the centre, the point of contact and the external point form a right triangle with the 5 cm distance as hypotenuse. The radius is the square root of 25 minus 16, that is 3 cm.

why_wrong.1: 5 cm is the distance from the centre to the external point, which is the hypotenuse and so must be the longest of the three.
why_wrong.2: 7 cm is larger than the hypotenuse, which is impossible in a right triangle.
why_wrong.3: 10 cm is larger still. Notice this is the 3, 4, 5 triangle, with the tangent 4 and the distance 5, so the radius is 3.

why_correct: The cube's volume is 22 cubed, that is 10648 cubic centimetres, and seven eighths of it is filled, giving 9317. Each marble has radius 0.25, so its volume is four thirds pi times 0.25 cubed, about 0.0654762. Dividing 9317 by that gives 142296 marbles.

why_wrong.1: 142396 is 100 more than the correct figure and would need a slightly larger filled volume than seven eighths.
why_wrong.2: 142496 is 200 too many. The three wrong options here differ only in the hundreds digit, so the arithmetic has to be carried right through rather than estimated.
why_wrong.3: 142596 is 300 too many. Work with the radius of 0.25 cm, not the diameter of 0.5, since that single slip changes the answer eightfold.

why_correct: The astrologer had knifed a man in a village quarrel, thrown him into a well and fled, believing he had killed him. He never went home again, and that flight is what put him under the tamarind tree in a strange town.

why_wrong.0: He had no education and no interest in getting one. Narayan is careful to tell us he knew nothing of the stars and lived entirely by his wits.
why_wrong.2: The army is never mentioned. His trade was chosen because it needed no capital and no training, not because of any service.
why_wrong.3: He is not a priest and makes no claim to be. His turban, his vermilion and his cowrie shells are a costume for a business.

why_correct: Narayan tells us plainly that the astrologer's success came from shrewd guesswork and a lifetime of studying faces and troubles. Within five minutes of listening he knew what a customer wanted to hear.

why_wrong.0: He had run away from the fields precisely to avoid a life of farming. His trade is the opposite of that.
why_wrong.1: He had no magical power at all, and knew it. The story's irony is that a complete fraud delivers, by accident, the one true and life-changing reading of his career.
why_wrong.3: He does not practise medicine. His prescriptions are sacred ash and charms, not remedies.

why_correct: Guru Nayak had come looking for the man who stabbed him and left him for dead, meaning to kill him in return. The whole tension of the story is that he is sitting opposite that very man and does not know it.

why_wrong.0: He speaks of no lost wealth. He offers money rather than seeking it.
why_wrong.1: There is no missing brother in the story. He seeks an enemy, not a relative.
why_wrong.3: No child is involved. The astrologer's own wife and child appear only at the very end, at home.

why_correct: Nivedita records that Swamiji's love of India was total and reverent. He spoke of her past with pride and of her future with hope, and he wished his disciples to feel the same devotion.

why_wrong.0: Indifference is the opposite of everything Nivedita describes. India was the subject he returned to constantly.
why_wrong.2: He felt no fear for India. He was critical of her weaknesses, but criticism from love is not fear.
why_wrong.3: He grieved over poverty and superstition, so there is a grain of truth in disappointment, but Nivedita's account is of pride and devotion, not despondency.

why_correct: For Swamiji India was not a territory but the Divine Mother herself, an object of worship. Nivedita describes him teaching her to see the country in exactly that light.

why_wrong.0: A political unit is what a map shows. Swamiji's vision was religious, and he spoke of India as a living presence rather than a state.
why_wrong.1: Commerce plays no part in his idea of India. He measured her by her spiritual inheritance.
why_wrong.3: Military power is not his theme either. His call was to strength of character and of soul.

why_correct: The Amarnath pilgrimage crosses high and difficult mountain country in Kashmir, and Nivedita's account dwells on the hard climbing, the cold and the exhaustion of the road.

why_wrong.0: There is no desert on the route. The hardship of Amarnath is altitude and ice, not sand.
why_wrong.2: No sea is crossed. The whole journey is inland and upward.
why_wrong.3: Forest is passed on the lower slopes, but what the pilgrims struggle with is the mountain path itself.

why_correct: What struck Nivedita most deeply was Swamiji's own experience inside the cave. He came out shaken and transfigured, and she writes that he felt he had been granted a vision of Shiva.

why_wrong.0: No market figures in the account. The journey is a pilgrimage, not a visit to a town.
why_wrong.1: The cave and its ice lingam are impressive, and she describes them, but her attention is fixed on what happened to Swamiji there. The question asks what impressed her most.
why_wrong.3: Local rulers play no part in the episode.

why_correct: Wordsworth sees London in the early morning before it wakes. The houses seem asleep and the mighty heart is lying still, so the city appears calm and at peace.

why_wrong.0: Noise and crowds are what London would be at any other hour, which is exactly the contrast the poet is drawing. He catches it at the one moment it is silent.
why_wrong.2: The city is not dark. It is bright and bare in the smokeless air, glittering in the first sunlight.
why_wrong.3: Smokeless is Wordsworth's own word. He is struck by how clean the air is at that hour.

why_correct: The city wears the beauty of the morning like a garment. The image makes the beauty something put on, temporary and fitting, which is why the moment must be caught before the day begins.

why_wrong.0: No jewel appears in the poem. Wordsworth's images are of clothing, of open fields and of a sleeping body.
why_wrong.2: The river glideth at his own sweet will, so the Thames is in the poem, but as one of the things seen rather than as the comparison for the city's beauty.
why_wrong.3: Towers, domes, theatres and temples are listed, but they are the city itself and not what its beauty is likened to.

why_correct: The whole sonnet is an act of stillness: silent, bare, calm, and a deep, sweet-tasting quiet. Serenity is the quality of nature that Wordsworth finds unexpectedly in the middle of a great city.

why_wrong.0: There is no violence anywhere in the poem.
why_wrong.1: Restlessness is what a city normally offers and what the poem is a relief from. Judge by the words: calm, still, asleep.
why_wrong.3: The scene is clear rather than mysterious. Wordsworth can see everything, all bright and glittering, which is part of the wonder.

why_correct: Sarojini Naidu's silver and blue bangles are for the maiden, likened to mountain mist and the bud of a new-born leaf. They stand for a girl on the edge of womanhood.

why_wrong.0: Childhood is not one of the stages the poem sets out. It moves from maiden to bride to matron.
why_wrong.2: The bangles are cheap glass, carried to a village fair. Wealth is not what they signify.
why_wrong.3: The poem has no sorrow in it. Even the last stanza, on the older woman, is written with dignity and warmth.

why_correct: The bride's bangles are flame-bright, likened to the fire of her marriage and to her bridal laughter and tears. Red and gold, they carry the colour of the wedding fire itself.

why_wrong.0: Mountain mist belongs to the maiden's silver and blue bangles, not the bride's.
why_wrong.1: Flowers appear as images elsewhere in Naidu's work but not for the bride's bangles here.
why_wrong.3: Morning clouds again suit the pale colours of the maiden's stanza. The bride's stanza is deliberately hot and bright by contrast.

why_correct: The poem's three stanzas of bangles correspond to three stages of a woman's life: the maiden, the bride and the mother who has raised her children. The bangle seller's tray is a way of showing a whole life.

why_wrong.0: Nothing industrial appears. The bangles are handmade and sold at a village fair.
why_wrong.2: There is no war and no heroism in the poem.
why_wrong.3: Naidu was a political figure, but this poem is not political. Its subject is domestic life.

why_correct: Yeats opens with the falcon turning in a widening gyre and unable to hear the falconer. The trained bird has lost touch with its master, which is his image for a civilisation that has lost its centre.

why_wrong.0: Falconry is the image, and the man who flies the bird is the falconer. A hunter is a different figure.
why_wrong.2: There is no shepherd in the poem. The rough beast of the second stanza is the only animal besides the falcon.
why_wrong.3: No king appears. The authority that has failed is not political but something deeper.

why_correct: Things fall apart, the centre cannot hold. Yeats is describing a world whose old order is disintegrating, with anarchy loosed and the best lacking all conviction while the worst are full of passionate intensity.

why_wrong.0: Perfect order is precisely what the poem says has ended.
why_wrong.1: The poem describes the opposite of stability. Written just after the First World War, it is a vision of collapse.
why_wrong.3: There is no peace. The poem ends with a rough beast slouching towards Bethlehem, which is a threat rather than a consolation.

why_correct: Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and the equal protection of the laws. It opens the Right to Equality, which runs from Article 14 to Article 18.

why_wrong.1: Article 19 gives the six freedoms, including speech and expression, and belongs to the Right to Freedom.
why_wrong.2: Article 21 protects life and personal liberty, the article on which much of modern Indian rights law is built. Also under the Right to Freedom.
why_wrong.3: Article 32 is the right to constitutional remedies, which Ambedkar called the heart and soul of the Constitution. It is the way to enforce the other rights, not a right to equality.

why_correct: UNESCO has its headquarters in Paris, where it was founded in 1946. It is the UN agency for education, science and culture, and it maintains the World Heritage list.

why_wrong.0: Geneva houses the WHO, the ILO and the UN Office at Geneva, so it is a major UN city but not UNESCO's home.
why_wrong.1: New York is the headquarters of the United Nations itself. The agency and the parent body are in different cities, which is the point of the question.
why_wrong.3: Vienna hosts the International Atomic Energy Agency and the UN Office at Vienna.

why_correct: Mars is the Red Planet, coloured by the iron oxide dust that covers its surface. That is simply rust, and it is visible even to the naked eye from Earth.

why_wrong.0: Venus is the hottest planet, veiled in thick sulphuric acid cloud, and appears whitish yellow.
why_wrong.2: Jupiter is the largest planet and shows bands of cream and brown. Its Great Red Spot is a storm, not the planet's colour.
why_wrong.3: Saturn is the ringed planet, pale gold in colour.

why_correct: Mother Teresa won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 for her work with the destitute and dying in Kolkata. She was an Indian citizen, which is what makes her the first Indian woman to receive the prize.

why_wrong.0: Indira Gandhi was Prime Minister and won the Bharat Ratna, but never a Nobel Prize.
why_wrong.2: Sarojini Naidu was a poet and freedom fighter called the Nightingale of India, and the first woman governor of an Indian state. Many firsts, but not this one.
why_wrong.3: Kalpana Chawla was the first woman of Indian origin in space. An astronaut, not a Nobel laureate.

why_correct: The Blue Revolution refers to the rapid growth of fish production and aquaculture in India. Blue for water, and it is associated with Dr Hiralal Chaudhuri.

why_wrong.0: Milk is the White Revolution, or Operation Flood, led by Dr Verghese Kurien. The best known of these colour revolutions and the usual wrong answer here.
why_wrong.2: Oilseeds are the Yellow Revolution.
why_wrong.3: Poultry and eggs are the Silver Revolution. It is worth learning the whole set together: green for food grains, white for milk, blue for fish, yellow for oilseeds.

why_correct: Gujarat has the longest coastline of any Indian state, about 1,600 kilometres, because of the deeply indented shores of the Gulf of Kachchh and the Gulf of Khambhat.

why_wrong.0: Tamil Nadu has a long coast of roughly 1,000 kilometres, but a much straighter one.
why_wrong.1: Andhra Pradesh is second at about 970 kilometres after the separation of Telangana.
why_wrong.3: Maharashtra's Konkan coast runs about 720 kilometres. Note that the longest coastline of any Indian territory belongs to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, but that is a union territory, not a state.

why_correct: The currency of Japan is the yen. Its symbol is a Y with two strokes, and it is one of the most traded currencies in the world.

why_wrong.0: The won is the currency of South Korea and, separately, of North Korea.
why_wrong.1: The yuan is the currency of China, more formally the renminbi. Yuan and yen are easily confused because both descend from the same Chinese word for a round coin.
why_wrong.3: The ringgit is the currency of Malaysia.

why_correct: Jawaharlal Nehru wrote The Discovery of India in 1944 while imprisoned at Ahmednagar Fort. He also wrote Glimpses of World History and an autobiography.

why_wrong.0: Gandhi wrote The Story of My Experiments with Truth and Hind Swaraj.
why_wrong.1: Ambedkar wrote Annihilation of Caste and The Problem of the Rupee.
why_wrong.3: Patel was not an author of note. Nehru is the one of these four remembered as much for his books as for his politics.

why_correct: The Antarctic is the largest desert in the world, about 14 million square kilometres. A desert is defined by how little precipitation it receives, not by heat, and Antarctica is the driest place on Earth.

why_wrong.0: The Sahara, about 9 million square kilometres, is the largest hot desert, and that is the answer most people give. The question asks for the largest of all deserts, and the two polar deserts are bigger.
why_wrong.1: The Gobi, in Mongolia and China, is a cold desert but far smaller, about 1.3 million square kilometres.
why_wrong.2: The Arabian Desert is roughly 2.3 million square kilometres, large but well short of the Sahara, let alone Antarctica.

why_correct: The International Court of Justice sits at the Peace Palace in The Hague, in the Netherlands. It is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations and settles disputes between states.

why_wrong.0: Geneva houses many UN agencies but not the Court.
why_wrong.2: Brussels is the seat of the European Union and of NATO, neither of which is a UN body.
why_wrong.3: Washington D.C. is the headquarters of the World Bank and the IMF. Note that the ICJ is the only principal organ of the UN not based in New York.

why_correct: Economics studies how people behave when resources are scarce and wants are unlimited. Robbins defined it as the science of choice under scarcity, and choice is what the subject is really about.

why_wrong.0: Weather is the province of meteorology. Economics may study the effect of a monsoon on crops, but that is the human response, not the weather itself.
why_wrong.2: Plants belong to botany. Agriculture is studied by economists only as an economic activity.
why_wrong.3: Machines belong to engineering. An economist treats a machine as capital, that is as a factor of production.

why_correct: Adam Smith is called the father of economics for An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, which gave the subject its first systematic treatment and the idea of the invisible hand.

why_wrong.0: Karl Marx wrote Das Kapital and founded the socialist critique of capitalism, nearly a century later.
why_wrong.2: J. M. Keynes founded modern macroeconomics with his General Theory of 1936, and is called the father of macroeconomics.
why_wrong.3: Alfred Marshall is called the father of modern or neoclassical economics, for his Principles of Economics of 1890. Marshall and Smith are the two most often confused, and the word modern is what separates them.

why_correct: Consumer behaviour concerns how an individual consumer allocates income among goods, so it is a microeconomic topic. Micro deals with individual units.

why_wrong.0: National income measures the output of the whole economy, so it is macroeconomic.
why_wrong.1: Inflation is a rise in the general price level across the economy, again macro.
why_wrong.3: Unemployment concerns the economy-wide labour market. All three wrong options describe the economy as a whole, which is exactly the dividing line.

why_correct: The central problem arises because resources are scarce while wants are unlimited. If resources were plentiful enough for every want, no choice would be necessary and there would be no economic problem.

why_wrong.0: Resources are not unlimited. That is the very opposite of scarcity.
why_wrong.1: Wants are unlimited, not limited. Satisfy one and another appears.
why_wrong.3: Production is not easy, and even if it were, the inputs it needs would still be limited.

why_correct: PPC is the Production Possibility Curve, which shows the different combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its resources fully and efficiently employed. It is also called the transformation curve.

why_wrong.0: Public Production Curve is not a term in economics.
why_wrong.2: Price Production Curve is invented. There is a price consumption curve in consumer theory, which is a different thing.
why_wrong.3: Product Planning Curve is not an economic concept either. The curve is about what is possible to produce, which is what the word possibility carries.

why_correct: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative that must be given up to get something. It is the real cost of a choice, measured in what was forgone rather than in money.

why_wrong.0: Fixed cost is an accounting classification, a cost that does not vary with output.
why_wrong.1: Extra income is a gain, not a cost.
why_wrong.3: Market price is the money paid. A free good has a market price of zero but can still carry a heavy opportunity cost in time.

why_correct: A capitalist economy is based on private ownership of the means of production, with decisions guided by the profit motive and the price mechanism. The United States is the usual example.

why_wrong.0: A socialist economy has state ownership of the means of production and central planning.
why_wrong.2: A mixed economy has both private and public ownership side by side, so it is not based on private ownership alone.
why_wrong.3: A planned economy is directed by the government's plan rather than by prices, and is another name for the socialist type.

why_correct: In a mixed economy the public and private sectors coexist, with the state running key industries and providing services while private enterprise operates elsewhere. India is a mixed economy.

why_wrong.0: Government ownership alone describes a socialist or planned economy.
why_wrong.1: A purely private sector describes capitalism.
why_wrong.3: There is certainly a government in a mixed economy; indeed its participation is what makes the economy mixed.

why_correct: Utility is the want-satisfying power of a commodity, that is the satisfaction a consumer gets from consuming it. It is subjective and differs from person to person.

why_wrong.0: Cost of production is what the producer spends, which is quite separate from what the consumer feels.
why_wrong.2: Income earned is a receipt of money, not a satisfaction from consuming.
why_wrong.3: Market demand is the total quantity buyers will purchase. Utility helps explain demand but is not the same as it.

why_correct: In economics demand means desire backed by both the ability and the willingness to pay. A wish without purchasing power behind it is not demand.

why_wrong.0: Desire alone is not demand. A poor man may desire a car without adding anything to its demand.
why_wrong.2: Need is not demand either. Many needs go unmet precisely because no purchasing power supports them.
why_wrong.3: Supply is the seller's side of the market, the opposite of demand.

why_correct: The law of demand says that, other things remaining equal, a rise in price causes a fall in quantity demanded and a fall in price causes a rise. Price and quantity move in opposite directions, which is why the demand curve slopes downward.

why_wrong.0: Moving together would give an upward sloping curve, which is the rare exception of Giffen and Veblen goods, not the law.
why_wrong.1: Demand certainly changes, with price and with other factors.
why_wrong.3: The law describes what happens when price changes, so a constant price would leave nothing to state.

why_correct: A change in consumers' income shifts the whole demand curve, because at every price a different quantity is now demanded. Income is one of the other things held equal in the law of demand.

why_wrong.0: A change in the commodity's own price causes movement along the curve, not a shift of it. This is the single most important distinction in the topic.
why_wrong.2: Quantity supplied belongs to the supply side and does not shift demand.
why_wrong.3: Cost of production affects supply. Its effect on demand is only indirect, through the price it leads to.

why_correct: Supply is the quantity of a commodity that sellers are willing and able to offer for sale at different prices in a given period. Like demand, it is a schedule of quantities against prices, not a single number.

why_wrong.0: Stock is what exists and is available, whereas supply is the part actually offered for sale at a given price. A trader may hold stock back if the price is poor.
why_wrong.2: Total production is what has been made, and some of it may not be offered for sale.
why_wrong.3: Demand is the buyer's side of the market.

why_correct: Equilibrium is reached where the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied. At that price there is neither surplus nor shortage, so there is no force pushing the price to change.

why_wrong.0: Demand exceeding supply is a shortage, and the price will be bid up until the gap closes.
why_wrong.1: Supply exceeding demand is a surplus, and the price will fall.
why_wrong.3: A price of zero would apply to a free good, which is not what equilibrium means.

why_correct: Marginal utility is the addition to total satisfaction from consuming one more unit of a commodity. It is the change in total utility caused by a one-unit change in quantity.

why_wrong.0: Total utility is the whole satisfaction from all units taken together.
why_wrong.2: Average utility is total utility divided by the number of units.
why_wrong.3: Cost of production belongs to the producer's side and has nothing to do with the consumer's satisfaction.

why_correct: The law says that as more units of a commodity are consumed, the satisfaction from each successive unit falls. The first cup of tea gives more pleasure than the fourth.

why_wrong.0: Utility always increasing is the opposite of the law. Total utility does keep rising for a while, but at a slowing rate, and it is marginal utility that falls.
why_wrong.1: Constant utility would mean every unit gave the same satisfaction, which experience contradicts.
why_wrong.3: The law is about satisfaction, not about prices, though it is the reason demand curves slope downward.

why_correct: The primary sector covers activities that draw directly on nature: agriculture, fishing, forestry and mining. Farming is its central example.

why_wrong.0: The secondary sector manufactures, turning raw materials into finished goods.
why_wrong.1: The tertiary sector provides services such as banking, transport and education.
why_wrong.3: Service sector is another name for the tertiary sector, so it is the same wrong answer twice. Note that a flour mill is secondary even though it handles a farm product.

why_correct: National income is the total income earned by all the factors of production of a country in a year, that is rent, wages, interest and profit taken together. It measures the whole economy's earnings, not the government's.

why_wrong.0: Government income is only one part, coming largely from taxes.
why_wrong.2: Export earnings are one component of the flow of income from abroad, not the whole.
why_wrong.3: Tax revenue is a transfer from citizens to the state and is not itself new income earned.

why_correct: GDP is Gross Domestic Product, the money value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a year, whoever produces them.

why_wrong.1: General Domestic Price is not a term. The general price level is a separate idea used in measuring inflation.
why_wrong.2: Gross Development Plan is invented.
why_wrong.3: Government Domestic Product is not a term either. Note the contrast with GNP, which counts what a country's nationals produce anywhere, while GDP counts what is produced inside its borders.

why_correct: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, which means each rupee buys less than before. It is measured by index numbers such as the Consumer Price Index.

why_wrong.0: A fall in prices is deflation, the opposite condition.
why_wrong.2: An increase in production is growth, and it usually works against inflation by increasing the supply of goods.
why_wrong.3: An increase in exports affects the balance of trade. The word general matters: a rise in the price of one commodity is not inflation.

why_correct: Money is anything generally accepted as a medium of exchange. That function is its defining one, because it removes the double coincidence of wants that made barter so difficult.

why_wrong.0: A consumer good is used to satisfy a want directly. Money satisfies no want by itself; it is useful only for what it buys.
why_wrong.1: A capital good is used to produce other goods, such as a machine.
why_wrong.3: A luxury good is a classification of consumer goods by necessity. Money buys luxuries but is not one.

why_correct: The Reserve Bank of India, established in 1935, is the central bank of the country. It issues currency, controls credit, acts as banker to the government and regulates the whole banking system.

why_wrong.0: Commercial banks such as the State Bank of India take deposits and lend to the public. The RBI is their regulator, not one of them.
why_wrong.2: A foreign bank is one incorporated outside India but operating here.
why_wrong.3: A cooperative bank is owned by its members and serves them, mainly in rural and semi-urban areas.

why_correct: All three are functions of money. It is a medium of exchange for transactions, a measure of value for comparing goods, and a store of value that can be held over time. A fourth, the standard of deferred payment, is usually added.

why_wrong.0: Measure of value is a genuine function, but naming only one leaves the others out.
why_wrong.1: Medium of exchange is the primary function, and still only one of them.
why_wrong.2: Store of value is also correct on its own. When several options are each true and the last says all of these, check whether any is actually false before ruling it out.

why_correct: Unemployment means people who are willing and able to work at the prevailing wage cannot find work. Willingness is essential to the definition, which is why students and retired people are not counted.

why_wrong.0: Working part time is underemployment, not unemployment, since the person does have work.
why_wrong.2: Low income describes poverty. A person may work hard and still be poor, so the two problems are distinct.
why_wrong.3: High prices describe inflation, a separate problem.

why_correct: Economics has two main branches: microeconomics, which studies individual units, and macroeconomics, which studies the economy as a whole. The division is due to Ragnar Frisch.

why_wrong.1: Three branches would require a third division of the same kind, and there is none. Fields such as public finance are applications within these two.
why_wrong.2: Four is not a recognised division.
why_wrong.3: Five is not either. Do not confuse the two branches with the four factors of production or the three sectors of the economy.

why_correct: Education is a Latin word. It comes from the Latin roots educare, educere and educatum, which is why the study of the term always begins with Latin.

why_wrong.1: French has shaped much English vocabulary, but this word reaches English from Latin.
why_wrong.2: The word is used in English, but the question asks where it comes from, not where it is used.
why_wrong.3: Greek gave philosophy many terms, such as metaphysics and pedagogy, but not this one.

why_correct: The word education comes from the Latin educere, meaning to lead out or to draw out. The idea is that the child already carries powers and possibilities within, and the teacher's work is to bring them out rather than to supply them from outside. This is the sense the syllabus asks for, and it is the sense on which the whole modern child centred view of education rests.

why_wrong.0: To nourish is the sense of the related Latin word educare. It is a genuine root of the word, and it is why some books gloss education as nourishing the child, but it is not the meaning this question is after.
why_wrong.1: To bring up is again educare, the upbringing and rearing of the child. It is close, and it was the printed key, but the term the syllabus wants here is the drawing out one.
why_wrong.3: To put in is the exact opposite idea, the old picture of the child as an empty vessel into which information is poured. The educere definition exists precisely to reject it.

why_correct: Swami Vivekananda defined education as the manifestation of the perfection already in man. The idea is that nothing is put into the child from outside; what is already there is uncovered.

why_wrong.0: Sri Aurobindo gave the philosophy of integral education, aiming at the full development of body, mind and spirit.
why_wrong.1: Gandhi gave Basic Education, or Nai Talim, built round a craft and the mother tongue.
why_wrong.3: Tagore founded Santiniketan and taught in the open air, close to nature. All four are Indian thinkers on education, so the definition itself must be recognised.

why_correct: In the broader sense education is a lifelong process that begins at birth and ends only at death. The child begins learning from the family long before any institution is involved.

why_wrong.0: School is where formal education begins, which is the narrow sense of the word. The question specifies the broader sense.
why_wrong.2: College comes later still in the formal ladder.
why_wrong.3: University is later again. The narrow sense means deliberate instruction in an institution, while the broad sense means every influence that shapes a person.

why_correct: The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, which is why that day is celebrated as Republic Day. The date was chosen to honour the Purna Swaraj declaration of 1930.

why_wrong.1: 26 November 1949 is when the Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution, and it is kept as Constitution Day. Adoption and commencement are two months apart, and that gap is exactly what this question tests.
why_wrong.2: 26 January 1949 is a year too early.
why_wrong.3: 26 November 1950 mixes the adoption date with the wrong year.

why_correct: The 86th Constitutional Amendment of 2002 inserted Article 21A, making free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen a fundamental right.

why_wrong.0: 2000 is when the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan was being framed, but no amendment was made.
why_wrong.1: 2001 is when the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan was launched. The scheme came first and the right the following year.
why_wrong.3: 2003 is after the amendment. Note that the Right to Education Act, which gave the right practical effect, came only in 2009 and took force in 2010.

why_correct: The family is an informal agency of education. It teaches without any syllabus, timetable or deliberate plan, simply through daily living, and its influence is the earliest and deepest a child receives.

why_wrong.0: Formal agencies are schools, colleges and universities, with a fixed curriculum and a planned course.
why_wrong.2: Non-formal agencies are organised but flexible, such as open schooling and adult literacy programmes. Organised but outside the school system, which is not the same as informal.
why_wrong.3: The family belongs to one category only, and it is the informal one.

why_correct: The National Council of Educational Research and Training was established in 1961, by merging seven existing national institutions, to advise the central and state governments on school education.

why_wrong.1: 1960 is a year too early, and nothing of note was founded then in this field.
why_wrong.2: 1959 is two years too early. The institutions that were merged existed before this, but the Council itself did not.
why_wrong.3: 1962 is a year late. A useful anchor is that NCERT came shortly after the Secondary Education Commission and before the Kothari Commission of 1964.

why_correct: NCTE is the National Council for Teacher Education, a statutory body set up in 1993 to plan and coordinate teacher education and to lay down norms for teacher training institutions.

why_wrong.0: Commission is wrong. A commission is usually a temporary body appointed to report, while a council is a permanent one.
why_wrong.2: Training Education is not the name, and it reads oddly, since teacher education is the phrase used.
why_wrong.3: Committee is wrong for the same reason as commission. Read such acronyms word by word: council, teacher, education.

why_correct: Metaphysics is the branch of philosophy dealing with the ultimate nature of reality, asking what truly exists and what the universe is made of. In educational philosophy it shapes what a system takes to be real and therefore worth teaching.

why_wrong.0: Axiology is the study of values, covering ethics and aesthetics, and it shapes the aims of education.
why_wrong.1: Ontology is the study of being and existence. It is close, but it is a division within metaphysics rather than the branch itself, and metaphysics is the broader term the question asks for.
why_wrong.3: Epistemology is the study of knowledge, asking what we can know and how we come to know it, which shapes teaching method.

why_correct: The Ashtangika Marga, or Noble Eightfold Path, is the Buddhist way to the cessation of suffering. It is the fourth of the Four Noble Truths and runs from right view to right concentration.
