why_wrong.0: Jainism teaches the Triratna, the Three Jewels of right faith, right knowledge and right conduct, together with the five vows.
why_wrong.2: Vedanta is based on the Upanishads and teaches the identity of the individual soul with Brahman.
why_wrong.3: Nyaya is the school of logic and the means of valid knowledge.

why_correct: Swami Vivekananda held that all knowledge, material and spiritual, is already within a person and is only hidden by ignorance. Education, on this view, removes the curtain rather than adding anything.

why_wrong.0: Plato held that learning is recollection of what the soul knew before birth, which is a related idea but from a different tradition and a different phrasing.
why_wrong.1: Gandhi's emphasis was on education through craft and on character rather than on innate knowledge.
why_wrong.2: Tagore stressed freedom, nature and creative self-expression. This saying belongs with Vivekananda's definition of education as manifestation of perfection, and the two go together.

why_correct: NCERT's chief function is extension work with State Education Departments to improve school education, through curriculum design, textbooks, teacher training and research.

why_wrong.0: Higher education is the concern of the University Grants Commission.
why_wrong.2: Secondary education is only one stage of school education. NCERT covers the whole school range from pre-primary upward, so this is too narrow.
why_wrong.3: Technical education is looked after by the All India Council for Technical Education.

why_correct: IQ is mental age divided by chronological age, multiplied by 100. So a ten-year-old with a mental age of twelve has an IQ of 120. The formula is due to William Stern.

why_wrong.0: Dividing mental age by 100 and then multiplying by 100 simply returns the mental age, and leaves chronological age out altogether.
why_wrong.1: This inverts the fraction. Chronological age over mental age would give a bright child an IQ below 100, which is the wrong way round.
why_wrong.3: This is the same inverted formula printed a second time. Whichever of the two you picked, the error is the same: mental age belongs on top.

why_correct: The home is the main centre of informal education. It is where the child first learns language, habits, manners and values, and it works continuously without any deliberate teaching.

why_wrong.1: Society is an informal agency too, and a powerful one, but its influence comes later and is more diffuse than the home's.
why_wrong.2: Radio and television are informal agencies of the modern kind, but they reach the child well after the home has begun its work.
why_wrong.3: Newspapers are likewise an informal agency, and they require literacy the child must first acquire elsewhere.

why_correct: The family educates informally, through imitation, affection and the routine of daily life, without a syllabus or a fixed method. The child learns without either party quite intending a lesson.

why_wrong.0: Formal teaching needs a planned curriculum and trained teachers, which the family does not have.
why_wrong.2: Deliberately is wrong because most family learning is unplanned. Parents do teach some things on purpose, but that is not what characterises the agency.
why_wrong.3: Regularly suggests a timetable. Family influence is constant rather than scheduled, and those are different things.

why_correct: John Dewey described the school as a miniature society, holding that it should reproduce the life of the community in small so that the child learns democracy by living it. He is the leading figure of pragmatism in education.

why_wrong.0: B. F. Skinner developed operant conditioning and programmed instruction.
why_wrong.1: E. L. Thorndike gave the laws of learning and the theory of trial and error.
why_wrong.2: J. F. Herbart gave the five formal steps of teaching and the doctrine of apperception. The other three are learning theorists; Dewey is the social philosopher of education.

why_correct: Plato set out his scheme of education in The Republic, which describes the ideal state and the long training of its guardians. It is the earliest systematic treatment of education in Western philosophy.

why_wrong.1: Educational Philosophy is not a work of Plato's.
why_wrong.2: Education of Plato is not a book he wrote; if anything it names a topic others have written on.
why_wrong.3: Emile is by Jean-Jacques Rousseau, published in 1762, and it is the other great classic of educational writing. Plato and Rousseau are the pair most often confused here.

why_correct: Mahavira was the twenty-fourth and last Tirthankara of Jainism. He gave the faith its final form in the sixth century BCE and added the vow of chastity to the four taught by Parshvanatha.

why_wrong.1: Jinasena was a Jain scholar and author of the Adipurana, not a Tirthankara.
why_wrong.2: Rishabhanatha was the first Tirthankara, at the opposite end of the list.
why_wrong.3: Kshemendra was a Kashmiri poet and writer, not a Jain Tirthankara at all.

why_correct: Rishabha, also called Rishabhanatha or Adinatha, was the first of the twenty-four Tirthankaras of Jainism. His symbol is the bull.

why_wrong.0: Mahavira was the twenty-fourth and last, so he is at the other end of the same list.
why_wrong.2: Parshvanatha was the twenty-third, and the first for whom there is historical evidence.
why_wrong.3: Padmaprabha was the sixth Tirthankara. The two worth fixing firmly are the first, Rishabha, and the last, Mahavira.

why_correct: Patanjali is regarded as the founder of the Yoga school, having compiled the Yoga Sutras, which set out the eight limbs of yoga from yama to samadhi.

why_wrong.1: Kapila founded the Samkhya school, which is the philosophical partner of Yoga.
why_wrong.2: Jaimini founded the Mimamsa school, concerned with the interpretation of Vedic ritual.
why_wrong.3: Shankara was the great exponent of Advaita Vedanta. All four founded or led schools of Indian philosophy, so the association must be learnt pair by pair.

why_correct: Buddha, in the sixth century BCE, taught that a person's worth comes from their conduct and not from the family they are born into. His Sangha admitted men and women of every caste, and that open order is what is counted as the first organised challenge to the caste system.

why_wrong.1: Tilak was a nationalist leader of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. His fight was against British rule, more than two thousand years after the period this question is about.
why_wrong.2: Gandhi campaigned hard against untouchability, but in the twentieth century. Had the question asked who fought untouchability he would be the answer; it asks who was first, and he comes far too late for that.
why_wrong.3: Mahavira also rejected birth-based hierarchy, and he and Buddha belonged to the same Sramana movement, so this is the one option a well-read student may want to defend. The answer expected here is Buddha, because the Sangha was the first order to open its doors to every caste as a matter of rule.

why_correct: Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment in 2002, makes free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen a fundamental right. It sits alongside Article 21, the right to life.

why_wrong.0: Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in public employment.
why_wrong.1: Article 46 directs the state to promote the educational interests of the weaker sections, but it is a Directive Principle and so not enforceable in court.
why_wrong.2: Article 45 originally directed the state to provide free education up to fourteen, again as a Directive Principle. The 86th Amendment moved that promise into the enforceable fundamental rights as 21A, and Article 45 now covers early childhood care.

why_correct: Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and other forms of forced labour. It falls under the Right against Exploitation, together with Article 24 on child labour.

why_wrong.0: Article 39 is a Directive Principle on the distribution of resources and on protecting children and workers.
why_wrong.1: Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.
why_wrong.2: Article 16 concerns equality of opportunity in public employment. The block to remember is 23 and 24 for exploitation, with 24 barring the employment of children under fourteen in hazardous work.

why_correct: Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan was launched in 2001 to universalise elementary education, aiming to bring every child aged six to fourteen into school.

why_wrong.1: 2002 is the year of the 86th Amendment, which made education a fundamental right. The programme came first and the constitutional right the year after.
why_wrong.2: 2003 is after both the programme and the amendment, and marks neither of them.
why_wrong.3: 2004 is later still. The sequence worth holding is SSA in 2001, the amendment in 2002 and the RTE Act in 2009.

why_correct: The environment is usually described as having three dimensions: physical, biological and social or cultural. Financial is not among them, being a human institution rather than a component of the surroundings.

why_wrong.0: The physical dimension covers the non-living surroundings, that is land, water, air, light and temperature.
why_wrong.1: The biological dimension covers all living things, from microbes to plants, animals and human beings.
why_wrong.2: The social dimension covers the institutions, customs and relationships within which people live. Economic activity does affect the environment powerfully, but it acts through these three rather than forming a fourth.

why_correct: Sustainable development means meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. That is the Brundtland Commission's definition of 1987.

why_wrong.0: Unlimited use would exhaust resources and leave nothing for those who come after, which is exactly what the idea guards against.
why_wrong.1: Ignoring the future is the opposite of sustainability. The concern for future generations is the heart of the definition.
why_wrong.3: Rapid industrialisation alone often damages the environment. Sustainable development balances economic, social and environmental goals rather than pursuing one.

why_correct: The Earth Summit is the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development, held at Rio de Janeiro in 1992. It produced Agenda 21, the Rio Declaration and the conventions on climate change and biodiversity.

why_wrong.0: The Stockholm Conference of 1972 was the first UN conference on the human environment, and it began the whole process, but the title Earth Summit belongs to Rio.
why_wrong.2: The Kyoto Conference of 1997 produced the Kyoto Protocol on greenhouse gas emissions.
why_wrong.3: The Paris Summit of 2015 produced the Paris Agreement on climate change.

why_correct: The United Nations Conference on the Human Environment was held at Stockholm in 1972. It was the first world conference on the environment, and 5 June, its opening day, is now World Environment Day.

why_wrong.0: 1962 is the year Rachel Carson published Silent Spring, which awakened public concern but was not a conference.
why_wrong.2: 1982 saw a review meeting in Nairobi, ten years on, but not the original conference.
why_wrong.3: 1992 is the Rio Earth Summit, twenty years after Stockholm. The pair to fix is Stockholm 1972 and Rio 1992.

why_correct: Solar energy is renewable, since it is replenished continuously and cannot be exhausted by use. Wind, tidal, geothermal and biomass energy are renewable for the same reason.

why_wrong.0: Coal is a fossil fuel, formed over millions of years, so it is non-renewable on any human timescale.
why_wrong.1: Petroleum is likewise a fossil fuel and finite.
why_wrong.3: Natural gas is a fossil fuel too. Three of the four options are fossil fuels, which makes the odd one out easy to spot.

why_correct: A growing population needs more food, water, fuel, housing and land, and produces more waste, so pressure on the environment rises directly with numbers.

why_wrong.0: Conservation becomes harder, not easier, as more people draw on the same resources.
why_wrong.2: Biodiversity generally falls as population grows, because habitat is cleared for settlement and farming.
why_wrong.3: Forest cover tends to shrink under population pressure, as land is taken for cultivation and building.

why_correct: When trees are removed, their roots no longer bind the soil and their canopy no longer breaks the fall of rain, so the topsoil is washed or blown away. Soil erosion is the most immediate consequence of deforestation.

why_wrong.0: Biodiversity falls sharply when forests go, because habitat is destroyed.
why_wrong.2: Rainfall usually decreases, since forests return moisture to the air by transpiration and help form clouds.
why_wrong.3: Climate worsens rather than improves. Forests moderate temperature and absorb carbon dioxide, and removing them does the reverse.

why_correct: The Green Revolution of the 1960s aimed at raising agricultural production, above all of wheat and rice, through high-yielding varieties, irrigation, fertilisers and pesticides. M. S. Swaminathan led it in India.

why_wrong.0: Industrial production is a separate matter, and the colour revolutions are all agricultural.
why_wrong.2: Forest cover was not its aim, and in places the expansion of cropland reduced it.
why_wrong.3: Population was not its target. Note the environmental cost that followed: falling water tables, soil salinity and pesticide residues.

why_correct: Child labour is a social factor affecting development. It arises from poverty and lack of schooling, and it holds back development by denying children the education that would raise their future productivity.

why_wrong.0: Political factors concern governance and policy. Laws against child labour are political, but the practice itself is social and economic.
why_wrong.2: Climatic factors are matters of weather and temperature.
why_wrong.3: Geological factors concern the earth's structure and mineral resources.

why_correct: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, set up in 1988 by the UN Environment Programme and the World Meteorological Organization, assesses the science of climate change and issues periodic assessment reports.

why_wrong.0: The World Health Organization deals with global public health.
why_wrong.1: UNESCO deals with education, science and culture, including World Heritage sites.
why_wrong.3: The International Monetary Fund deals with international monetary cooperation and financial stability.

why_correct: The Ramsar Convention of 1971 is the treaty for the conservation and wise use of wetlands. India has many Ramsar sites, including the Sundarbans and Chilika Lake.

why_wrong.0: Forests are covered by other agreements, such as the forest principles agreed at Rio.
why_wrong.2: Mountains have no single convention of this kind.
why_wrong.3: Oceans are governed by the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. Ramsar is named after the Iranian city where it was signed, and it deals only with wetlands.

why_correct: The Kyoto Protocol of 1997 is an agreement under the climate change convention, binding industrialised countries to reduce their emissions of greenhouse gases.

why_wrong.0: Ozone depletion is the subject of the Montreal Protocol. Kyoto and Montreal are the pair most often swapped: Montreal for the ozone layer, Kyoto for the climate.
why_wrong.2: Wildlife conservation is covered by CITES and by the Convention on Biological Diversity.
why_wrong.3: Desertification has its own UN convention, agreed in 1994.

why_correct: Carbon dioxide is the principal greenhouse gas responsible for global warming. Other gases trap more heat per molecule, but carbon dioxide is released in such volume by burning fossil fuels that its total effect is greatest.

why_wrong.0: Oxygen is essential to life and to combustion but does not trap infrared radiation.
why_wrong.1: Nitrogen makes up most of the atmosphere yet is not a greenhouse gas at all.
why_wrong.3: Hydrogen is barely present in the atmosphere and is not a greenhouse gas. Abundance in the air and warming effect are quite separate things.

why_correct: All three work together. Eco-clubs involve students directly, formal education builds understanding over years, and campaigns reach the wider public quickly. Awareness needs all three channels.

why_wrong.0: Eco-clubs are effective but reach only those who join them.
why_wrong.1: Education is powerful but slow, and it reaches those in school.
why_wrong.2: Campaigns reach many people but their effect fades without the other two behind it. Each option is genuinely true, which is what makes all of these the answer.

why_correct: Coal is non-renewable. It formed from plant matter buried over millions of years, and once burnt it cannot be replaced within any human timescale.

why_wrong.0: Wind energy is renewable, driven by the sun's uneven heating of the earth.
why_wrong.1: Water is renewable through the water cycle, though it can be locally exhausted or polluted by overuse.
why_wrong.3: Solar energy is renewable and effectively inexhaustible.

why_correct: The Montreal Protocol of 1987 protects the ozone layer by phasing out chlorofluorocarbons and other ozone-depleting substances. It is the most successful environmental treaty so far, and the ozone hole is now shrinking.

why_wrong.0: Forests are not its subject.
why_wrong.2: Rivers are covered by national laws and by basin-specific agreements.
why_wrong.3: Wildlife is covered by CITES and the biodiversity convention. Keep Montreal for ozone and Kyoto for climate.

why_correct: The Brundtland Commission, formally the World Commission on Environment and Development, popularised sustainable development in its 1987 report Our Common Future. It was chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland of Norway.

why_wrong.1: The World Bank lends for development projects and has adopted the idea, but did not originate it.
why_wrong.2: UNESCO works on education, science and culture.
why_wrong.3: The IMF deals with monetary and financial stability. The report's title, Our Common Future, is worth remembering along with the commission's name.

why_correct: Air pollution degrades the environment by lowering the quality of the air and harming health, crops and buildings. Environmental degradation means any deterioration in the quality of the environment.

why_wrong.0: Afforestation is planting trees on land that had none, which improves the environment.
why_wrong.1: Rainwater harvesting conserves water and recharges groundwater.
why_wrong.3: Recycling reduces waste and the demand for raw materials. Three of the four options are remedies, so the one that is a harm stands out.

why_correct: Education does all three. It makes people aware of environmental problems, changes how they behave, and so leads to the actual conservation of resources. Awareness without behaviour would achieve nothing.

why_wrong.0: Raising awareness is real but is only the first step.
why_wrong.1: Promoting responsible behaviour follows from awareness and is the second step.
why_wrong.2: Conserving resources is the outcome of the first two. Since each is true and they form a chain, all of these is the answer.

why_correct: Land reclamation means restoring degraded or unusable land to productive use, for instance by draining marsh, levelling mined ground or treating saline soil.

why_wrong.0: Destroying forests is deforestation, which makes land less productive rather than more.
why_wrong.2: Mining degrades land and often creates the very damage that reclamation must later repair.
why_wrong.3: Soil erosion is a form of degradation, so it is the problem rather than the remedy.

why_correct: Agenda 21 was adopted at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992. It is a comprehensive action plan for sustainable development in the twenty-first century, to be carried out globally, nationally and locally.

why_wrong.0: The Stockholm Conference of 1972 produced a declaration and an action plan, but not Agenda 21.
why_wrong.2: The Kyoto Conference produced the Kyoto Protocol on emissions.
why_wrong.3: The Basel Convention concerns the movement of hazardous waste. The 21 in the name refers to the twenty-first century, which places it in 1992.

why_correct: Human beings can think, foresee consequences and choose between courses of action, so they can take responsibility for the environment. That capacity for reasoned decision is what makes them rational partners rather than mere occupants.

why_wrong.1: Depending on machines is not rationality, and machines are themselves a product of human choices.
why_wrong.2: Human beings affect the environment more than any other species, which is precisely why their choices matter.
why_wrong.3: No one lives independently of nature. Human beings depend on air, water and soil like every other organism.

why_correct: The Basel Convention of 1989 controls the transboundary movement of hazardous wastes and their disposal. It was framed to stop rich countries dumping toxic waste in poorer ones.

why_wrong.0: Biodiversity is covered by the Convention on Biological Diversity, agreed at Rio.
why_wrong.2: Wetlands are covered by the Ramsar Convention.
why_wrong.3: Population control is not the subject of any such convention. Each of these treaties is named after the city where it was signed, so they are best learnt as city and subject pairs.

why_correct: All three are genuine forms of public participation. Tree planting, clean-up campaigns and eco-club work all involve ordinary citizens acting directly rather than leaving protection to the government.

why_wrong.0: Tree plantation drives are one good example among several.
why_wrong.1: Community clean-ups are another, and they involve the wider neighbourhood.
why_wrong.2: Eco-club activities are a third, based in schools. When several options are each true examples of the same idea, look carefully before rejecting all of these.

why_correct: Environmental education aims to build awareness of environmental problems and to translate that awareness into responsible action. Knowledge that changes nothing would fall short of the objective.

why_wrong.0: Industrial growth is an economic aim, and unchecked growth is often part of the problem.
why_wrong.2: Increasing population adds to environmental pressure.
why_wrong.3: Encouraging excessive use of resources is the opposite of what the subject teaches.

why_correct: Eratosthenes, the Greek scholar and librarian of Alexandria, first used the word geographia in the third century BCE. He also measured the circumference of the Earth with remarkable accuracy.

why_wrong.0: Aristotle wrote on the natural world and argued the Earth was a sphere, but he did not coin the term.
why_wrong.2: Herodotus is called the father of history, and he described many lands, but the word is not his.
why_wrong.3: Strabo wrote a great Geographica in the first century, well after Eratosthenes had named the subject.

why_correct: Human geography studies the spatial distribution of human activities and the relationship between people and their environment. It covers population, settlement, economic activity and culture.

why_wrong.0: Geomorphology studies landforms and the processes that shape them, and belongs to physical geography.
why_wrong.1: Climatology studies climate and its patterns, again a branch of physical geography.
why_wrong.3: Oceanography studies the seas. All three wrong options are physical, and the question asks about human activity.

why_correct: Kant's nebular hypothesis, developed by Laplace, holds that the Solar System formed from a hot, rotating cloud of gas that cooled, contracted and shed rings which condensed into planets.

why_wrong.0: A giant meteorite plays no part in the hypothesis. Meteorite impacts shaped planetary surfaces later.
why_wrong.2: Black holes were unknown when the hypothesis was framed, and none is involved in forming a solar system.
why_wrong.3: A supercontinent is a feature of Earth's own history, as in Pangaea, and belongs to continental drift rather than to the origin of the system.

why_correct: The Big Bang theory is the modern explanation of the origin of the universe, holding that it began about 13.7 billion years ago from an extremely dense, hot state and has been expanding ever since.

why_wrong.0: The planetesimal theory of Chamberlin and Moulton concerns the origin of the Solar System, not the universe.
why_wrong.1: The nebular theory likewise explains the Solar System only. Note the difference of scale the question turns on: the Solar System is one star among billions.
why_wrong.3: Continental drift explains the movement of the Earth's landmasses, a far smaller matter still.

why_correct: The core is composed mainly of nickel and iron, and is therefore called NIFE. It is the densest layer and is the source of the Earth's magnetic field.

why_wrong.0: SIAL is the upper continental crust, rich in silica and aluminium.
why_wrong.1: SIMA is the oceanic crust, rich in silica and magnesium.
why_wrong.2: The mantle is composed largely of silicate rocks rich in iron and magnesium, but it is not the nickel-iron layer. The three names SIAL, SIMA and NIFE run in order of increasing density.

why_correct: The Mohorovicic discontinuity, or Moho, separates the crust from the mantle. It was identified by the Croatian seismologist Andrija Mohorovicic from a sudden change in the speed of seismic waves.

why_wrong.0: The Gutenberg discontinuity separates the mantle from the core.
why_wrong.1: The Conrad discontinuity lies within the crust, between its upper and lower parts.
why_wrong.3: The Lehmann discontinuity separates the outer core from the inner core. Each boundary is named for the seismologist who found it, and they are best learnt in order from the surface down.

why_correct: S-waves are transverse, needing a medium that can resist shearing, and liquids cannot. Their failure to pass through the outer core is the main evidence that it is liquid.

why_wrong.0: P-waves are longitudinal and travel through solids, liquids and gases alike, which is why they are the first to arrive.
why_wrong.2: Surface waves travel along the ground surface and cause most earthquake damage, but the question concerns passage through the interior.
why_wrong.3: Long waves, or L-waves, are a kind of surface wave and again do not travel through the deep interior.

why_correct: The asthenosphere lies in the upper mantle, roughly 100 to 200 kilometres down. It is partly molten and plastic, and the rigid plates of the lithosphere move over it.

why_wrong.1: The lower mantle is under greater pressure and behaves more rigidly.
why_wrong.2: The outer core is liquid but lies far deeper, beyond the Gutenberg discontinuity.
why_wrong.3: The inner core is solid despite its heat, because of the immense pressure. The asthenosphere matters because it is the layer that makes plate tectonics possible.

why_correct: Volcanism originates within the Earth, driven by internal heat, so it is an endogenic process. Endogenic processes build landforms up.

why_wrong.0: Weathering acts at the surface, driven by the atmosphere, so it is exogenic.
why_wrong.1: Mass wasting is the downslope movement of material under gravity, again a surface process.
why_wrong.3: Erosion is exogenic too. The dividing question is simply where the energy comes from: inside the Earth or outside it.

why_correct: Fold mountains are formed when compressional forces at converging plate margins squeeze layers of sedimentary rock into folds. The Himalayas, Alps and Andes were all raised this way.

why_wrong.0: Denudation wears land down rather than building it up.
why_wrong.1: Volcanism builds volcanic mountains such as Fujiyama, which are formed from erupted material rather than by folding.
why_wrong.3: River action carves valleys and builds plains, working on a far smaller scale than mountain building.

why_correct: Weathering is driven by the atmosphere, water and living things acting at the surface, so it is an exogenic process. Exogenic processes wear landforms down.

why_wrong.0: Earthquakes arise from movement within the crust and are endogenic.
why_wrong.1: Folding is caused by internal compressional forces, again endogenic.
why_wrong.2: Faulting is caused by internal tensional or compressional forces. Three of the four originate inside the Earth, so the surface process is the odd one out.

why_correct: Weathering is the breakdown of rock in situ, that is in its own place, without any transport. Adding movement to it is what makes erosion.

why_wrong.0: Erosion involves both breakdown and removal by an agent such as water, wind or ice.
why_wrong.2: Deposition is the laying down of material at the end of transport.
why_wrong.3: Transportation is the carrying of weathered material away, the middle stage of the sequence. In situ is the phrase that settles this question.

why_correct: Insolation is incoming solar radiation, the energy the Earth receives from the Sun. The word is a contraction of incoming solar radiation.

why_wrong.1: Outgoing terrestrial radiation is the long-wave heat the Earth radiates back, which is a separate part of the heat budget.
why_wrong.2: Atmospheric pressure is the weight of the air, measured by a barometer.
why_wrong.3: Wind is air in motion, caused by pressure differences that insolation helps create, but not insolation itself.

why_correct: Carbon dioxide contributes the largest share of the enhanced greenhouse effect among the gases released by human activity, because it is emitted in such quantity by burning fossil fuels.

why_wrong.0: Oxygen is not a greenhouse gas, since its molecule cannot absorb infrared radiation.
why_wrong.1: Nitrogen is the most abundant gas in the air but is not a greenhouse gas either.
why_wrong.3: Argon is inert and plays no part. Note that water vapour is in absolute terms the largest natural contributor, but it is not one of the options here and is not the gas driving the human-caused change.

why_correct: The barometer measures atmospheric pressure, either as a column of mercury or, in the aneroid type, by the flexing of a sealed metal box.

why_wrong.0: A hygrometer measures humidity, that is the moisture content of the air.
why_wrong.1: An anemometer measures wind speed.
why_wrong.3: A thermometer measures temperature. Each instrument goes with one element of weather, and they are best learnt as a set.

why_correct: Human geography studies the relationship between people and their environment, including how people adapt to nature and how they modify it. That reciprocal relationship is its central subject.

why_wrong.0: Rocks and minerals belong to geology and geomorphology.
why_wrong.2: Ocean currents belong to oceanography.
why_wrong.3: Earthquakes belong to seismology and geomorphology, which are branches of physical geography.

why_correct: Primary activities extract resources directly from nature: agriculture, fishing, forestry, mining and gathering. They are closest to the physical environment of all economic activities.

why_wrong.0: Secondary activities process and manufacture what the primary sector extracts.
why_wrong.1: Tertiary activities provide services such as transport, trade and education.
why_wrong.3: Quaternary activities involve knowledge work, research and information handling.

why_correct: Software development is a quaternary activity, since it is knowledge-based work concerned with creating and processing information rather than with goods or ordinary services.

why_wrong.0: Primary activity extracts from nature.
why_wrong.1: Secondary activity manufactures goods.
why_wrong.2: Tertiary activity provides general services. Software is often lumped with services, which makes this the tempting answer, but the quaternary sector was defined precisely to separate high-knowledge work from routine service work.

why_correct: India lies entirely in the Northern and Eastern Hemispheres, extending from about 8 degrees to 37 degrees north and from 68 degrees to 97 degrees east.

why_wrong.0: The Western Hemisphere lies west of the Prime Meridian, and no part of India does.
why_wrong.2: No part of India lies south of the Equator. The southernmost point, Indira Point in the Nicobars, is still about 6 degrees north.
why_wrong.3: A country cannot lie entirely in both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres, since the Equator separates them.

why_correct: The Tropic of Cancer passes through eight Indian states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram. It runs west to east across the middle of the country.

why_wrong.0: 6 is short by two. A useful check is to trace the line on the map from Gujarat in the west to Mizoram in the east.
why_wrong.1: 7 is short by one, and usually comes from omitting Tripura or Chhattisgarh.
why_wrong.3: 9 is one too many, and often comes from wrongly including a neighbouring state such as Odisha or Manipur.

why_correct: The Northern Plains were formed by alluvium deposited over millions of years by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra and their tributaries as they emerged from the Himalayas. The soil is deep, fertile and renewed by flooding.

why_wrong.0: Wind-blown sediment forms loess plains, as in China, not these.
why_wrong.1: Lava flows formed the Deccan Trap, in peninsular India, which is a very different landform.
why_wrong.2: Glacial deposits occur in the high Himalayas, but the plains themselves are river-built.

why_correct: The Peninsular Plateau is made largely of ancient crystalline igneous and metamorphic rocks. It is one of the oldest landmasses on Earth, a fragment of the former Gondwanaland, and is rich in minerals.

why_wrong.0: Young fold mountains are the Himalayas, geologically recent and still rising, while the plateau is stable and very old.
why_wrong.1: Alluvial deposits form the Northern Plains.
why_wrong.3: Volcanic islands describe the Andamans and Barren Island. The Deccan Trap is volcanic in origin, but it covers only part of the plateau, whose foundation is crystalline.

why_correct: The Himalayas are called the Water Tower of Asia because their snowfields and glaciers feed the Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra and other great rivers, supplying water to a large part of the continent all year round.

why_wrong.0: The Northern Plains receive that water rather than supplying it.
why_wrong.1: The Indian Desert is the driest region of the country.
why_wrong.3: The Coastal Plains lie at the seaward end of the rivers' journey. The name captures the idea of a raised store that feeds the lowlands below.

why_correct: The Kosi is called the Sorrow of Bihar. It carries enormous silt from Nepal, which raises its bed and makes it shift its channel repeatedly, flooding wide areas of north Bihar.

why_wrong.0: The Damodar was called the Sorrow of Bengal before the Damodar Valley Corporation dams tamed it. The two sorrows are the pair most often confused.
why_wrong.2: The Mahanadi flows through Chhattisgarh and Odisha and was controlled by the Hirakud dam.
why_wrong.3: The Son is a tributary of the Ganga in Bihar but does not carry this name.

why_correct: The Ganga and Brahmaputra together form the Sundarbans delta, the largest in the world, spread across India and Bangladesh. It carries the world's largest mangrove forest.

why_wrong.0: The Godavari has a large delta on the east coast but a far smaller one.
why_wrong.1: The Krishna delta is smaller still, and adjoins the Godavari's.
why_wrong.3: The Mahanadi forms a delta in Odisha, again much smaller. The size follows from the two rivers' combined discharge and their vast silt load from the Himalayas.

why_correct: Dendrochronology is the study of tree rings, so it works on the remains of plants. Each year a tree adds a ring, and their widths give both a date and a record of past climate.

why_wrong.0: Furniture may be dated by the method, but only because it is made of wood, so the material studied is still the plant.
why_wrong.1: Animal remains are dated by other means, such as radiocarbon dating of bone.
why_wrong.2: Pottery is dated by thermoluminescence or by its style and stratigraphy. The clue is in the name: dendron is Greek for tree.

why_correct: The rock and pillar edicts of Ashoka, cut in the middle of the third century BCE, are the oldest deciphered inscriptions found in India. They were read for the first time in 1837, when James Prinsep worked out the Brahmi script, and they are the foundation of everything we know about the Mauryan empire from its own words.

why_wrong.1: The Allahabad inscription, the Prayag Prashasti composed by Harisena in praise of Samudragupta, dates from about 350 CE. It is also engraved on an Ashokan pillar, which is a useful reminder of which of the two came first.
why_wrong.2: The Mehrauli iron pillar inscription of Chandra dates from about 400 CE, some six and a half centuries later than the Ashokan edicts. The pillar is famous for resisting rust, not for its age, and this was the printed key.
why_wrong.3: The Aihole inscription of Pulakeshin the Second, composed by Ravikirti in 634 CE, is the latest of the four by a wide margin.

why_correct: The Mesopotamians invented writing first, developing cuneiform in Sumer around 3400 BCE. It began as pictographic records of grain and cattle pressed into clay with a reed stylus.

why_wrong.1: The Harappan script appeared around 2600 BCE, later than cuneiform, and it remains undeciphered.
why_wrong.2: Egyptian hieroglyphs appeared around 3200 BCE, close behind Mesopotamia but not first. These two are the pair to keep in order.
why_wrong.3: Mayan writing developed in Central America much later, in the first millennium BCE.

why_correct: Quintus Curtius Rufus, a Roman historian of the first century, wrote the Historiae Alexandri Magni, which covers Alexander's campaigns including his invasion of India and the battle against Porus.

why_wrong.0: Herodotus is the father of history but wrote of the Persian Wars, a century before Alexander was born.
why_wrong.1: Plato was a philosopher, and he died before Alexander's campaigns began.
why_wrong.3: Homer composed the Iliad and Odyssey, epics of the legendary Trojan War, centuries earlier.

why_correct: Statements two and four are true and one and three are false. Marx did urge intellectuals to join the working-class movement, and he interpreted history materially, through the economic base of society.

why_wrong.0: This makes statement one true, but Marx understood society from below, starting from the material conditions of production and the working class, not from above.
why_wrong.1: This adds statement three, but Marx was a critic of imperialism, not a champion of empire building.
why_wrong.2: This option lists statement four as both true and false, so it contradicts itself. Read each of the four statements against what you know before matching them to an option.

why_correct: Of the four travellers, Fa-Hien came earliest. The Chinese pilgrim visited India in the early fifth century, during the reign of Chandragupta II, and recorded what he saw in his account of the Buddhist kingdoms.

why_wrong.0: Jean-Baptiste Tavernier was a French jeweller who travelled in India in the seventeenth century, under the Mughals, so he is the latest of the four.
why_wrong.1: Taranath was a Tibetan Buddhist historian of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
why_wrong.3: Hiuen-Tsang came in the seventh century, during Harsha's reign, two hundred years after Fa-Hien. The two Chinese pilgrims are often confused, and Fa-Hien is the earlier.

why_correct: The Euphrates formed the traditional frontier between the Roman empire and the Iranian empires, first Parthian and later Sasanian. Control of the crossings was fought over for centuries.

why_wrong.0: The Danube was Rome's northern frontier, against the Germanic peoples.
why_wrong.1: The Nile flows through Egypt, which was a Roman province rather than a border with Iran.
why_wrong.3: The Tigris is the other great Mesopotamian river and lies further east, well inside Iranian territory for most of this period.

why_correct: All three worked together. Pressure on the frontiers and barbarian invasion strained the army, internal corruption weakened government, and economic trouble with debased coinage and inflation undermined the whole structure.

why_wrong.0: External pressure was severe, but the empire had survived invasions before when it was internally sound.
why_wrong.1: Internal mismanagement mattered greatly, but by itself it does not explain the collapse.
why_wrong.2: Economic troubles were serious, especially the debasement of the currency. Historians treat the decline as a case of several causes reinforcing one another, which is why all of the above is right.

why_correct: All three mention slavery. Hammurabi's Code regulates the treatment of slaves in Babylon, Homer's epics describe captives taken in war, and the Twelve Tables set out the legal position of slaves in early Rome.

why_wrong.0: The Code of Hammurabi does deal with slaves, but so do the others.
why_wrong.1: The Iliad and the Odyssey are full of slaves and war captives.
why_wrong.2: The Twelve Tables likewise cover them. The point the question makes is that slavery was near universal in the ancient world, which is why every one of these sources touches on it.

why_correct: Vespasian began the Colosseum around 72 CE, and it was completed under his son Titus in 80 CE. Its formal name, the Flavian Amphitheatre, comes from their dynasty.

why_wrong.0: Nero built the Golden House on the same site, and the Colosseum was deliberately raised over its lake as a gift back to the people.
why_wrong.1: Trajan built the forum and column that bear his name, a generation later.
why_wrong.2: Augustus was the first emperor, a century earlier, and is remembered for saying he found Rome brick and left it marble.

why_correct: Menander I, known in Indian sources as Milinda, is credited with the first gold coins issued in India. He ruled the largest of the Indo-Greek kingdoms and appears in the Buddhist text Milindapanha, which records his dialogue with the monk Nagasena.

why_wrong.0: Antimachus I was an earlier Indo-Greek ruler, known for his silver coinage and his portrait with a distinctive hat.
why_wrong.1: Demetrius I extended Greek rule into north-west India and is shown wearing an elephant-scalp headdress, but the gold issue is credited to Menander.
why_wrong.3: Apollodotus I ruled in the same region and issued bilingual silver coins in Greek and Kharosthi.

why_correct: Sparta and Athens were the two great city-states of ancient Greece, so statements one and two are true. Milan and Venice are Italian cities of a much later age, so three and four are false.

why_wrong.1: This reverses the truth, making the Greek cities false and the Italian ones Greek.
why_wrong.2: Venice is not a Greek city-state, and Athens certainly is.
why_wrong.3: Milan is not a Greek city-state, and Athens again is. Athens and Sparta are the two whose rivalry produced the Peloponnesian War, which fixes them firmly in Greece.

why_correct: Both statements are true and the reason does explain the assertion. Augustus ended a century of civil war, established the Pax Romana and presided over a flowering of literature and building, which is precisely why his age is called golden.

why_wrong.0: The assertion is correct, so this option fails at the first step.
why_wrong.2: Both are indeed correct, but this option stops short of saying the reason explains the assertion, and it plainly does. In assertion-reason questions the more precise correct option is the answer.
why_wrong.3: The reason is correct, not incorrect. Peace and stability after the civil wars are exactly what made the age prosperous.

why_correct: The passage says revolts were rare while escape was common, so slaves in ancient Greece preferred individual escape to collective rebellion. Scattered across many small households, they had little chance to organise together.

why_wrong.0: The passage says the opposite, that organised revolt was rare.
why_wrong.2: Contentment cannot be inferred from escape. Fleeing shows discontent, not satisfaction.
why_wrong.3: The passage states that slaves fled to obtain freedom, so the desire for it was clearly present. Answer a case-based question from the passage itself rather than from general knowledge.

why_correct: Aristotle wrote the Politics, in which he classified constitutions and called man a political animal. He also wrote the Nicomachean Ethics and the Poetics.

why_wrong.0: Thucydides wrote the History of the Peloponnesian War.
why_wrong.1: Herodotus wrote the Histories, on the Persian Wars.
why_wrong.2: Plato wrote The Republic and The Laws, which are also political works. Plato and Aristotle are teacher and pupil, and matching each to his titles is what the question tests.

why_correct: Cleisthenes is called the father of Athenian democracy. His reforms of 508 BCE reorganised the citizens into ten tribes cutting across old family loyalties, and gave real power to the assembly.

why_wrong.0: Aristotle analysed democracy as a philosopher and was in fact critical of it.
why_wrong.1: Plato was hostile to democracy, having seen it condemn his teacher to death.
why_wrong.2: Socrates was executed by the Athenian democracy in 399 BCE. Note that Solon's earlier reforms prepared the ground, but the title belongs to Cleisthenes.

why_correct: The sixteen Mahajanapadas are listed in the Anguttara Nikaya, a Buddhist text in the Pali canon. Jain sources such as the Bhagavati Sutra give a similar list.

why_wrong.0: The Ramayana is an epic and does not give this administrative list.
why_wrong.2: The Mahabharata is likewise epic rather than a record of the sixteen states.
why_wrong.3: The Gita is a philosophical dialogue within the Mahabharata. The list comes from Buddhist literature, which places it in the sixth century BCE, exactly when these states existed.

why_correct: Buddhist sources record both Bimbisara and Ajatashatru as lay followers of the Buddha. Bimbisara gave the Venuvana grove to the sangha, and Ajatashatru is said to have hosted the First Buddhist Council at Rajgir after the Buddha's death.

why_wrong.0: Mahavira was their contemporary, and Jain tradition also claims both kings, calling them Shrenika and Kunika. So this is not a baseless answer, and historians note that the two traditions compete for them. What the question asks for is the association recorded in the Buddhist canon, which is with the Buddha.
why_wrong.1: Parshvanatha was the twenty-third Jain Tirthankara and lived some two hundred and fifty years before these kings, so he cannot have been their teacher.
why_wrong.3: Both kings are firmly connected with the new religions of their day, so none of the above is wrong.

why_correct: The Mauryan empire had its centre in Magadha, with its capital at Pataliputra on the Ganga. Magadha's iron, its fertile land and its river routes had already made it the strongest of the Mahajanapadas.

why_wrong.0: Malwa in central India was a province rather than the centre.
why_wrong.2: Gandhara in the north-west was the frontier region, where Ashoka's inscriptions appear in Greek and Aramaic.
why_wrong.3: Kashi was an earlier Mahajanapada, absorbed by Magadha during its rise.

why_correct: Alexander fought Porus at the Battle of the Hydaspes in 326 BCE, on the river now called the Jhelum. Alexander won but was so impressed by Porus that he restored his kingdom to him.

why_wrong.0: The siege of Tyre in 332 BCE was in Phoenicia, on the Mediterranean coast.
why_wrong.1: The Battle of Issus in 333 BCE was against Darius III of Persia.
why_wrong.2: The Battle of Gaugamela in 331 BCE was the decisive defeat of Darius. All three came earlier, on Alexander's march east, and the Indian campaign is the last of them.

why_correct: Statements two and three are true and one and four are false. The Smritishastras were composed in this age and Kalidasa wrote then, but the medium of Gupta literature was Sanskrit, not Pali, and Latin never reached India.

why_wrong.0: This makes statement one true, but Pali belongs to the earlier Buddhist literature, whereas the Gupta age is the great age of Sanskrit.
why_wrong.1: This makes statement four true, but Latin was the language of Rome and had no currency in India.
why_wrong.2: This again accepts statement four. The quickest way through is to spot that Latin in India is impossible, which eliminates every option that calls statement four true.

why_correct: The passage states directly that the Ottoman emperors monitored their officials in order to maintain public welfare and progress. The answer to a case-based question must come from the passage itself.

why_wrong.1: Punishing corrupt officials would be a means of achieving the purpose, not the purpose itself, and the passage does not mention punishment.
why_wrong.2: Increasing tax is not mentioned, and it would conflict with the stated aim of public welfare.
why_wrong.3: Reducing administrative cost is not mentioned either. When a passage names the purpose in so many words, resist the option that sounds more sophisticated.

why_correct: Idealism holds that reality is ultimately spiritual and that the individual is part of a universal mind or spirit. On that view the child is an integral part of the ultimate universe, and education draws out the spiritual self already present.

why_wrong.0: Realism holds that the material world exists independently of the mind, and treats the child as one object among others in it.
why_wrong.1: Pragmatism judges ideas by their practical consequences and sees no fixed ultimate reality to be part of.
why_wrong.2: Existentialism begins from the individual's own freedom and choice, and resists absorbing the person into any larger whole.

why_correct: Rabindranath Tagore taught that education must take place in communion with nature. At Santiniketan classes were held in the open air under the trees, because he believed a child shut indoors is cut off from the source of learning.

why_wrong.0: Vivekananda's emphasis was on man-making education and the manifestation of inner perfection.
why_wrong.1: Sri Aurobindo taught integral education, aiming at the full development of the physical, vital, mental and spiritual being.
why_wrong.3: Gandhi's Basic Education centred on a productive craft and the mother tongue. All four are Indian educationists, so the phrase itself is the clue.

why_correct: Naturalism advocates discipline by natural or direct consequences, an idea from Rousseau. A child who breaks a window and must sit in the cold learns from the consequence itself rather than from punishment.

why_wrong.0: Existentialism emphasises self-chosen responsibility rather than a scheme of consequences.
why_wrong.1: Pragmatism favours social discipline, learnt through group activity and shared purpose.
why_wrong.3: Realism favours discipline through training and habit formation. Each philosophy has its own view of discipline, and natural consequences belong to the naturalists.

why_correct: Epistemology is the theory of knowledge, dealing with what knowledge is, where it comes from and how it is validated. A teacher whose business is to promote knowledge is therefore directly concerned with it.

why_wrong.0: Values are the province of axiology, which shapes the aims of education rather than its content.
why_wrong.1: Truth is close, and epistemology certainly examines it, but the teacher's day-to-day aim is stated as promoting knowledge, which is the wider term.
why_wrong.3: Skills matter in teaching, but the branch of philosophy that studies them is not epistemology in the first instance.

why_correct: Caste is named the major constraint on social change in India because it is a hereditary structure that fixes status, occupation and marriage from birth, and it resists change from within rather than merely slowing it.

why_wrong.1: Education is an agent of social change rather than a constraint on it, which makes it the odd one out here.
why_wrong.2: Religion can obstruct change where it sanctions custom, so it is a genuine constraint. But religious belief itself has also driven reform, from Buddha to the Brahmo Samaj, so its effect runs both ways.
why_wrong.3: Poverty is a real barrier too, and it keeps people from schooling and mobility. It is, however, a condition that change aims to remove, whereas caste is the structure that has most persistently resisted removal.

why_correct: Buddhist education admitted students by interest and aptitude rather than by birth, opening the monasteries to all castes. That openness is one of the ways Buddhism broke with the Vedic order.

why_wrong.0: Islamic education was organised in maktabs and madrasas around religious instruction.
why_wrong.1: Vedic education restricted study of the Vedas by caste, with the upper varnas alone admitted.
why_wrong.3: Jainistic education was also open in spirit, but the phrase and the practice described here belong to the Buddhist system, with its great universities at Nalanda and Taxila.

why_correct: Albert Bandura's social learning theory is also called observational learning or modelling. His Bobo doll experiment showed that children copy behaviour they have merely watched, without being rewarded for it themselves.

why_wrong.0: Insight learning is Kohler's, demonstrated with chimpanzees who solved a problem suddenly rather than by trial and error.
why_wrong.2: Sign learning is Tolman's theory, in which the learner builds a cognitive map of signs leading to goals.
why_wrong.3: Verbal learning concerns the acquisition of words and associations, studied by Ebbinghaus among others.

why_correct: Pragmatism judges education by its usefulness in life, so it favours a vocational and activity-based curriculum. Learning by doing is its central method, and Dewey is its leading figure.

why_wrong.0: Realism emphasises scientific knowledge and the study of the material world.
why_wrong.1: Naturalism emphasises free growth according to the child's own nature, without imposed ends.
why_wrong.3: Idealism emphasises the humanities, moral and spiritual values, and would regard a purely vocational aim as too narrow.

why_correct: The aim of idealistic education is self-realisation, that is the full unfolding of the spiritual self and its union with the ultimate reality. All other aims are subordinate to it.

why_wrong.1: Physical development is stressed by naturalism, which begins from the body and the senses.
why_wrong.2: Intuition is valued in idealism, but as a means of apprehending reality rather than as the aim.
why_wrong.3: Practical usefulness is the pragmatist aim, and idealism is often criticised for neglecting it.

why_graced: This question has been graced: every candidate receives the mark, whatever they wrote and even if they left it blank. Jainism has the five great vows, the pancha mahavrata, and Buddhism has the five precepts, the panchashila, and both are literally five principles of conduct. Jainism was the intended answer, but Buddhism cannot honestly be called wrong, so the question was withdrawn from scoring.

why_wrong.0: Buddhism has the panchashila, the five precepts binding on every lay follower: to abstain from killing, from stealing, from sexual misconduct, from false speech and from intoxicants. That is a set of five principles of conduct, so this option is defensible as printed.
why_wrong.1: The Vedic tradition has no comparable fixed set of five rules of conduct. Its ethical scheme runs through the purusharthas and the duties of the ashramas, which are four, not five.
why_wrong.2: Jainism has the pancha mahavrata: ahimsa, satya, asteya, brahmacharya and aparigraha. This is the answer the setter intended, and it is correct.
why_wrong.3: Islam has the five pillars, but those are obligations of faith and worship, the creed, prayer, alms, fasting and the pilgrimage, rather than the ethical restraints the phrase principles of conduct points to. That a third option can be argued for at all is a further reason the question was withdrawn.

why_correct: Swami Vivekananda defined education as the manifestation of the perfection already existing in man. The teacher does not add anything but removes what obstructs, as a gardener does not make the plant grow but removes the weeds.

why_wrong.0: Gandhi defined education as an all-round drawing out of the best in child and man, in body, mind and spirit.
why_wrong.2: Tagore stressed harmony with nature and freedom of the creative spirit.
why_wrong.3: Sri Aurobindo taught integral education towards a higher consciousness. All four are close in spirit, so the exact wording must be matched to its author.

why_correct: Epistemology is the branch of philosophy dealing with the nature, sources and validity of knowledge. It asks what we can know and how we come to know it.

why_wrong.1: Metaphysics deals with the nature of ultimate reality, asking what exists rather than how we know it.
why_wrong.2: Logic deals with the principles of valid reasoning and correct inference.
why_wrong.3: Ethics deals with right and wrong conduct, and belongs with aesthetics under axiology.

why_correct: John Locke denied innate ideas in his Essay Concerning Human Understanding, arguing that all knowledge comes from experience through sensation and reflection. He is the founder of British empiricism.

why_wrong.1: David Hume was an empiricist too and pushed the position further into scepticism, but the explicit attack on innate ideas is Locke's.
why_wrong.2: Descartes maintained the opposite, holding that certain ideas such as God and extension are innate.
why_wrong.3: Leibniz also defended innate ideas, replying directly to Locke in his New Essays. The rationalists affirm innate ideas and the empiricists deny them, and that is the divide being tested.

why_correct: John Locke described the mind at birth as a tabula rasa, a blank slate on which experience writes. It is the same doctrine as the denial of innate ideas, stated as an image.

why_wrong.0: Bishop Berkeley held that to be is to be perceived, a form of subjective idealism.
why_wrong.2: Hume analysed the mind into impressions and ideas and denied a permanent self, which is a further step rather than this one.
why_wrong.3: John Stuart Mill was a utilitarian and a logician of the following century.

why_correct: Descartes took mathematics as the model of certain knowledge, because its truths are clear, distinct and independent of the senses. He built his whole method on that ideal.

why_wrong.0: Christian Wolff systematised Leibniz's philosophy but is not the source of this claim.
why_wrong.1: Spinoza wrote his Ethics in geometrical form, so he certainly admired mathematical method, but the doctrine is credited to Descartes.
why_wrong.3: Leibniz was a great mathematician and co-inventor of the calculus, yet the statement belongs to Descartes.

why_correct: The playground is an informal agency of education. There is no syllabus and no teacher, yet a child learns cooperation, fair play, leadership and how to lose, simply by playing.

why_wrong.1: A library is part of the formal system, organised deliberately to support study.
why_wrong.2: A seminar is a planned academic meeting, so it is formal.
why_wrong.3: A classroom is the most formal agency of all. The test is whether the learning is planned and deliberate, and only the playground's is not.

why_correct: Charvaka is materialist and holds that man is nothing but the physical body, formed from the four elements. Consciousness arises from that combination and ends with it, so there is no soul surviving death.

why_wrong.1: A self distinct from the body is what Charvaka expressly denies.
why_wrong.2: Consciousness for Charvaka is a property that emerges from matter, like the intoxicating power that arises when ingredients ferment, not an independent reality.
why_wrong.3: Charvaka has a definite answer here, so none of these is wrong.

why_correct: For Shankara the Self is Brahman, exactly as the mahavakya ayam atma brahma declares. And Brahman is eternal, without birth or death, and transcendent, beyond the whole empirical world. So each of the three descriptions is true of the Self, and All of These is the only complete answer.

why_wrong.0: Brahman is a true description of the Self and is the heart of Shankara's teaching, and it was the printed key. But it is not the whole of what the options offer. When a question ends with All of These, test every statement before settling on the first true one.
why_wrong.1: Eternal is likewise true. The Self is unborn, undying and unchanging. But by itself it is incomplete.
why_wrong.2: Transcendent is also true, since the Self as Brahman is beyond the world of name and form. Again incomplete on its own.

why_correct: Charvaka accepts perception alone as a valid means of knowledge and rejects both inference and testimony, because neither can be verified by the senses. That is what makes it the most radical of the Indian schools.

why_wrong.0: Inference is rejected, but so is testimony, so naming only one is incomplete.
why_wrong.1: Testimony is rejected as well, and for the same reason.
why_wrong.3: Charvaka certainly challenges both. Its whole epistemology reduces to pratyaksha, direct perception, which is why it can deny the soul, God and life after death.

why_correct: Liberation in Buddhism is nirvana, the extinction of craving and thereby of suffering and rebirth. The word literally means blowing out, as of a flame.

why_wrong.1: Moksha is the term used in Hindu philosophy for release from the cycle of birth and death.
why_wrong.2: Mukti is another Hindu term for the same release, used interchangeably with moksha.
why_wrong.3: There is a proper term, so none of these is wrong. Each tradition has its own word, and matching word to tradition is what the question tests.

why_correct: Jainism prescribes all three. Penance burns away accumulated karma, self-control prevents new karma from binding, and detachment from possessions and passions frees the soul. Together they lead to liberation.

why_wrong.0: Penance, or tapas, is essential in Jainism but is only one part of the path.
why_wrong.1: Self-control through the vows is likewise necessary but not sufficient by itself.
why_wrong.2: Detachment, aparigraha, is the third element. Since each is genuinely required, all of these is the answer, and the path is often summed up as the Three Jewels of right faith, right knowledge and right conduct.

why_correct: Charvaka neglects liberation altogether. Being materialist, it denies the soul and rebirth, so there is nothing to be liberated and nothing to be liberated from. Its aim is pleasure in this life.

why_wrong.1: Jainism makes liberation central, achieved by shedding karma until the soul rises to the top of the universe.
why_wrong.2: Buddhism makes nirvana its whole purpose, set out in the Four Noble Truths.
why_wrong.3: Vedanta makes moksha the highest of the four ends of life. Charvaka is the one Indian school that rejects the framework entirely, which is why it is called nastika in the strongest sense.

why_correct: Swami Vivekananda held that all knowledge, material and spiritual, is already within us and is merely veiled by ignorance. It follows that education uncovers rather than supplies.

why_wrong.0: Tagore's emphasis was on freedom, nature and creative expression.
why_wrong.2: Gandhi's emphasis was on craft, character and self-reliance.
why_wrong.3: Plato held that learning is recollection of what the soul knew before birth, which is a genuinely similar doctrine from another tradition. The Indian phrasing about the curtain of ignorance is Vivekananda's.

why_correct: Rabindranath Tagore founded Santiniketan, beginning with a school in 1901 that grew into Visva-Bharati University in 1921. Teaching there was done in the open air, in close contact with nature.

why_wrong.1: Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission.
why_wrong.2: Gandhi founded Sabarmati and Sevagram ashrams and the scheme of Basic Education.
why_wrong.3: Sri Aurobindo founded the ashram at Pondicherry and its Centre of Education.

why_correct: The Vedic view is that creation is without beginning and without end, an eternal cycle of creation, preservation and dissolution repeating without a first moment or a last.

why_wrong.0: Without beginning is only half the doctrine, and leaving out the second half changes the meaning.
why_wrong.1: Without an end is the other half, and it is equally incomplete on its own.
why_wrong.3: Creation at a particular moment is the view of the Semitic traditions, and it is precisely what the cyclical Vedic conception denies.

why_correct: A State has four essential elements: population, territory, government and sovereignty. Religion is not among them, and a State may have any religion or none, as a secular State does.

why_wrong.0: Population is essential; there can be no State without people.
why_wrong.1: Government is essential, being the machinery through which the State acts.
why_wrong.2: Sovereignty is essential, and it is what distinguishes a State from any other association. Territory is the fourth, and it is the one missing from this list of options.

why_correct: Pluralists hold that sovereignty is not the monopoly of the State but is shared among the many associations to which people belong: churches, trade unions, universities and local bodies. Laski and MacIver argued this against the monistic view.

why_wrong.0: Absolute and indivisible sovereignty is the monistic theory of Bodin, Hobbes and Austin, which pluralism was framed to attack.
why_wrong.2: Sovereignty held only by the monarch is the doctrine of divine right and absolute monarchy.
why_wrong.3: Sovereignty exercised only by the judiciary describes no theory, and would make the courts supreme over the legislature.

why_correct: Thomas Hobbes is most closely associated with the State of Nature, which he described in Leviathan as a war of every man against every man, where life was solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short.

why_wrong.0: Karl Marx explained the State as an instrument of class domination and predicted its withering away.
why_wrong.2: J. S. Mill wrote on liberty and representative government, not on a pre-political condition.
why_wrong.3: T. H. Green was an idealist who saw the State as removing obstacles to the good life. Locke and Rousseau also used the term, but of the four names offered only Hobbes belongs to that tradition.

why_correct: Individualists describe the State as a necessary evil. They hold that its interference restricts liberty, so it is an evil, but that it is needed to maintain order and protect rights, so it is necessary.

why_wrong.1: Idealists such as Hegel and Green regard the State as a positive good and even as the march of God on earth.
why_wrong.2: Socialists want the State to do more, not less, in order to secure economic equality.
why_wrong.3: Fascists glorify the State absolutely, holding that the individual exists for it.

why_correct: The Social Contract Theory explains the State as arising from an agreement among people who left the state of nature to secure order. Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau each gave their own version of it.

why_wrong.0: The Force Theory holds that the State arose from conquest by the strong.
why_wrong.1: The Divine Origin Theory holds that the State was created by God and the ruler is His representative.
why_wrong.3: The Evolutionary Theory holds that the State grew gradually from the family, without any single founding act.

why_correct: Rousseau located sovereignty in the General Will, the will of the community aiming at the common good. It is not the mere sum of individual wills but what all would will as citizens.

why_wrong.0: Hobbes placed sovereignty in an absolute ruler to whom people surrendered all rights.
why_wrong.1: Locke placed ultimate authority with the people but expressed it through a limited government and the right of resistance, not through a general will.
why_wrong.3: Austin placed sovereignty in a determinate human superior whose commands are habitually obeyed.

why_correct: John Austin gave the legal or monistic theory of sovereignty, defining the sovereign as a determinate human superior who receives habitual obedience and owes it to no one else. Law, for him, is the sovereign's command.

why_wrong.0: Harold Laski was the leading pluralist and a critic of exactly this theory.
why_wrong.1: J. A. Hobson wrote on imperialism and economics.
why_wrong.3: MacIver was a sociologist who also criticised the monistic view and distinguished the State from society.

why_correct: The external aspect of sovereignty is independence from foreign control, meaning the State is free to conduct its own affairs and is not subject to any other State.

why_wrong.0: Law-making power is internal, exercised over the State's own people and territory.
why_wrong.1: Taxation is likewise an internal power.
why_wrong.3: Judicial authority is internal too. The division is simply direction: inward over its own subjects, outward against other States.

why_correct: The Force Theory holds that the State originated in conquest, the strong subduing the weak and imposing their rule. War, said the theory's critics, made the king and the king made war.

why_wrong.0: Origin from the family is the Evolutionary or Patriarchal theory.
why_wrong.1: Creation by divine command is the Divine Origin Theory.
why_wrong.3: Gradual evolution is again the Evolutionary Theory, which is the modern and most accepted explanation.

why_correct: Sir Henry Maine is the chief exponent of the Evolutionary Theory, tracing the growth of the State from family to gens, tribe and finally State, and describing the movement from status to contract.

why_wrong.1: Rousseau is a social contract theorist.
why_wrong.2: Austin gave the legal theory of sovereignty, not an account of the State's origin.
why_wrong.3: Bodin first systematised the concept of sovereignty in the sixteenth century.

why_correct: Locke supported limited government. He held that people surrender only some rights, that the government is a trustee bound by natural law, and that people may resist it if it breaks the trust.

why_wrong.0: Hobbes argued for an absolute sovereign, since only unlimited power could prevent a return to the war of all against all.
why_wrong.2: Mussolini founded fascism, which subordinates the individual entirely to the State.
why_wrong.3: Austin's sovereign is legally unlimited and subject to no restraint. Hobbes and Locke are the pair to keep straight: both use the contract, but reach opposite conclusions about how much power the ruler should have.

why_correct: Popular sovereignty means that ultimate authority rests with the people, from whom all governmental power is derived. The Indian Constitution opens with We, the people of India, on that principle.

why_wrong.0: Sovereignty in the king is monarchical sovereignty, defended by the divine right theory.
why_wrong.2: Sovereignty in Parliament alone is legal sovereignty, as in the British doctrine. Popular sovereignty lies behind it, since Parliament is elected.
why_wrong.3: Sovereignty in the military describes a dictatorship, which is the negation of the idea.

why_correct: The Divine Origin Theory rests on faith rather than evidence. It cannot be tested historically, and it was largely abandoned once the Reformation, the rise of science and democratic ideas undermined it.

why_wrong.0: The Evolutionary Theory is supported by anthropological and historical evidence of tribal societies developing into States.
why_wrong.1: The Force Theory has considerable historical support, since many States were indeed founded by conquest.
why_wrong.3: The Social Contract Theory is criticised as unhistorical, which makes it a fair guess, but it is at least argued from reason rather than from faith.

why_correct: Hegel regarded the State as an ethical institution, the highest expression of the moral idea, in which the individual realises true freedom. His idealism was later developed by T. H. Green and Bosanquet.

why_wrong.1: Locke saw the State as a limited trustee for protecting life, liberty and property.
why_wrong.2: Bentham was a utilitarian and judged the State by whether it produced the greatest happiness of the greatest number.
why_wrong.3: Laski was a pluralist who denied the State any such moral supremacy over other associations.

why_correct: Political sovereignty in a democracy rests with the electorate, the body of voters behind the legal sovereign. Their verdict at elections is the power that legal authority must ultimately answer to.

why_wrong.1: The army is subordinate to civilian authority in a democracy.
why_wrong.2: The bureaucracy executes policy but does not make or legitimise it.
why_wrong.3: The judiciary interprets the law. Legal sovereignty lies with the law-making body and political sovereignty behind it with the voters, and that pairing is what the question tests.

why_correct: Sovereignty is inalienable, meaning it cannot be given away, and territory is not one of its characteristics at all. Transferability of territory is therefore not a feature of sovereignty.

why_wrong.0: Permanence is a genuine feature: sovereignty lasts as long as the State does, whoever governs.
why_wrong.1: Absoluteness is a feature in the monistic theory, meaning the sovereign is subject to no higher legal power.
why_wrong.2: Universality within the territory is a feature, since sovereignty extends over every person and association inside the State. Alongside these go indivisibility, inalienability and exclusiveness.

why_correct: Locke wrote to justify constitutional, limited government, and his Two Treatises defended the English Glorious Revolution of 1688. His ideas later shaped the American Declaration of Independence.

why_wrong.0: Absolute monarchy is what Hobbes's version of the contract justified, and what Locke was arguing against.
why_wrong.2: Military rule finds no support anywhere in Locke.
why_wrong.3: Theocracy is government by religious authority, which Locke opposed in his Letter Concerning Toleration.

why_correct: Aristotle defined the State in his Politics as a union of families and villages having for its end a perfect and self-sufficing life. He held that the State comes into being for life and continues for the good life.

why_wrong.1: Plato described an ideal state in The Republic built on justice and the division of classes, but this definition is Aristotle's.
why_wrong.2: Rousseau wrote of the general will and the social contract.
why_wrong.3: T. H. Green defined the State as removing hindrances to the good life, which is a related idea from a much later idealist.

why_correct: The Divine Origin Theory supported absolute monarchy, since a king who ruled by God's will was answerable to God alone and could not be resisted or judged by his subjects.

why_wrong.0: Democracy rests on popular sovereignty, which is the opposite claim.
why_wrong.1: Constitutionalism means limited government under law, which divine right rejects.
why_wrong.3: Socialism concerns economic organisation and arose centuries later. James I of England and Louis XIV of France are the standard examples of rulers who invoked the theory.

why_correct: Commercial sovereignty is not a recognised form. The forms discussed in political science are legal, political, popular, de jure, de facto and titular sovereignty.

why_wrong.0: Legal sovereignty is the authority recognised by law to issue commands.
why_wrong.1: Political sovereignty is the power behind the legal sovereign, in modern States the electorate.
why_wrong.2: Popular sovereignty is the doctrine that ultimate authority rests with the people. Trade and commerce are regulated by a sovereign State, but they are not a kind of sovereignty.

why_correct: Austin held that in every political society there is a determinate human superior who receives habitual obedience from the bulk of the people and renders obedience to no one. That obedience is the mark of sovereignty.

why_wrong.1: People's participation belongs to popular sovereignty, and Austin's theory is legal rather than democratic.
why_wrong.2: Group autonomy is the pluralist position, framed in opposition to Austin.
why_wrong.3: International cooperation limits sovereignty in practice, and Austin's theory makes no room for it. His three key terms are determinate, habitual obedience and legally unlimited.

why_correct: The chief criticism of Hobbes is that his contract justifies absolute authority. People surrender all their rights irrevocably to a sovereign who is party to no agreement, leaving them no right of resistance however tyrannical he becomes.

why_wrong.0: Hobbes does not promote democracy. He preferred monarchy as the most effective form of absolute rule.
why_wrong.2: He does not oppose sovereignty; he makes it unlimited.
why_wrong.3: Pluralism is the opposite of his position, which concentrates all authority in one sovereign.

why_correct: Harold Laski was the strongest critic of the monistic theory. He argued that the State is only one association among many and has no moral right to unlimited obedience, and that in reality power is federal and divided.

why_wrong.0: Bodin founded the monistic theory in the sixteenth century.
why_wrong.1: Austin gave it its classic legal statement.
why_wrong.3: Hobbes gave it its philosophical defence. The other three built the theory; Laski attacked it.

why_correct: The evolutionary explanation holds that the State grew gradually out of the family, kinship, religion, war and political consciousness working together over long ages. It is the explanation historians and anthropologists accept.

why_wrong.0: Creation in a single event describes the social contract theory, and evolution denies any such founding moment.
why_wrong.2: Foundation by God is the divine origin theory.
why_wrong.3: Military conquest alone is the force theory. Force did play a part in evolution, but as one factor among several rather than the whole explanation.

why_correct: Jean Bodin first gave a systematic account of sovereignty in his Six Books of the Commonwealth in 1576, defining it as supreme power over citizens and subjects, unrestrained by law.

why_wrong.1: Aristotle wrote on the State and its forms but had no developed concept of sovereignty, which is a modern idea tied to the nation-state.
why_wrong.2: Marx analysed the State in class terms in the nineteenth century.
why_wrong.3: T. H. Green was a nineteenth-century idealist. The sequence to remember runs Bodin, then Hobbes, then Austin.

why_correct: Accounting is the process of identifying, recording, classifying and summarising financial transactions, and then communicating the results. Recording is the step the other three depend on.

why_wrong.0: Selling goods is a business activity. Accounting records the sale; it does not make it.
why_wrong.2: Manufacturing is production. It creates transactions for accounting to record, but is not accounting itself.
why_wrong.3: Advertising is marketing. Note the pattern: the three wrong options are all things a business does, while accounting is how a business keeps track of what it did.

why_correct: The business entity concept treats the business as separate and distinct from its owner. That is why the owner's capital is shown as a liability of the business, and why drawings are recorded at all.

why_wrong.0: The money measurement concept says only what can be expressed in money is recorded, which is why staff morale never appears in the books.
why_wrong.2: The cost concept records assets at their purchase price rather than their market value.
