why_wrong.0: High temperature and low pressure is precisely when a real gas behaves most nearly ideally, so this has it exactly backwards.
why_wrong.2: High temperature works against deviation, because fast molecules are little affected by attractions.
why_wrong.3: Low pressure works against deviation too, since the molecules are then far apart. Both conditions must push the molecules together for deviation to show.

why_correct: Hydrogen peroxide can act both ways. Oxygen in it is in the intermediate minus one state, so it can be reduced to minus two, making peroxide an oxidising agent, or oxidised to zero, making it a reducing agent.

why_wrong.0: Oxidising is only half the truth. Against a stronger oxidising agent such as potassium permanganate, peroxide is itself oxidised and gives off oxygen.
why_wrong.1: Reducing is likewise only half. Against iodide, peroxide is the oxidising agent.
why_wrong.3: One of the options is correct. The general rule is that an element in an intermediate oxidation state can usually go either way.

why_correct: Silicon tetrachloride hydrolyses rapidly because silicon has vacant d orbitals that let water attack it. The product is silicic acid, together with hydrogen chloride.

why_wrong.0: Silica, SiO2, is what remains after silicic acid is strongly heated and loses water. It is a later product, not the immediate one.
why_wrong.1: Silica gel is a dried, porous form of silica used as a drying agent, further along the same path.
why_wrong.3: Silicon carbide is made by heating silica with carbon at very high temperature and has nothing to do with hydrolysis. Note the contrast with carbon tetrachloride, which does not hydrolyse because carbon has no d orbitals.

why_correct: A minus B is the part of A outside B, so the union is that part together with all of B, with no overlap between them. That gives n of A union B equal to 47 plus 326, which is 373.

why_wrong.0: 173 is far too small. The union must be at least as large as B alone, which is already 326.
why_wrong.1: 273 is likewise smaller than B, so it can be ruled out without any calculation.
why_wrong.3: There is a correct option, so none of these does not apply. Note that n of A is not needed at all here, and it is offered to tempt you into adding 115 and 326.

why_correct: Statement 1 is true, since removing B from A removes exactly the elements of A that lie in B. Statement 2 is true, because every element of A either lies in B or does not. Statement 3 is false, so only 1 and 2 hold.

why_wrong.0: This includes statement 3, which is wrong. The correct identity is A minus B union C equals A minus B intersection A minus C, with an intersection rather than a union. This is one of De Morgan's laws for sets.
why_wrong.1: Statement 2 is true, but so is statement 1, so only 2 is too narrow.
why_wrong.2: This again accepts statement 3. Test it with a small example: take A as 1 and 2, B as 1 and C as 2, and the two sides come out different.

why_correct: The domain of a relation is the set of first elements of its ordered pairs. Those first elements here are 1, 2 and 2, so the domain is the set containing 1 and 2.

why_wrong.1: 2 and 3 mixes a first element with a second. 3 appears only as a second element, so it belongs to the range.
why_wrong.2: 1 and 3 makes the same mistake with 3.
why_wrong.3: The whole of A would be the domain only if every element of A appeared as a first element, but 3 never does. The domain is a subset of A, not necessarily all of it.

why_correct: The range is the set of second elements. Those are b, c and c, so the range is the set containing b and c.

why_wrong.0: a and b takes a as a range element, but a appears only in the first position, so it is in the domain.
why_wrong.2: a and c makes the same error with a.
why_wrong.3: All three would require a to appear as a second element somewhere, and it never does. Domain and range are read from opposite sides of the pairs.

why_correct: Since cosec is the reciprocal of sin, a number plus its reciprocal equals 2 only when that number is 1. So sin theta is 1, and 1 to the hundredth plus 1 to the hundredth is 2.

why_wrong.1: 2 to the power 100 would come from raising the whole given expression to the hundredth power, which is not what the question asks.
why_wrong.2: 2 to the power 99 is another version of the same mistake.
why_wrong.3: There is a correct option. The key insight is that x plus 1 over x is at least 2 for positive x, with equality only at x equal to 1, so the condition pins sin theta exactly.

why_correct: If 8 theta is pi then 7 theta is pi minus theta, and cos of pi minus theta is minus cos theta. So the sum is minus cos theta plus cos theta, which is 0.

why_wrong.1: Minus 1 would need the two terms to differ by 1 rather than cancel. They are exact opposites.
why_wrong.2: 1 would need them to be equal and each a half, which they are not.
why_wrong.3: 2 would need both to equal 1, which would require theta to be 0, contradicting 8 theta equal to pi. Using the supplementary identity is quicker than evaluating cos of pi over 8.

why_correct: sin of 180 plus theta is minus sin theta, and sin of 180 minus theta is plus sin theta. Their product is minus sin squared theta, and multiplying by cosec squared theta, which is 1 over sin squared theta, gives minus 1.

why_wrong.0: 0 would need one of the factors to vanish, but none does for general theta.
why_wrong.2: 1 comes from getting both signs positive. Only one of the two shifts changes the sign of sine: adding 180 does, subtracting from 180 does not.
why_wrong.3: There is a definite answer, so none of these is wrong.

why_correct: From alpha plus beta equal to pi over 2 we get alpha equal to pi over 2 minus beta, and putting that into beta plus gamma equal to alpha gives gamma equal to pi over 2 minus 2 beta. So tan gamma is cot 2 beta. Writing t for tan beta, cot 2 beta is one minus t squared over 2t, so tan beta plus twice tan gamma is t plus one minus t squared over t, which collapses to one over t. And one over tan beta is cot beta, which is tan of pi over 2 minus beta, that is tan alpha. Check it with beta equal to 20 degrees: alpha is 70 and gamma is 50, tan alpha is 2.747, and tan 20 plus twice tan 50 is 0.364 plus 2.384, which is 2.747.

why_wrong.0: Twice tan beta plus twice tan gamma doubles both terms. At beta equal to 20 degrees it gives 3.111 against the true value 2.747.
why_wrong.2: Twice tan beta plus tan gamma puts the factor 2 on the wrong term. Beware of testing this one at beta equal to 30 degrees, because then gamma is also 30 and the two expressions happen to agree by accident. Take beta equal to 20 instead and it gives 1.920 against 2.747. When you check an identity numerically, avoid the angle that makes two of the quantities equal.
why_wrong.3: Tan beta plus tan gamma is what you get if the factor 2 is dropped altogether. At beta equal to 20 degrees it gives 1.556, not 2.747.

why_correct: Multiplying by minus 1 rotates a complex number by half a turn. If the argument of z is negative, lying between minus pi and 0, then adding pi keeps the result within the principal range, so the difference of the arguments is pi.

why_wrong.1: Minus pi would be the answer if the argument of z were positive, since then pi would have to be subtracted to stay in the principal range. That is why the question specifies a negative argument.
why_wrong.2: Pi over 2 is a quarter turn, which corresponds to multiplying by i, not by minus 1.
why_wrong.3: Minus pi over 2 is a quarter turn the other way.

why_correct: The modulus is a distance, so the condition says z is nearer to 4 than to 2. The dividing line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them, at 3, and the nearer side to 4 is where the real part exceeds 3.

why_wrong.0: The real part being greater than 0 is far too wide. The point 1, for instance, satisfies it but is nearer to 2 than to 4.
why_wrong.1: The real part being less than 0 is on the wrong side altogether.
why_wrong.3: Greater than 2 includes points between 2 and 3, which are still nearer to 2. The boundary is the midpoint of 2 and 4, which is 3, not 2.

why_correct: The number minus 4 lies on the negative real axis, so its amplitude, measured from the positive real axis, is pi.

why_wrong.0: Pi over 2 is the positive imaginary axis, which would be a purely imaginary number such as 4i.
why_wrong.1: Pi over 3 would need equal-signed real and imaginary parts in a particular ratio, but this number has no imaginary part at all.
why_wrong.3: Pi over 6 likewise requires an imaginary part. Sketching the point on the Argand plane settles this immediately.

why_correct: The sum of the roots is 5, so beta is 5 minus alpha. Putting that into 3 alpha plus 2 beta equal to 12 gives alpha equal to 2, so beta is 3, and K is the product, 6.

why_wrong.0: 5 is the sum of the roots, not their product. The coefficient of x gives the sum and the constant gives the product.
why_wrong.2: 8 would need roots multiplying to 8 and adding to 5, and no such pair satisfies the extra condition.
why_wrong.3: 10 similarly fails. Check any answer by confirming that both the sum condition and the given relation hold.

why_correct: For every real x, x squared is at least 0 and 3 times the modulus of x is at least 0, so the left side is at least 2 and can never be 0. There are no real solutions.

why_wrong.1: 1 would require the expression to touch zero exactly once, but its smallest value is 2, at x equal to 0.
why_wrong.2: 2 is what you would get by treating this as x squared plus 3x plus 2, forgetting the modulus. That version does have two roots, minus 1 and minus 2, but both are negative and the modulus rules them out.
why_wrong.3: 4 would be the count if the modulus produced two quadratics each with two roots, but neither branch has real roots here.

why_correct: Let the roots be alpha and 2 alpha. Their sum is 3 alpha, which equals minus 2b over a, and their product is 2 alpha squared, which equals c over a. Eliminating alpha between the two gives 8b squared equal to 9ac.

why_wrong.0: 4b squared equal to ac has the wrong numerical factors. Both the 3 from the sum and the 2 from the product must survive into the final relation.
why_wrong.1: 4b squared equal to 3ac is the result of squaring only part of the substitution.
why_wrong.2: b squared equal to 9ac drops the factor from the doubled root in the product. A useful check is that the relation must reduce correctly when the two roots are equal, which is a separate condition.

why_graced: This question has been graced: every candidate receives the mark, whatever they wrote and even if they left it blank. The double inequality splits into two. From 2x minus 5 less than or equal to 5x plus 4 we get minus 9 less than or equal to 3x, that is x greater than or equal to minus 3. From 5x plus 4 strictly less than 19 we get 5x less than 15, that is x strictly less than 3. So the solution over the integers is minus 3 less than or equal to x less than 3, which is the integers from minus 3 to 2. The paper prints no option that says this, because the intended option writes the right hand end as less than or equal to 3 and so wrongly admits x equal to 3. The printed paper was checked and it really does print the strict sign, so the question was withdrawn from scoring.

why_wrong.0: Minus 2 less than or equal to x less than or equal to 3 is wrong at both ends. The left hand inequality gives minus 3, not minus 2, and the right hand one is strict.
why_wrong.1: Minus 2 less than or equal to x less than 23 has the strictness right but both numbers wrong. The 23 comes from mishandling the right hand inequality.
why_wrong.2: Minus 3 less than or equal to x less than or equal to 4 has the left hand end right but stretches the right hand end well past 3. Substituting x equal to 4 gives 24, which is not less than 19.
why_wrong.3: Minus 3 less than or equal to x less than or equal to 3 is the intended answer and is correct except for one integer. Put x equal to 3 into the middle expression: 5 times 3 plus 4 is 19, and the question demands strictly less than 19, so 3 is not a solution.

why_correct: The first inequality gives x between minus 4 and 6. The second gives x at most minus 2 or at least 2. Both must hold, so the answer is the part of minus 4 to 6 that survives, namely minus 4 to minus 2 together with 2 to 6.

why_wrong.0: The symbol here is intersection, but those two intervals have no point in common, so the intersection would be empty. The two pieces are joined by union.
why_wrong.2: The empty set is wrong, since x equal to 3 satisfies both conditions.
why_wrong.3: Only the negative piece leaves out the whole of 2 to 6, which also satisfies both. The modulus condition on x alone splits into two branches, and both must be kept.

why_correct: The inequality says the modulus of x minus 4 is less than 2, which gives x between 2 and 6. Since x equal to 4 is excluded by the question, the solution is 2 to 4 together with 4 to 6.

why_wrong.0: The open interval from 2 to 6 forgets to remove 4, where the expression is undefined.
why_wrong.2: Extending to infinity is wrong. Large values of x make the fraction small, so the inequality fails there.
why_wrong.3: Extending to minus infinity is wrong for the same reason. Multiplying an inequality by a modulus is safe here because the modulus is positive, but the excluded point must still be removed.

why_correct: Writing both permutations as factorials, the ratio simplifies to n plus 5 times n plus 4, all over 4. Setting that equal to 11 times n minus 1 over 2 gives the quadratic n squared minus 13n plus 42 equal to 0, whose roots are 6 and 7. Of these, 6 is the option offered.

why_wrong.0: 5 does not satisfy the equation. Substituting it gives 90 over 4 on the left and 22 on the right.
why_wrong.2: 8 fails as well, since the quadratic factorises as n minus 6 times n minus 7.
why_wrong.3: 10 is far outside the solution set. Always simplify the permutation ratio to a small product before solving, rather than expanding the factorials.

why_correct: Every such number has four digits with the thousands digit 1, 2 or 3, giving 3 choices. Each of the other three digits may be any of the five, giving 5 cubed, that is 125. So the count is 3 times 125, which is 375.

why_wrong.0: 125 counts only one choice of leading digit instead of three.
why_wrong.1: 105 does not arise from any correct counting here and looks like an arithmetic slip.
why_wrong.3: 625 is 5 to the fourth, which would allow 0 and 4 as leading digits too. That would let in numbers below 1000 and at or above 4000, both excluded.

why_correct: If nCr equals nCs with r not equal to s, then r plus s equals n. Here 2 plus 3 gives n equal to 5, and 5C4 is 5.

why_wrong.0: 3 would be the answer if n were smaller, but the condition fixes n at 5.
why_wrong.1: 4 comes from confusing the answer with the lower index. 5C4 equals 5C1, which is 5.
why_wrong.3: 7 does not arise from any correct step. The identity to remember is nCr equals nC n minus r.

why_correct: From each vertex of an n sided polygon you can draw a diagonal to every vertex except itself and its two neighbours, which is n minus 3 of them. Doing that at all n vertices counts every diagonal twice, so the number of diagonals is n times n minus 3, all divided by 2. For a heptagon that is 7 times 4 over 2, which is 14.

why_wrong.0: 7 is the number of vertices, and also the number of sides. It is the count you start from, not the answer.
why_wrong.1: 21 is 7 choose 2, the number of straight lines joining any two of the seven vertices. That total includes the 7 sides, which are not diagonals; 21 minus 7 gives the 14 we want. This was the printed key.
why_wrong.3: 13 corresponds to no reading of the question. If you reached it, recount with the formula rather than by drawing, since diagonals are very easy to miss or double count in a sketch.

why_correct: The function is 1 for positive x and minus 1 for negative x. So f of x and f of minus x are always opposite in sign, their difference is plus or minus 2, and its modulus is 2.

why_wrong.0: 0 would require f to be an even function, taking the same value at x and minus x. This function is odd instead.
why_wrong.1: 1 is the value of the function itself for positive x, not of the difference.
why_wrong.2: Minus 1 cannot be right, since the question takes a modulus and a modulus is never negative.

why_correct: Approaching 0 from the right the expression is 1, and from the left it is minus 1. The one-sided limits differ, so the limit does not exist.

why_wrong.0: 0 would need the function to approach zero, but it only ever takes the values 1 and minus 1.
why_wrong.1: Minus 1 is the left-hand limit alone. A limit exists only if both sides agree.
why_wrong.2: 1 is the right-hand limit alone, and the same objection applies. Whenever a modulus sits over the variable at the point in question, check both sides separately.

why_correct: At x equal to 3 the expression is 0 over 0, so rationalise the numerator. Multiplying above and below by the sum of the roots gives x squared minus 9 over x minus 3 times the sum, which cancels to x plus 3 over the sum, and at x equal to 3 that is 6 over 2 root 19, or 3 over root 19.

why_wrong.0: 0 would be the answer only if the numerator vanished faster than the denominator, but here they vanish at the same rate.
why_wrong.1: 6 over root 19 forgets to halve when the two square roots in the denominator are added at x equal to 3. Each is root 19, so the sum is 2 root 19.
why_wrong.3: Root 19 over 6 is the correct answer turned upside down.

why_correct: Expand both terms about zero. e to the x squared is 1 plus x squared plus higher powers, and cos x is 1 minus x squared over 2 plus higher powers. Subtracting, the ones cancel and the numerator is three halves of x squared plus higher powers, so dividing by x squared and letting x tend to zero gives three halves. L'Hopital agrees: differentiating top and bottom once gives 2x times e to the x squared plus sin x, over 2x, which is e to the x squared plus sin x over 2x, tending to 1 plus one half, that is three halves.

why_wrong.0: One quarter does not come out of any correct step here. If you reached it, redo the problem by L'Hopital's rule, which needs no series at all.
why_wrong.1: Two thirds is the reciprocal of the right answer, and it was the printed key. If your working produced three halves, do not turn it upside down at the last moment.
why_wrong.3: 1 is what you get if you expand the exponential but treat cos x as simply 1, forgetting the minus x squared over 2 term. That term contributes the extra one half, and leaving it out is the commonest slip in this question.

why_correct: Power is work divided by time. Work has dimensions ML2T−2, so dividing by T gives ML2T−3.

why_wrong.1: MLT is not the dimension of any standard quantity, and it carries no negative power of time, which every rate must have.
why_wrong.2: ML2T2 has time in the numerator rather than the denominator. Power is energy per unit time, so T must appear as a negative power.
why_wrong.3: M2LT3 squares the mass, and no mechanical quantity of this kind depends on mass squared.

why_correct: Torque plays the same role in rotation that force plays in straight-line motion: it is what produces angular acceleration. The rotational form of Newton's second law is torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration.

why_wrong.0: The rotational analogue of mass is moment of inertia, since both measure resistance to a change of motion.
why_wrong.1: The rotational analogue of linear momentum is angular momentum, not torque. Torque is what changes angular momentum, just as force changes momentum.
why_wrong.3: Kinetic energy has a rotational form of its own, half I omega squared, but energy is not the analogue of torque.

why_correct: Instantaneous power is the dot product of force and velocity, P equals F dot v. It follows from power being the rate of doing work and work being force dot displacement.

why_wrong.0: Mass times velocity is momentum, which is a vector, not power.
why_wrong.2: Torque times time gives angular impulse, which equals the change in angular momentum.
why_wrong.3: Force dot displacement is work itself, not power. Power is the rate at which that work is done, so a division by time is still needed.

why_correct: To just complete a vertical loop the string must stay taut at the top, so the minimum speed there is root gr. Using energy conservation between top and bottom, with a height difference of 2r, gives the minimum speed at the lowest point as root 5gr.

why_wrong.0: Root gr is the minimum speed at the highest point, where gravity alone supplies the centripetal force. The question asks about the lowest point.
why_wrong.1: Root 3gr is the minimum speed at the side of the loop, at the level of the centre.
why_wrong.3: Root 2gr is the speed gained by falling through a height r, which is not the condition here. The three heights give three different answers, so identify the point first.

why_correct: Friction is non-conservative because the work it does depends on the path taken, not just on the endpoints, and the energy it removes is lost as heat rather than stored.

why_wrong.0: Gravity is conservative. Work done against it is stored as potential energy and can be recovered in full.
why_wrong.1: The electrostatic force is conservative too, with its own potential energy.
why_wrong.3: The elastic force of a spring is conservative, storing energy as half k x squared and giving it back. The test is whether the work round a closed path is zero, and only friction fails it.

why_correct: The slope of a graph is the rate of change of the quantity on the vertical axis with respect to the one on the horizontal axis. On a displacement time graph that is the rate of change of displacement with time, which is precisely the definition of velocity. A steeper line means a faster body, and a horizontal line means the body is at rest.

why_wrong.0: Displacement is what the graph reads off the vertical axis at a given instant, not what its slope measures. The height and the steepness are two different pieces of information.
why_wrong.1: Acceleration is the slope of a velocity time graph, one differentiation further on. On a displacement time graph acceleration shows up in the curvature, not the slope. This was the printed key, and question 14 on this same paper asks the same idea and keys it correctly as velocity.
why_wrong.3: Time is the horizontal axis. An axis variable is never what a slope represents.

why_correct: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy. It follows directly from Newton's second law and holds whether the forces are conservative or not.

why_wrong.0: The change in potential energy equals the negative of the work done by a conservative force alone. The theorem concerns the net work of all forces.
why_wrong.2: Change in momentum equals impulse, that is force times time, which is a different theorem.
why_wrong.3: Acceleration is not an energy at all, so it cannot equal a quantity of work.

why_correct: The spring force is kx, and it grows from zero as the spring stretches. The work done is the area under the force-extension graph, a triangle of base x and height kx, which gives half k x squared.

why_wrong.0: kx is the force at extension x, not the energy stored.
why_wrong.1: Half kx has the dimensions of force, since the half changes nothing dimensionally. Energy needs x squared.
why_wrong.3: kx squared is twice the correct value. It is what you would get by treating the force as constant at kx throughout, forgetting that it started at zero.

why_correct: The angle of repose is the greatest incline on which a body just stays at rest, and setting the component of gravity along the slope equal to limiting friction gives tan of that angle equal to the coefficient of friction. Since the angle of friction has the same tangent, the two angles are equal.

why_wrong.1: 90 degrees would be a vertical surface, on which nothing could rest by friction alone.
why_wrong.2: 0 degrees would mean nothing could rest even on level ground.
why_wrong.3: The angle of banking concerns a road curved to help a vehicle turn. Related in that it also involves a tangent, but a different quantity.

why_correct: Limiting friction is the largest value static friction can reach, just before the body begins to slide. Beyond that point the friction becomes kinetic and drops slightly.

why_wrong.0: Kinetic friction acts once the body is already sliding, and it is smaller than the limiting value.
why_wrong.1: Rolling friction acts when one body rolls over another, and it is smaller again than either.
why_wrong.3: Dynamic friction is another name for kinetic friction, so it names motion already under way rather than the threshold before it.

why_correct: Static friction is self-adjusting: it takes whatever value is needed to balance the applied force and keep the body at rest, growing as the applied force grows, up to the limiting value.

why_wrong.0: Kinetic friction is very nearly constant once sliding begins, and does not adjust itself to the applied force.
why_wrong.2: Rolling friction is also roughly constant for a given pair of surfaces.
why_wrong.3: Sliding friction is another name for kinetic friction, and is likewise fixed rather than self-adjusting.

why_correct: From E equals h nu, h is energy divided by frequency. Energy is ML2T−2 and frequency is T−1, so h has dimensions ML2T−1, which is the same as angular momentum.

why_wrong.1: MLT−2 is the dimension of force.
why_wrong.2: ML2T−2 is energy itself, which is what you get by forgetting to divide by frequency.
why_wrong.3: M2L2T−1 squares the mass, and nothing in E equals h nu introduces a mass squared.

why_correct: A carousel is accelerating, since its riders are continually changing direction, so a frame fixed to it is non-inertial. Newton's laws do not hold in it unless pseudo-forces such as the centrifugal force are introduced.

why_wrong.0: An inertial frame is one at rest or moving with constant velocity. Circular motion involves centripetal acceleration, so the frame cannot be inertial.
why_wrong.2: There is no absolute frame in mechanics. Newton proposed one, but it plays no part in this classification.
why_wrong.3: Linear is not a category of reference frame. Frames are either inertial or non-inertial.

why_correct: The slope of a position-time graph is the change in position divided by the change in time, which is precisely the definition of velocity.

why_wrong.0: Acceleration is the slope of a velocity-time graph, one derivative further on.
why_wrong.1: Displacement is read off the vertical axis directly, not from the slope.
why_wrong.3: Momentum is mass times velocity, and a graph of position against time carries no information about mass.

why_correct: Constant speed in a straight line means the velocity is unchanging in both size and direction, so the rate of change of velocity is zero and there is no acceleration.

why_wrong.0: Positive acceleration would mean the speed was increasing, which contradicts constant speed.
why_wrong.1: Negative acceleration would mean it was slowing down. Careful: constant speed on a curved path does involve acceleration, because the direction changes, but here the path is straight.
why_wrong.3: Infinite acceleration has no physical meaning and would require an infinite force.

why_correct: At the top of its path the projectile has stopped rising and has not yet begun to fall, so its vertical velocity is momentarily zero. The horizontal velocity, however, is unchanged throughout.

why_wrong.0: The vertical velocity is greatest at launch and at landing, not at the peak.
why_wrong.2: The horizontal velocity does continue at the top, and it equals the initial horizontal component, but the question asks about the vertical velocity, which is zero.
why_wrong.3: g is an acceleration, not a velocity. The acceleration at the top is still g downward, which is exactly why the projectile does not stay there.

why_correct: The first law says a body continues at rest or in uniform motion unless a force acts on it. That statement defines force, as the thing that changes the state of motion, and introduces inertia, as the tendency to resist that change.

why_wrong.1: Momentum is defined in connection with the second law, which relates force to the rate of change of momentum.
why_wrong.2: Kinetic energy comes from the work-energy theorem, not from any of Newton's three laws directly.
why_wrong.3: Work is defined separately, as force times displacement along the force.

why_correct: For a uniform solid cylinder about its own long axis the moment of inertia is half MR squared, the same as for a solid disc, since a cylinder is a stack of discs about the same axis.

why_wrong.0: MR squared is the moment of inertia of a thin ring or hollow cylinder, where all the mass sits at the rim. A solid cylinder has mass nearer the axis, so its value must be smaller.
why_wrong.2: Two fifths MR squared belongs to a solid sphere.
why_wrong.3: Two thirds MR squared belongs to a hollow sphere.

why_correct: The radius of gyration k is defined by I equal to Mk squared, so k is the square root of I over M. For a thin ring about the central axis perpendicular to its plane, every particle of the ring sits at exactly the same distance R from the axis, so I equals MR squared with no numerical factor at all. Hence k equals R. This is the one case where the radius of gyration is obvious without any integration.

why_wrong.0: R over 2 is the radius of gyration of a circular disc about a diameter, where I equals MR squared over 4. It belongs to a different body and a different axis.
why_wrong.1: R over root 2 is the answer for a ring about a diameter, where the perpendicular axis theorem gives I equal to MR squared over 2. This was the printed key: it is the right calculation for the wrong axis. The question asks about the central perpendicular axis, not a diameter.
why_wrong.3: 2R is impossible for any body about an axis through its centre. Every particle lies within R of that axis, so k, being a kind of average of those distances, can never be larger than R.

why_correct: Leading zeros are never significant, but trailing zeros after a decimal point are. So in 0.005020 the digits 5, 0, 2 and the final 0 count, giving four significant figures.

why_wrong.0: 3 comes from dropping the final zero. That zero is written deliberately after the decimal point and does carry information about precision.
why_wrong.2: 5 counts one of the leading zeros, which merely fix the position of the decimal point.
why_wrong.3: 6 counts every digit shown, including both leading zeros.

why_correct: Volume goes as the cube of the radius, and for a product or power the percentage errors add with the power as a multiplier. So the error in volume is three times 2 per cent, that is 6 per cent.

why_wrong.0: 2 per cent would be right if volume were proportional to radius itself.
why_wrong.1: 4 per cent corresponds to squaring, which is the error in surface area, not volume.
why_wrong.3: 8 per cent would come from cubing the error rather than multiplying it by three. The rule is to multiply the percentage error by the power, not to raise it to that power.

why_correct: The candela is the SI base unit of luminous intensity. The seven base units are the metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela.

why_wrong.0: The joule is a derived unit of energy, equal to a newton metre.
why_wrong.1: The newton is derived, equal to kilogram metre per second squared.
why_wrong.3: The watt is derived, equal to a joule per second. All three of the wrong options are named after scientists and are derived; the candela is the odd one out.

why_correct: Torque is force times perpendicular distance, so its dimensions are ML2T−2, exactly those of work. The two are physically different, one a vector and the other a scalar, but dimensionally identical.

why_wrong.0: Momentum has dimensions MLT−1.
why_wrong.1: Force has dimensions MLT−2, one power of length short.
why_wrong.2: Power has an extra division by time, giving ML2T−3. This question is a reminder that equal dimensions do not mean equal quantities.

why_correct: Starting from rest, s equals half a t squared, so displacement is proportional to the square of the time. Doubling the time quadruples the distance covered.

why_wrong.0: Displacement proportional to t describes uniform velocity, that is no acceleration at all.
why_wrong.2: Root t would mean the body covered ground ever more slowly, which is the reverse of accelerating.
why_wrong.3: t cubed would require the acceleration itself to be increasing steadily, but here it is uniform.

why_correct: Drawing the hands back lengthens the time over which the ball is stopped. Since impulse equals force times time and the impulse is fixed by the ball's momentum, a longer time means a smaller force on the hands.

why_wrong.0: The impulse is not reduced. It is fixed by the change in the ball's momentum, which must be brought to zero however the catch is made.
why_wrong.2: The ball's momentum is likewise fixed by its mass and speed on arrival, and all of it must be removed.
why_wrong.3: The time of catch is increased, not reduced, and that increase is exactly the mechanism. This is the same principle as crumple zones in cars and mattresses under high jumpers.

why_correct: Ruskin Bond's narrator first sees the girl on the platform at Deoli, during the brief halt his train makes there. The whole story turns on that platform, because it is the only place he ever meets her.

why_wrong.0: There is no marketplace scene. The narrator never leaves the station at Deoli.
why_wrong.2: His college is where he travels from, not where he meets her.
why_wrong.3: No fair appears in the story. The setting is deliberately narrow: a small station, a short halt, and a train that will not wait.

why_correct: The narrator passes through Deoli on his way to Dehra Dun, travelling to his grandmother's house in the holidays. Deoli is simply a small station on that line where the train stops for ten minutes.

why_wrong.0: Delhi is not his destination in the story.
why_wrong.1: Kolkata does not appear at all.
why_wrong.3: Mumbai is not mentioned either. The journey to Dehra matters because it is a routine one, repeated every holiday, which is what makes the girl's disappearance so haunting.

why_correct: The girl sells baskets on the platform. She carries them on her arm and moves along the train while it waits, which is how the narrator comes to speak to her.

why_wrong.0: She is not a flower seller.
why_wrong.1: Tea is sold at Indian stations by others, but not by her.
why_wrong.2: Fruit sellers are a common sight on platforms too, which is what makes these tempting. Bond is specific: baskets.

why_correct: The girl simply disappears from the station. On later journeys she is not there, the stall keeper says he does not know what became of her, and the narrator never learns the truth.

why_wrong.0: He does not change his route. He goes on making the same journey and looking for her each time.
why_wrong.1: The train continues to stop at Deoli, which is precisely why he keeps hoping.
why_wrong.3: He never forgets her. He thinks of her for years, and the story ends with him choosing not to look further, so that the possibility remains alive.

why_correct: In Strong Roots, A. P. J. Abdul Kalam describes his childhood home on Mosque Street in Rameswaram, close to both the mosque and the ancient Shiva temple. That closeness shaped his lifelong belief in shared living.

why_wrong.0: A railway station is not part of his description of the house.
why_wrong.2: A marketplace is not what he emphasises. What he stresses is the nearness of two places of worship.
why_wrong.3: There is no factory. Rameswaram in his childhood was a small pilgrim town.

why_correct: Kalam's upbringing stressed hard work, honesty, self-discipline and generosity. His family was not wealthy, and he learned austerity and values rather than comfort.

why_wrong.0: Wealth and status were absent from his childhood. His father owned neither luxury nor position, though he was widely respected.
why_wrong.2: Competition is not his theme. His father taught service and self-reliance rather than getting ahead of others.
why_wrong.3: Political influence was never sought. His father declined the comforts that his standing could have brought.

why_correct: Kalam's father held that adversity always presents opportunities for self-discovery, so difficulties help a person understand themselves better. Hardship, on this view, is instructive rather than merely painful.

why_wrong.0: Fame is not the point. His father lived quietly and sought no recognition.
why_wrong.1: Earning money is not the lesson either, and his family lived simply by choice.
why_wrong.3: Avoiding responsibility is the opposite of what he taught. His father's answer to difficulty was to face it and learn from it.

why_correct: Chekhov's story opens at a party where the guests argue over capital punishment and life imprisonment. The banker calls the death penalty more humane, the lawyer says he would choose life imprisonment, and the bet follows from that disagreement.

why_wrong.0: Religion is discussed only later, when the lawyer reads theology during his confinement.
why_wrong.1: Politics is not the subject of the argument.
why_wrong.3: Education is not debated, though the lawyer's reading amounts to an education of a kind.

why_correct: The lawyer agrees to fifteen years of solitary confinement. The banker had suggested five, and the lawyer raised it to fifteen himself, to make the point more forcefully.

why_wrong.0: 5 years is what the banker first proposed, and the lawyer rejected it as too easy.
why_wrong.1: 10 years is not the figure agreed.
why_wrong.3: 20 years is too many. The detail matters because the lawyer walks out five hours before the fifteen years expire, forfeiting everything deliberately.

why_correct: The bet is for two million rubles. The sum is large enough that losing it would ruin the banker, which is why he contemplates murder as the term draws to a close.

why_wrong.0: One million understates it.
why_wrong.2: Five million is too high.
why_wrong.3: Ten million is far too high. Chekhov's irony depends on the amount: the banker who once had money to throw away is nearly destroyed by the same sum fifteen years later.

why_correct: The lawyer spends his confinement reading, working through languages, philosophy, history, theology and the natural sciences, and in the later years hundreds of volumes at a time.

why_wrong.0: He does not pass the years asleep. His activity is what makes the story's ending possible.
why_wrong.2: He plays the piano in the early years, but games are not his occupation.
why_wrong.3: Exercise is not described. His confinement is of the mind, and it is the reading that changes him.

why_correct: Fifteen years of reading leave the lawyer contemptuous of everything the world values, including money. He renounces the two million to show his scorn, walking out hours before he would have won it.

why_wrong.0: He does not forget. His letter states his reasons at length and with great deliberation.
why_wrong.1: He gains no wealth in confinement. He leaves with nothing, by choice.
why_wrong.3: He knows nothing of the banker's murderous intention, since the banker enters and leaves without waking him.

why_correct: Toru Dutt's casuarina tree is bound up with memories of childhood and of the brother and sister who played beneath it and are now dead. The tree is loved for their sake, not for its own.

why_wrong.1: There are no political events in the poem.
why_wrong.2: Business has no place in it.
why_wrong.3: War is not its subject. The poem is elegiac and personal, and its emotion comes from loss rather than from any public event.

why_correct: A huge creeper winds round the tree like a python, scarring its trunk. Yet the tree bears the strangling grip and still flourishes, crowned with crimson flowers.

why_wrong.0: No rose vine appears in the poem.
why_wrong.2: Bamboo is not mentioned anywhere in the poem, and it would not wind round a trunk as the creeper does.
why_wrong.3: Ivy would suit an English poem, but Dutt's image is of a creeper compared to a python, which is a deliberately Indian picture.

why_correct: The poet's memories are joyful and nostalgic. She recalls happy hours under the tree with her brother and sister, and the sweetness of that recollection is inseparable from the grief of having lost them.

why_wrong.0: There is no fear in the poem, though the creeper is likened to a python.
why_wrong.2: There is no bitterness. Dutt writes with tenderness even about her loss.
why_wrong.3: Indifference is impossible here. She wishes the tree to be consecrated in verse so that it may outlive her, which is the opposite of indifference.

why_correct: India is the largest democracy in the world, with an electorate of over 900 million. It has held regular free elections under universal adult franchise since 1951.

why_wrong.0: The United States is the world's oldest continuous constitutional democracy, but its electorate is far smaller. Oldest and largest are different titles.
why_wrong.2: Brazil is the largest democracy in South America but has under 150 million voters.
why_wrong.3: Indonesia is the third largest democracy and the largest Muslim-majority one.

why_correct: The World Health Organization has its headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland. It was established in 1948, and 7 April is observed as World Health Day.

why_wrong.0: New York is the headquarters of the United Nations itself.
why_wrong.1: Paris is the headquarters of UNESCO.
why_wrong.3: Vienna houses the International Atomic Energy Agency. Geneva is the UN's second great centre and holds the WHO, the ILO and the WTO.

why_correct: Dr B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly and is called the Father of the Indian Constitution. He was also independent India's first Law Minister.

why_wrong.0: Dr Rajendra Prasad was President of the Constituent Assembly and later the first President of India. Presiding over the Assembly and drafting the Constitution are different roles, and this is the confusion the question rests on.
why_wrong.1: Sardar Patel chaired the committees on fundamental rights and minorities and integrated the princely states.
why_wrong.3: Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution, which became the basis of the Preamble, and was the first Prime Minister.

why_correct: Germany is not a permanent member of the Security Council. The five permanent members are China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the victors of the Second World War.

why_wrong.0: China is permanent, its seat passing from the Republic of China to the People's Republic in 1971.
why_wrong.1: France is permanent, and it is one of the two European members alongside the United Kingdom.
why_wrong.3: Russia is permanent, having inherited the Soviet Union's seat in 1991. Germany and Japan, the defeated powers of 1945, both seek permanent seats along with India and Brazil, which is why Germany is the natural distractor.

why_correct: The Green Revolution raised food grain production, above all wheat and rice, through high-yielding varieties, irrigation, fertilisers and pesticides. It made India self-sufficient in food grains.

why_wrong.0: Horticulture is the Golden Revolution.
why_wrong.1: Fisheries are the Blue Revolution.
why_wrong.2: Dairy is the White Revolution, or Operation Flood, led by Dr Verghese Kurien. The colour revolutions are worth learning as a set, and green is the one for grain.

why_correct: Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam is called the Missile Man of India for his work on the Agni and Prithvi missiles and the integrated guided missile programme. He served as President from 2002 to 2007.

why_wrong.0: Dr Homi J. Bhabha is the father of India's nuclear programme.
why_wrong.1: Dr Vikram Sarabhai is the father of India's space programme, and ISRO's founder.
why_wrong.3: Dr C. V. Raman won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930 for the Raman effect. Note that Kalam also wrote Strong Roots, which appears earlier on this same paper.

why_correct: The Kosi is called the Sorrow of Bihar. Carrying vast quantities of silt down from Nepal, it raises its own bed and shifts its channel, flooding wide tracts of north Bihar.

why_wrong.0: The Ganga floods too, but it does not carry this name.
why_wrong.2: The Yamuna is the Ganga's longest tributary and flows through Delhi and Agra.
why_wrong.3: The Son is another Bihar river but is not the one so called. The companion title is the Sorrow of Bengal, which belonged to the Damodar before it was dammed.

why_correct: The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded in Oslo, Norway, by a committee appointed by the Norwegian Parliament. Alfred Nobel's will laid down this single exception.

why_wrong.0: Stockholm is where all the other Nobel Prizes are awarded, which makes it the natural wrong answer.
why_wrong.1: Copenhagen has no role in the prizes.
why_wrong.2: Helsinki has none either. Norway and Sweden were in union when Nobel wrote his will, which is thought to explain the arrangement.

why_correct: Amartya Sen wrote The Argumentative Indian, a collection of essays on Indian history, culture and identity. He won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1998 for his work on welfare economics.

why_wrong.0: Shashi Tharoor wrote The Great Indian Novel and An Era of Darkness, so he is a plausible guess among Indian writers on similar themes.
why_wrong.2: R. K. Narayan wrote fiction set in Malgudi, including Swami and Friends and The Guide.
why_wrong.3: Chetan Bhagat writes popular contemporary fiction.

why_correct: The International Civil Aviation Organization, a UN agency based in Montreal, sets the standards and regulations for international air navigation and safety.

why_wrong.0: UNESCO deals with education, science and culture.
why_wrong.1: The ILO deals with labour standards and workers' rights.
why_wrong.3: The WTO regulates international trade. Read the acronym out in full and the answer follows: International Civil Aviation Organization.

why_correct: Wheat produced during the current year is newly created output, so its value is part of this year's GDP. GDP counts only goods and services actually produced within the period.

why_wrong.0: Second-hand furniture was produced and counted in an earlier year. Reselling it transfers ownership without creating anything new.
why_wrong.1: Buying shares is a financial transaction, an exchange of paper claims, not production.
why_wrong.3: A pension is a transfer payment, made without any good or service being supplied in return.

why_correct: Net means after allowing for the wearing out of capital, so NNP at market price is GNP at market price minus depreciation.

why_wrong.0: Adding depreciation moves the wrong way. Gross includes it and net excludes it, so going from gross to net means subtracting.
why_wrong.2: Subtracting net factor income from abroad converts national to domestic, which is a different adjustment entirely.
why_wrong.3: Adding subsidies to a factor cost figure moves towards market price, which is again a different step. Three separate adjustments run through these formulae: gross to net is depreciation, national to domestic is net factor income from abroad, and market price to factor cost is net indirect taxes.

why_correct: A teacher's salary is paid in return for a service actually rendered, so it is a factor payment and is included in national income. It is not a transfer.

why_wrong.0: An old-age pension is paid without any current service in return, so it is a transfer.
why_wrong.1: An unemployment allowance is likewise received without work being done.
why_wrong.3: A scholarship is a transfer too. The test is whether something is given in exchange, and only the teacher gives anything.

why_correct: Factor cost is what the factors of production actually receive, so indirect taxes are deducted from the market price and subsidies added back. National income is NNP at factor cost.

why_wrong.1: Adding depreciation to GDP gives a larger gross figure, not a net one at factor cost.
why_wrong.2: GDP minus depreciation gives NDP, which is still domestic and still at market price.
why_wrong.3: Adding net indirect taxes moves from factor cost towards market price, which is the wrong direction. Market price is higher than factor cost by the amount of net indirect taxes.

why_correct: The final value method counts only the value of final goods and services, so the value of intermediate goods is not counted twice. The value added method achieves the same result from the other direction.

why_wrong.1: Wholesale prices are used to construct price indices, not to measure output.
why_wrong.2: Retail prices are likewise used in price indices such as the CPI.
why_wrong.3: Consumption is one component of the expenditure method, not a remedy for double counting.

why_correct: Keynes held that employment depends on effective demand, that is on aggregate demand for goods and services. If demand is deficient, output and employment fall short of full employment.

why_wrong.1: Population determines the size of the labour force but not how much of it is employed.
why_wrong.2: Interest affects investment and so demand, but only indirectly, and Keynes argued that demand rather than the rate of interest is the governing factor.
why_wrong.3: Tax collection is one instrument of policy, not the determinant of employment. Keynes was writing against the classical view that supply creates its own demand.

why_correct: The consumption function is C equals a plus bY, where a is autonomous consumption, spent even at zero income, and b is the marginal propensity to consume. It is a straight line with a positive intercept.

why_wrong.1: A squared term would make consumption rise ever faster with income, which contradicts the observed pattern.
why_wrong.2: A negative slope would mean consumption falls as income rises, which is the reverse of what happens.
why_wrong.3: Y minus a would make the marginal propensity to consume exactly 1, leaving no saving at any level of income.

why_correct: The multiplier is 1 divided by 1 minus the MPC. With an MPC of 0.75 that is 1 over 0.25, which is 4. So a rise of one rupee in investment raises income by four.

why_wrong.0: 2 corresponds to an MPC of 0.5.
why_wrong.1: 3 corresponds to an MPC of two thirds.
why_wrong.3: 5 corresponds to an MPC of 0.8. The multiplier is also 1 divided by the marginal propensity to save, which here is 0.25.

why_correct: The average propensity to consume is total consumption divided by total income, C over Y. It shows what proportion of income is spent.

why_wrong.1: Y over C inverts the ratio and has no standard meaning.
why_wrong.2: S over Y is the average propensity to save, the companion measure, and the two add to 1.
why_wrong.3: The change in C over the change in Y is the marginal propensity to consume. Average uses totals, marginal uses changes, and that is the distinction being tested.

why_correct: The break-even point is where consumption equals income, so nothing is left over and saving is exactly zero. Below it saving is negative and above it positive.

why_wrong.0: Saving is positive above the break-even level of income, not at it.
why_wrong.1: Saving is negative below it, financed by past savings or borrowing.
why_wrong.3: Investment is a separate variable and is not necessarily zero anywhere. At this point the consumption function crosses the 45 degree line.

why_correct: Export of software services is an export of services, which belongs to the current account of the Balance of Payments. The current account records trade in goods and services, income and current transfers.

why_wrong.0: Foreign direct investment is a capital account item, since it creates an asset or a liability.
why_wrong.1: Careful here. Import of machinery is trade in goods and does belong to the current account, so this option is arguably right too. The one the question intends is the service export, and either way the capital account items are the two clearly wrong ones.
why_wrong.3: External commercial borrowing creates a liability, so it is a capital account item.

why_correct: A deficit means the country's total payments to the rest of the world exceed its total receipts, so it must draw down reserves or borrow to meet the gap.

why_wrong.0: Receipts exceeding payments is a surplus, the opposite case.
why_wrong.2: Exports equalling imports would be a balance in trade, and the Balance of Payments covers more than trade in any case.
why_wrong.3: A deficit tends to weaken the currency rather than strengthen it.

why_correct: Under a flexible or floating rate, the exchange rate is set by the demand for and supply of foreign exchange in the market, and it moves freely as those change.

why_wrong.0: Government order fixes the rate, which is the fixed exchange rate system.
why_wrong.1: An RBI notification would again be an administered rate. In practice India has a managed float, where the RBI intervenes to smooth movements without setting the rate.
why_wrong.3: Parliament does not set exchange rates.

why_correct: Depreciation lowers the external value of the currency, so foreigners need less of their own money to buy the same goods. Exports therefore become cheaper abroad and more competitive.

why_wrong.0: Imports become more expensive, not exports.
why_wrong.2: The effect is substantial, which is why depreciation is watched so closely.
why_wrong.3: Nothing becomes illegal. Note the difference from devaluation: depreciation happens through the market, devaluation by official decision.

why_correct: The Reserve Bank of India holds and manages the country's foreign exchange reserves, and intervenes in the currency market to keep movements orderly.

why_wrong.0: SEBI regulates the securities market.
why_wrong.1: NABARD refinances rural and agricultural credit.
why_wrong.3: NITI Aayog is a policy think tank and successor to the Planning Commission. Managing reserves is a classic central bank function, alongside issuing currency and acting as banker to the government.

why_correct: British rule brought deindustrialisation. Indian handicrafts, above all textiles, were destroyed by competition from machine-made British goods and by policies that opened India to them, throwing artisans back on the land.

why_wrong.0: India was not rapidly industrialised. Modern industry grew slowly and late, and mainly where British interests were served.
why_wrong.2: Capital formation stayed very low, one reason growth was near stagnant.
why_wrong.3: Technology was imported and controlled from abroad, so self-reliance did not develop.

why_correct: The railways are usually named as a positive legacy. They were built to serve British commercial and military needs, but they broke down geographical isolation and left India with a network it still uses.

why_wrong.0: The drain of wealth was a pure loss, the transfer of India's resources to Britain without any return.
why_wrong.2: The decline of handicrafts destroyed livelihoods on a vast scale.
why_wrong.3: Famines were frequent and devastating under colonial policy. The three wrong options are all straightforwardly harms, which makes the odd one out easy to see.

why_correct: Dadabhai Naoroji developed the drain of wealth theory in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, arguing that a large part of India's wealth was being drained to Britain each year without any equivalent return.

why_wrong.1: Gandhi criticised colonial economic policy and championed swadeshi, but the theory is Naoroji's.
why_wrong.2: Nehru wrote on colonial exploitation in The Discovery of India, drawing on the idea rather than originating it.
why_wrong.3: Ambedkar wrote on caste and on currency, but not this theory. Naoroji is also remembered as the Grand Old Man of India and as the first Indian in the British Parliament.

why_correct: The tertiary or service sector contributes the largest share of India's GDP, well over half. India moved from agriculture to services without a large manufacturing phase in between, which is unusual.

why_wrong.0: The primary sector still employs the largest number of people, but contributes far less to output. That gap between employment share and output share is the important point.
why_wrong.1: The secondary sector contributes less than services.
why_wrong.3: Mining is a small part of the primary sector.

why_correct: Liberalisation officially began in 1991 with the New Economic Policy, introduced during a severe balance of payments crisis. Industrial licensing was largely abolished and the economy opened to trade and foreign investment.

why_wrong.0: 1947 is independence, after which India adopted planning and extensive controls, the opposite of liberalisation.
why_wrong.1: 1969 saw bank nationalisation, again a move towards state control.
why_wrong.3: By 2000 liberalisation was already a decade old. The three strands of 1991 are liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation.

why_correct: Liberalisation means removing restrictions, so increasing import restrictions is the opposite of it. Tariffs and quotas were reduced after 1991, not raised.

why_wrong.0: Reduction of licensing is central to liberalisation, dismantling the old permit system.
why_wrong.1: Greater private participation is another of its features.
why_wrong.3: Market-oriented reform is what the whole policy amounts to. Three of the four options loosen controls, so the one that tightens them stands out.

why_correct: The Human Development Index combines three dimensions: a long and healthy life, measured by life expectancy; knowledge, measured by schooling; and a decent standard of living, measured by income per head. It was devised by Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen.

why_wrong.0: Income alone was the older measure the HDI was designed to replace, precisely because income says too little about how people actually live.
why_wrong.2: Inflation and unemployment are macroeconomic indicators but are not part of the HDI.
why_wrong.3: Exports and imports concern external trade.

why_correct: The Green Revolution raised the output of wheat and rice above all, through high-yielding varieties, irrigation, fertilisers and pesticides. Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh gained most.

why_wrong.0: Pulses were largely left out, and their output per head actually fell, which remains a problem for Indian nutrition.
why_wrong.2: Cotton is a commercial crop and was not the focus.
why_wrong.3: Tea is a plantation crop, untouched by the programme. The narrowness of the gains, in crops and in regions, is one of the standard criticisms.

why_correct: Cooperative banks are an institutional source of agricultural credit, along with commercial banks, regional rural banks and NABARD. Institutional means regulated, with fair interest rates and proper terms.

why_wrong.0: The village moneylender is the classic non-institutional source, charging very high interest.
why_wrong.1: Traders lend informally against the crop and are non-institutional.
why_wrong.3: Landlords lending to tenants are non-institutional too. Expanding institutional credit was a main aim of bank nationalisation in 1969.

why_correct: Indian agriculture depends heavily on the monsoon, since a large part of the cropped area is unirrigated. A weak or late monsoon can cut output sharply, which is why farming is often called a gamble in the rains.

why_wrong.0: Mechanisation is uneven and limited, not excessive everywhere. Small holdings make machinery uneconomic for many farmers.
why_wrong.2: Irrigation is far from surplus; large areas have none at all.
why_wrong.3: Labour is generally surplus in Indian agriculture rather than short, with much disguised unemployment.

why_correct: The University Education Commission was appointed in 1948 under Dr S. Radhakrishnan, the first education commission of independent India. It reported on the reform of higher education.

why_wrong.0: 1950 is the year the Constitution came into force, not the year of this commission.
why_wrong.2: 1947 is the year of independence, and the commission followed a year later.
why_wrong.3: 1957 belongs to no major education commission. The sequence worth holding is Radhakrishnan 1948, Mudaliar 1952, Kothari 1964.

why_correct: The Indian Education Commission, better known as the Kothari Commission, was appointed in 1964 under Dr D. S. Kothari and reported in 1966. It reviewed education at every stage and led to the first National Policy on Education in 1968.

why_wrong.1: 1948 is the Radhakrishnan or University Education Commission, which dealt with higher education alone.
why_wrong.2: 1952 is the Mudaliar or Secondary Education Commission.
why_wrong.3: 1986 is the second National Policy on Education, not a commission.

why_correct: EWS stands for Economically Weaker Section, the category used for reservation and for the free seats private schools must provide under the Right to Education Act.

why_wrong.1: Educationally weaker is not the term; the criterion is income, not schooling.
why_wrong.2: Society is wrong as well as educationally, so this misses twice.
why_wrong.3: Essentially is not the word. The word economically is what carries the meaning, since the classification is made by family income.

why_correct: The three-language formula was recommended by the Kothari Commission of 1964 to 1966: the mother tongue or regional language, Hindi or another Indian language, and English.

why_wrong.0: The National Policy of 1986 endorsed and continued the formula but did not originate it.
why_wrong.1: The Mudaliar Commission of 1952 dealt with secondary education and its diversified courses.
why_wrong.3: The Radhakrishnan Commission of 1948 dealt with universities. The Kothari Commission is the source of most of the structural ideas still in use, including the 10+2+3 pattern.

why_correct: Rabindranath Tagore founded Visva-Bharati at Santiniketan, beginning as a school in 1901 and becoming a university in 1921. It was declared a central university in 1951.

why_wrong.0: Rabindra Bharati University in Kolkata is named after Tagore but was founded in 1962, long after his death.
why_wrong.1: Avinashilingam University in Tamil Nadu was founded by T. S. Avinashilingam.
why_wrong.3: Calcutta University was established by the British in 1857. Named after and founded by are quite different, which is the trap in the first option.

why_correct: Swami Vivekananda defined education as the manifestation of the perfection already in man. On this view the teacher uncovers what is already present rather than adding anything from outside.

why_wrong.0: Gandhi defined education as an all-round drawing out of the best in child and man, in body, mind and spirit.
why_wrong.2: Aurobindo taught integral education, aiming at a higher consciousness.
why_wrong.3: Radhakrishnan was a philosopher and chaired the University Education Commission. All four wrote on education, so the exact wording must be matched to its author.

why_correct: Emile, or On Education was written by Jean-Jacques Rousseau in 1762. It argues for natural education, letting the child develop freely according to his own nature, and is the founding text of naturalism in education.

why_wrong.1: John Dewey wrote Democracy and Education and The School and Society.
why_wrong.2: Friedrich Frobel founded the kindergarten and wrote The Education of Man.
why_wrong.3: Maria Montessori developed the Montessori method and wrote The Montessori Method.

why_correct: Tagore held that nature is the child's best teacher, which is why classes at Santiniketan were held in the open air under the trees. He believed a child shut inside four walls is cut off from the source of learning.

why_wrong.0: Experience is central to Dewey's pragmatism rather than to Tagore's teaching.
why_wrong.1: Elders have a place, but Tagore's emphasis was on freedom rather than authority.
why_wrong.3: Discipline imposed from outside is precisely what Tagore resisted, preferring self-discipline grown in freedom.

why_correct: Savitribai Phule is regarded as India's first woman teacher. With her husband Jyotirao Phule she opened a school for girls at Pune in 1848, facing heavy social opposition.

why_wrong.1: Pandita Ramabai was a scholar and reformer who founded the Sharada Sadan for widows, a generation later.
why_wrong.2: Begum Rokeya pioneered girls' education among Muslims in Bengal in the early twentieth century.
why_wrong.3: Tarabai Shinde wrote Stri Purush Tulana, an early feminist tract, but was not a teacher.

why_correct: Inclusive education places children with special needs in ordinary classrooms and adapts the school to suit them, so that no child is separated out. It is the approach the Right to Education Act adopts.

why_wrong.0: Special schools educate such children separately, which segregates them from their peers.
why_wrong.1: Integrated education places them in ordinary schools but expects the child to adjust to the school. Inclusion reverses that: the school adjusts to the child, and that reversal is the whole distinction.
why_wrong.3: There is a correct answer, so none of these is wrong.

why_correct: The Delors Commission named four pillars: learning to know, learning to do, learning to live together and learning to be. Learning to have is not among them, and its acquisitive sense runs against the report's spirit.

why_wrong.0: Learning to be is the fourth pillar, concerning the full development of the person.
why_wrong.2: Learning to know is the first, concerning understanding and the tools of learning.
why_wrong.3: Learning to live together is the third, concerning tolerance and interdependence. The missing fourth option, learning to do, completes the set.

why_correct: Indira Gandhi National Open University was established in 1985 as India's first national open university, offering distance education across the country.

why_wrong.1: 1986 is the National Policy on Education, which endorsed open learning but came a year after IGNOU.
why_wrong.2: 1988 is after its founding.
why_wrong.3: 1966 is the year the Kothari Commission reported. Note that Andhra Pradesh Open University, now Dr B. R. Ambedkar Open University, was founded in 1982 and was India's first open university, but not a national one.

why_graced: This question has been graced: every candidate receives the mark, whatever they wrote and even if they left it blank. The Delors Commission, formally the International Commission on Education for the Twenty-first Century, was constituted by UNESCO in 1993, and its report Learning: The Treasure Within appeared in 1996. Since 1993 is not among the options, no candidate could have answered correctly, so the question was withdrawn from scoring by Umar Iqbal's ruling of 5 August 2026.

why_wrong.0: 1998 is two years after the report was even published.
why_wrong.1: 1994 is a year after the commission was set up.
why_wrong.2: 1996 is the year the report was published, which is why it is the most tempting of the four. Formation and publication are three years apart.
why_wrong.3: 1992 is a year before the commission was constituted.

why_correct: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act was passed by Parliament in 2009. It gives effect to Article 21A, which the 86th Amendment had inserted in 2002.

why_wrong.0: 2007 is before the Act was passed.
why_wrong.2: 2010 is the year it came into force, which is a separate step from being passed. That gap is exactly what this question and the last one on the paper test together.
why_wrong.3: 2008 is a year early, and nothing of note in this chain of events happened then.

why_correct: All four are objectives of the NCC. It aims to develop character, discipline and leadership, to encourage service to the community, and to provide organised recreation and adventure activity alongside them.

why_wrong.0: Entertainment sounds too light on its own, but adventure camps and organised recreation are genuinely part of the programme, so it cannot simply be dismissed.
why_wrong.1: Leadership is one of the NCC's stated aims and a central one.
why_wrong.2: Social welfare is another, through blood donation drives, tree planting and disaster relief.
why_wrong.3: Discipline is perhaps the best known of all. When each option is separately true, the combined option is the answer, and note that this question uniquely offers five choices rather than four.

why_correct: UNESCO is the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation, founded in 1946 with its headquarters in Paris. It maintains the World Heritage list.

why_wrong.1: Economical is wrong; the E stands for Educational.
why_wrong.2: Social is wrong; the S stands for Scientific.
why_wrong.3: Children is wrong, and it belongs to UNICEF, the United Nations Children's Fund. Read the acronym letter by letter and each substitution shows itself.

why_correct: For Dewey the teacher is a facilitator and guide, arranging experiences through which children learn by doing, rather than transmitting information to a passive class.

why_wrong.0: A delegator merely hands out tasks and steps back, which is not Dewey's active guiding role.
why_wrong.1: An instructor delivering knowledge is the traditional model Dewey argued against.
why_wrong.3: There is a correct answer here. Learning by doing is the phrase most associated with him.

why_correct: The Kothari Commission's report of 1966 is titled Education and National Development. Its opening line is famous: the destiny of India is now being shaped in her classrooms.

why_wrong.0: Learning Without Burden is the Yash Pal Committee report of 1993, on the weight of the curriculum.
why_wrong.1: An Enlightened and Humane Society is associated with the Acharya Ramamurti review of 1990.
why_wrong.2: Education and the People of India is not the title of this report. The word development in the title reflects the commission's central argument, that education is an investment in the nation.

why_correct: Education is in the Concurrent List, so both Parliament and the state legislatures can make laws on it. It was moved there from the State List by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.

why_wrong.1: Free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen is a fundamental right under Article 21A, but that is a right rather than a legislative list.
why_wrong.2: The Constitution as a whole is not a list.
why_wrong.3: Education was in the State List until 1976, which is why this remains the common wrong answer.

why_correct: The National Council of Educational Research and Training was established in 1961, by merging seven existing national institutions, to advise governments on school education.

why_wrong.0: 1956 is when the UGC was established as a statutory body.
why_wrong.1: 1960 is a year before NCERT was founded.
why_wrong.2: 1967 is well after. A useful anchor is that NCERT came between the Mudaliar Commission of 1952 and the Kothari Commission of 1964.

why_correct: The Fundamental Rights guarantee this. Article 25 gives freedom of religion, and Articles 29 and 30 give minorities the right to conserve their culture and to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.

why_wrong.0: Directive Principles guide state policy but are not enforceable in a court.
why_wrong.1: The Concurrent List determines who may legislate on education, not what rights citizens hold.
why_wrong.3: Democratic Right is not a category in the Constitution. Fundamental Rights are the enforceable part, which is what makes them the answer.

why_correct: The National Policy on Education 1986 recommended a National System of Education, with a common educational structure of 10+2+3 and a common core curriculum across the country.

why_wrong.1: IGNOU is a university, not a policy-making body.
why_wrong.2: NCTE regulates teacher education.
why_wrong.3: The Kothari Commission proposed the 10+2+3 structure and much of the thinking behind it, but the phrase National System of Education belongs to the 1986 policy.

why_correct: Wood's Despatch of 1854 is called the Magna Carta of English education in India. It laid down a complete scheme from primary school to university, recommended grants-in-aid and the founding of universities, and led to the three universities of 1857.

why_wrong.1: The Sergeant Report of 1944 was the last major colonial plan, proposing universal education within forty years.
why_wrong.2: Macaulay's Minute of 1835 settled the medium as English but was a short polemic rather than a complete scheme.
why_wrong.3: The Hunter Commission of 1882 reviewed the working of Wood's Despatch, so it came afterwards and built on it.

why_correct: The National Council for Teacher Education, given statutory status in 1993, is the apex body for teacher education. It lays down norms for teacher training institutions and grants them recognition.

why_wrong.0: The UGC is the apex body for higher education generally, coordinating universities and their standards.
why_wrong.1: The ministry is the government department, not a professional regulator.
why_wrong.2: NCERT advises on school education, curriculum and textbooks, but teacher education is NCTE's charge. All four are real bodies, so it is the scope of each that must be learnt.

why_correct: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act was passed by Parliament in August 2009 and received the President's assent that month, but it was brought into force on 1 April 2010, the beginning of the financial and academic year. India thus became one of the countries in which elementary education is a fundamental right of every child between six and fourteen.

why_wrong.1: 1 January 2010 is not the commencement date. Acts of this kind are normally brought into force at the start of an academic or financial year, not in the middle of one.
why_wrong.2: 1 January 2009 falls before the Act was even passed, which was in August of that year. A law cannot take effect before it exists.
why_wrong.3: 31 January 2009 is likewise months before the Act was passed. Take care to separate the year of passing, which question 14 on this same paper asks about, from the date of coming into force, which is what this question asks.

why_correct: Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms, taken at three levels: genetic diversity within a species, species diversity within an area, and ecosystem diversity across a region.

why_wrong.1: Minerals are non-living, so they belong to the abiotic environment.
why_wrong.2: Soils are abiotic too, though soil supports enormous biodiversity within it.
why_wrong.3: Industries are human creations and have nothing to do with the term. The word bio in biodiversity is the clue: it is about life.

why_correct: A biodiversity hotspot is a region exceptionally rich in species, with a high proportion found nowhere else, and under serious threat. India has four: the Himalayas, the Western Ghats, the Indo-Burma region and Sundaland.

why_wrong.0: Pollution has its own vocabulary of hotspots in casual use, but the technical term belongs to conservation.
why_wrong.2: Mining often threatens hotspots but does not define them.
why_wrong.3: Urbanisation is likewise a pressure on them rather than the meaning of the word. Norman Myers introduced the term, and a hotspot must be both rich and endangered.

why_correct: A national park conserves species in their natural habitat, so it is in-situ conservation. In situ means in place, protecting the whole living community where it already is.

why_wrong.0: A zoo keeps animals away from their habitat, which is ex-situ.
why_wrong.1: A botanical garden grows plants away from where they naturally occur, again ex-situ.
why_wrong.3: A seed bank stores seeds under controlled conditions, the clearest ex-situ method of all.

why_correct: A botanical garden conserves plants away from their natural habitat, so it is ex-situ conservation. Zoos, seed banks and gene banks work the same way.

why_wrong.0: A wildlife sanctuary protects animals in their own habitat, so it is in-situ.
why_wrong.1: A biosphere reserve protects a whole living landscape in place.
why_wrong.2: A national park is in-situ too. Three of the four options are in-situ, so the odd one out is the answer, and this question is the mirror image of the one before it.

why_correct: The Chipko Movement began in 1973 at Mandal in the Chamoli district of what is now Uttarakhand, then part of Uttar Pradesh. Villagers, mostly women, hugged trees to stop them being felled, and chipko means to cling.

why_wrong.0: West Bengal is not connected with Chipko.
why_wrong.1: Gujarat had its own environmental movements but not this one.
why_wrong.3: Kerala is associated with the Silent Valley movement of the late 1970s, which saved a rainforest from a dam. A different state and a different campaign.

why_correct: Environmental Impact Assessment is carried out before a development project such as a dam, mine, road or factory is approved, so that its likely effects can be weighed and mitigated in advance.

why_wrong.0: Ordinary agricultural activity does not require an EIA, though very large irrigation projects do.
why_wrong.2: Cultural programmes have no such requirement.
why_wrong.3: Sports events are not covered either. The point of an EIA is to look ahead, before the damage is done rather than after.

why_correct: The objective of an EIA is to identify and assess the environmental consequences of a proposed project in advance, so that harm can be avoided, reduced or compensated before work begins.

why_wrong.0: Increasing production is the project's aim, not the assessment's.
why_wrong.2: Tourism promotion is unrelated.
why_wrong.3: Population is not its subject. An EIA may recommend changes to a project, or that it not proceed at all.

why_correct: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 is India's law for controlling water pollution. It set up the Central and State Pollution Control Boards.

why_wrong.0: The Wildlife Protection Act of 1972 protects species and creates protected areas.
why_wrong.1: The Forest Conservation Act of 1980 restricts the diversion of forest land to other uses.
why_wrong.3: The Environment (Protection) Act of 1986 is the umbrella law covering the environment generally, passed after Bhopal. It is broader, whereas this question asks specifically about water.

why_correct: The Environment (Protection) Act was enacted in 1986, in the aftermath of the Bhopal gas tragedy of 1984. It is an umbrella law giving the central government wide powers over all aspects of the environment.

why_wrong.0: 1972 is the Wildlife Protection Act, and also the Stockholm Conference.
why_wrong.1: 1974 is the Water Act, which deals with water pollution alone rather than the environment generally.
why_wrong.2: 1981 is the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act. The sequence runs water in 1974, air in 1981 and the general environment law in 1986.

why_correct: The Wildlife (Protection) Act was passed in 1972, the same year as the Stockholm Conference. It created national parks and sanctuaries and listed protected species in schedules.

why_wrong.1: 1986 is the Environment (Protection) Act.
why_wrong.2: 1991 saw an important amendment to the Wildlife Act, but not its passing.
why_wrong.3: 2002 saw another amendment, adding conservation reserves and community reserves. Project Tiger was launched in 1973, the year after the Act.
