why_correct: A disaster caused by natural processes such as earthquakes, floods, cyclones and droughts is a natural disaster. Human action may worsen its effects, but the trigger is natural.

why_wrong.0: Man-made disasters are caused by human action, such as the Bhopal gas leak or an industrial fire.
why_wrong.2: Industrial disasters are a category of man-made disaster.
why_wrong.3: Social disasters such as riots are also human in origin. The classification turns on the cause, not on the scale of the damage.

why_correct: An earthquake is a natural disaster, caused by the sudden release of energy along a fault in the Earth's crust. It is a geological event that no human action initiates.

why_wrong.0: Biological disasters are epidemics and pest attacks.
why_wrong.1: Technological disasters arise from the failure of machines or systems.
why_wrong.3: Chemical disasters are leaks and spills of hazardous substances. Note that most earthquake deaths come from collapsing buildings, so how a society builds decides how disastrous the event is.

why_correct: Floods are mainly caused by excessive rainfall, particularly heavy monsoon rain that a river cannot carry away. Silting of riverbeds, deforestation and poor drainage all make them worse.

why_wrong.1: Deforestation does contribute, by increasing runoff, but the word only makes this too narrow.
why_wrong.2: Industrialisation is not a main cause of flooding.
why_wrong.3: Urbanisation contributes by covering ground with concrete so that water cannot soak in, but again only makes this wrong. Watch for absolute words in options: they are usually what makes a half-true answer fail.

why_correct: Preparedness comes first in the disaster management cycle, along with prevention and mitigation. Planning, training, early warning systems and drills are all done before a disaster strikes.

why_wrong.0: Relief comes immediately after the event, providing food, shelter and medical aid.
why_wrong.1: Rehabilitation follows relief, restoring livelihoods and normal life.
why_wrong.3: Reconstruction is the last stage, rebuilding what was destroyed. The cycle runs preparedness, response, relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction, and preparation is what most reduces the eventual loss.

why_correct: Sustainable use means using resources wisely enough to meet present needs without destroying the ability of future generations to meet their own. It is use with restraint, not without it.

why_wrong.0: Unlimited exploitation would exhaust the resource and leave nothing behind.
why_wrong.1: Ignoring the future is exactly what sustainability rules out.
why_wrong.3: Complete prohibition is the opposite extreme, and it would leave present needs unmet. Sustainability is a balance between the two, not either end.

why_correct: Solar energy is renewable, replenished continuously and impossible to exhaust by use. Wind, tidal, geothermal and biomass energy are renewable for the same reason.

why_wrong.0: Coal is a fossil fuel formed over millions of years, so it is non-renewable.
why_wrong.1: Petroleum is likewise fossil and finite.
why_wrong.3: Natural gas is a fossil fuel too. Three of the four options are fossil fuels, which makes the odd one out plain.

why_correct: The ozone layer in the stratosphere absorbs most of the sun's ultraviolet radiation, which would otherwise cause skin cancer, cataracts and damage to crops and plankton.

why_wrong.0: Infrared is heat radiation, trapped by greenhouse gases rather than by ozone. Ozone depletion and global warming are separate problems, and confusing them is the usual error here.
why_wrong.2: Radio waves pass through the atmosphere and are harmless.
why_wrong.3: Sound waves are mechanical and do not travel through space at all.

why_correct: Global warming is caused by greenhouse gases, chiefly carbon dioxide but also methane, nitrous oxide and CFCs. They absorb the infrared radiation the Earth emits and re-radiate it downwards.

why_wrong.1: Oxygen is essential to life and to burning but does not trap heat.
why_wrong.2: Nitrogen makes up most of the atmosphere yet is not a greenhouse gas.
why_wrong.3: Helium is inert and present only in traces. Abundance in the air and warming effect are quite separate things.

why_correct: The Central Pollution Control Board is the national body for environmental regulation of pollution, set up under the Water Act of 1974. It sets standards and coordinates the state boards.

why_wrong.0: The Reserve Bank of India is the central bank.
why_wrong.1: The UGC coordinates higher education.
why_wrong.3: The UPSC conducts recruitment for the central services.

why_correct: CPCB is the Central Pollution Control Board, constituted in 1974 under the Water Act and later given duties under the Air Act as well.

why_wrong.1: Public Conservation is not the phrase; the board's business is pollution.
why_wrong.2: It is a board, not a bureau, and its work is control rather than conservation.
why_wrong.3: Protection and bureau are both wrong. Read each letter: Central, Pollution, Control, Board.

why_correct: Afforestation is planting trees on land that had no forest before, such as barren or waste land. It increases forest cover and helps check erosion and absorb carbon dioxide.

why_wrong.0: Cutting forests is deforestation, the opposite.
why_wrong.2: Mining in forests destroys them.
why_wrong.3: Building industries in forests likewise removes cover. Note the related term reforestation, which is replanting where forest once stood, whereas afforestation creates forest on land that had none.

why_correct: The Bishnoi community of Rajasthan protects trees and wildlife as a matter of religious duty. In 1730 at Khejarli, Amrita Devi and more than three hundred Bishnois died hugging khejri trees to stop them being felled.

why_wrong.0: Rivers are the concern of movements such as Narmada Bachao.
why_wrong.2: Wetlands are protected under the Ramsar Convention.
why_wrong.3: Mountains are not the Bishnoi concern. The Khejarli sacrifice is regarded as the forerunner of the Chipko movement two and a half centuries later.

why_correct: A biosphere reserve protects entire ecosystems, with a strictly protected core zone, a buffer zone for research and a transition zone where people live and work. It conserves plants, animals and human culture together.

why_wrong.0: Plants alone would be a botanical reserve.
why_wrong.1: Animals alone would be a wildlife sanctuary.
why_wrong.3: Forests alone would be a forest reserve. The breadth of the concept, including the people living in it, is what distinguishes a biosphere reserve.

why_correct: Environmental legislation exists to protect the environment, by setting standards, restraining polluters and providing penalties. Everything else it does follows from that purpose.

why_wrong.0: Industrial growth is often restrained by such laws rather than promoted by them.
why_wrong.2: Trade is not their object.
why_wrong.3: Urbanisation is regulated by planning law. Such legislation gives effect to Article 48A and Article 51A(g) of the Constitution, which make protection of the environment a duty of both state and citizen.

why_correct: Our Common Future was published in 1987 by the World Commission on Environment and Development, chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland of Norway and therefore known as the Brundtland Commission. It gave sustainable development its standard definition.

why_wrong.1: UNEP is the UN Environment Programme, which set up the commission but did not write the report.
why_wrong.2: UNESCO deals with education, science and culture.
why_wrong.3: WWF is a conservation organisation working on species and habitats.

why_correct: Plate tectonic theory divides the lithosphere into seven major plates, together with a number of minor ones. The major plates are the Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian and Antarctic.

why_wrong.0: 5 is too few and leaves out the minor plates altogether.
why_wrong.2: 10 major plates overstates the count, and the word only wrongly excludes the minor ones.
why_wrong.3: 12 is the number sometimes given when several minor plates are counted as major, but the standard division is seven major plus minor. Every option except the answer contains the word only, which is what makes them wrong.

why_correct: The Himalayas were raised by the collision of the Indo-Australian plate with the Eurasian plate, which crumpled the sediments of the Tethys Sea between them. The collision continues, so the range is still rising.

why_wrong.0: The African and Eurasian plates collided to form the Alps and the Atlas mountains.
why_wrong.2: The Pacific plate meeting Eurasia produces the island arcs and trenches of Japan and the Philippines, a subduction rather than a continental collision.
why_wrong.3: The Nazca plate subducting under South America produced the Andes.

why_correct: Volcanism originates within the Earth, driven by internal heat, so it is an endogenic process. Endogenic processes build landforms up; exogenic ones wear them down.

why_wrong.0: Weathering acts at the surface through the atmosphere and water, so it is exogenic.
why_wrong.1: Erosion is exogenic, carried out by rivers, wind, glaciers and waves.
why_wrong.3: Mass wasting is the downslope movement of material under gravity, again a surface process. The dividing question is simply where the energy comes from.

why_correct: Exfoliation is physical weathering: the outer layers of rock peel away in sheets as the surface expands and contracts with heating and cooling faster than the interior. No chemical change occurs.

why_wrong.0: Chemical weathering alters the composition of the rock, through processes such as oxidation, carbonation and hydrolysis.
why_wrong.1: Biological weathering is caused by plants, animals and microbes, as when roots split rock.
why_wrong.3: River erosion involves transport by water, whereas weathering breaks rock down where it stands.

why_correct: Karst topography develops on limestone, which is dissolved by slightly acidic rainwater through carbonation. It produces caves, sinkholes, stalactites and underground drainage.

why_wrong.0: Granite is an igneous rock resistant to solution, weathering instead by exfoliation into rounded tors.
why_wrong.1: Basalt is igneous too and does not dissolve in this way.
why_wrong.3: Sandstone is porous but not soluble, so it does not form caverns of this kind. Solubility is the essential property, and only limestone has it.

why_correct: A floodplain is built by deposition, as a river in flood spreads across its valley and drops the silt it can no longer carry. Levees and deltas are formed the same way.

why_wrong.0: A gorge is cut by vertical erosion in the youthful stage of a river.
why_wrong.1: A waterfall is erosional, formed where the river crosses from hard rock to soft.
why_wrong.3: A V-shaped valley is erosional too, the classic form of a young river. Erosional features belong to the upper course and depositional ones to the lower.

why_correct: The Coriolis force arises from the rotation of the Earth, deflecting moving air and water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern. It is zero at the Equator and greatest at the poles.

why_wrong.0: Revolution is the Earth's yearly orbit around the Sun, which gives the seasons rather than this deflection.
why_wrong.2: The Moon's gravity causes tides.
why_wrong.3: Solar radiation causes the pressure differences that make winds blow, but the deflection of those winds comes from rotation.

why_correct: The doldrums, or equatorial low pressure belt, is the zone of calm near the Equator. Air rises there rather than blowing horizontally, so surface winds are light and variable, which once becalmed sailing ships for weeks.

why_wrong.0: The horse latitudes are the calm belts near 30 degrees north and south, under the subtropical highs. Also calm, but at a quite different latitude.
why_wrong.2: The polar front is where cold polar air meets warmer westerlies, around 60 degrees, and it is a zone of storms rather than calm.
why_wrong.3: The westerlies are strong winds blowing from the subtropical highs towards the poles.

why_correct: Convectional rainfall dominates the equatorial region. Intense heating makes air rise rapidly, cool and condense, giving heavy afternoon thunderstorms almost daily.

why_wrong.0: Cyclonic rainfall is associated with depressions in temperate latitudes and with tropical cyclones.
why_wrong.1: Orographic rainfall occurs where moist air is forced up over mountains, as on the windward slopes of the Western Ghats.
why_wrong.3: Frontal rainfall occurs where warm and cold air masses meet, which is characteristic of temperate regions.

why_correct: The average salinity of ocean water is about 35, meaning 35 grams of dissolved salt in every kilogram of sea water. It is properly written as 35 parts per thousand rather than as a percentage, which would be 3.5 per cent.

why_wrong.0: 15 is far too low; such water is brackish, as in the Baltic Sea.
why_wrong.1: 25 is still well below the ocean average.
why_wrong.3: 45 is far too high; salinity approaches that only in enclosed seas with heavy evaporation, such as the Red Sea or the Dead Sea. The figure to hold is 35, and the unit is parts per thousand.

why_correct: The Gulf Stream is the warm current flowing north-eastward along the eastern coast of North America and on across the Atlantic, where it keeps north-west Europe far milder than its latitude would suggest.

why_wrong.0: The Labrador Current is cold and flows south along the same coast further north. Where the two meet, off Newfoundland, fog and rich fishing grounds result.
why_wrong.1: The California Current is cold and flows along the western coast of North America.
why_wrong.3: The Peru or Humboldt Current is cold and flows along the western coast of South America.

why_correct: A biodiversity hotspot is a region exceptionally rich in endemic species, that is species found nowhere else, and at the same time under serious threat of habitat loss. Both conditions must hold.

why_wrong.0: High temperature has nothing to do with it, despite the word hot.
why_wrong.2: Deserts have low species richness and are not hotspots.
why_wrong.3: Industrial zones threaten biodiversity rather than harbouring it. India's four hotspots are the Himalayas, the Western Ghats, Indo-Burma and Sundaland.

why_correct: The tundra is characterised by permafrost, ground that stays frozen all year below a thin surface layer that thaws in summer. Only mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs can grow there.

why_wrong.0: Tropical rainforest is hot and wet all year, with the richest biodiversity on Earth.
why_wrong.1: Savanna is tropical grassland with a marked dry season.
why_wrong.3: Mediterranean regions have hot dry summers and mild wet winters. Permafrost is the defining feature, and it needs a climate cold enough that the ground never fully thaws.

why_correct: Population density is the number of people per unit area, usually per square kilometre. It measures how crowded a place is, whereas total population measures only how many people there are.

why_wrong.0: Birth rate minus death rate is the natural growth rate.
why_wrong.1: Females per thousand males is the sex ratio.
why_wrong.3: Workers as a proportion of population is the work participation rate. Each of these is a real measure, so the terms must be matched carefully.

why_correct: The demographic transition model as taught here has five stages, running from high birth and death rates, through falling death rates and then falling birth rates, to low rates in both and finally a declining population.

why_wrong.0: 3 stages is how the model is compressed in some textbooks, including NCERT, which treats it as high stationary, expanding and low stationary. Not baseless, but the fuller version separates the phases.
why_wrong.1: 4 stages is the classical version, which stops before the fifth declining stage now seen in Japan and much of Europe.
why_wrong.3: 6 stages is not a recognised form of the model.

why_correct: Nucleated or compact settlements are typical of fertile alluvial plains, where good soil and water support dense farming and houses cluster closely together, often around a well, temple or crossroads.

why_wrong.0: Dispersed settlements are found in hilly, forested or infertile country, where farms are scattered.
why_wrong.1: Isolated settlement is the extreme form of dispersal, a single dwelling standing alone.
why_wrong.3: Linear settlements follow a road, river or canal, so their shape is set by the feature they line rather than by soil fertility.

why_correct: A census town is one that meets the Census criteria without having a municipality: a population of at least 5,000, a density of at least 400 per square kilometre, and at least 75 per cent of male workers in non-agricultural work.

why_wrong.0: A metropolitan town has a population of more than a million.
why_wrong.1: A statutory town is one with a municipality, corporation or cantonment board, defined by law rather than by these numbers. Statutory against census is exactly the pair this question tests.
why_wrong.3: A municipality is a form of urban local government, which is what a census town by definition lacks.

why_correct: Uttar Pradesh is India's most populous state, with about 200 million people at the 2011 Census, more than the population of most countries.

why_wrong.0: Maharashtra is second, with about 112 million.
why_wrong.2: Bihar is third, with about 104 million, and has the highest population density among the large states.
why_wrong.3: West Bengal is fourth, with about 91 million. Note the difference between total population and density: Bihar is far more crowded than Uttar Pradesh.

why_correct: The Bhakra-Nangal project on the Sutlej is India's largest multipurpose river valley project. Bhakra dam is among the highest in the world, and the scheme provides irrigation, hydroelectricity and flood control to Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan.

why_wrong.0: The Damodar Valley Project of 1948 was India's first multipurpose project, modelled on the Tennessee Valley Authority, but it is smaller. First and largest are different titles.
why_wrong.1: The Hirakud project on the Mahanadi in Odisha has the longest earthen dam but is smaller overall.
why_wrong.3: The Tehri dam on the Bhagirathi is India's tallest dam, completed much later and controversial for the town it submerged.

why_correct: Solar energy is a non-conventional or renewable source, along with wind, tidal, geothermal and biomass. Non-conventional sources are inexhaustible and far less polluting.

why_wrong.0: Coal is a conventional fossil fuel.
why_wrong.1: Petroleum is conventional and fossil too.
why_wrong.2: Natural gas is likewise conventional. Three of the four are fossil fuels, which makes the odd one out plain.

why_correct: Chhattisgarh is the largest producer of coal in India, mining well over two hundred million tonnes a year, chiefly from the Korba coalfield. Note carefully that the question asks about production, which is how much is dug out in a year, and not about reserves, which is how much lies underground.

why_wrong.0: Odisha is a close second in production, with the Talcher and Ib valley fields, and it also holds very large reserves. It is the nearest rival to the right answer, but not the leader.
why_wrong.2: Jharkhand holds the largest coal reserves in the country and it is where Indian coal mining began, at Raniganj and Jharia, so many books call it the leading coal state. But its annual output is now below that of Chhattisgarh. Reserves and production are different things, and this was the printed key.
why_wrong.3: West Bengal has the Raniganj field, the oldest coalfield in India, but its present output is far behind the top three.

why_correct: The Green Revolution raised the output of wheat and rice above all, through high-yielding varieties, assured irrigation, chemical fertilisers and pesticides. Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh gained most.

why_wrong.0: Pulses were largely left out, and output per head actually fell, which remains a problem for Indian nutrition.
why_wrong.1: Oilseeds were the subject of the later Yellow Revolution.
why_wrong.3: Cotton is a commercial crop and was not the programme's focus. The narrowness of the gains, in crops and in regions, is one of the standard criticisms.

why_correct: Road transport carries by far the largest volume of freight in India, about seventy per cent of it, as the NCERT textbook states. Roads reach places no railway line does, they allow door to door delivery without transhipment, and they suit the small consignments and short hauls that make up most of the country's traffic.

why_wrong.0: Air transport is the fastest but carries the smallest volume of all, a tiny fraction of one per cent. It is used for goods that are light, valuable or urgent, not for bulk.
why_wrong.1: Water transport is the cheapest per tonne kilometre and is why it dominates India's overseas trade, but the inland waterways are little developed and carry very little of the country's internal freight.
why_wrong.3: Rail transport did carry the largest share until the 1980s and it still moves the heavy bulk goods, coal, iron ore, cement and foodgrains, over long distances. Road overtook it decades ago, and rail now carries roughly thirty per cent. This was the printed key.

why_correct: The World Trade Organization regulates international trade, framing the rules, hosting negotiations and settling disputes between member countries. It replaced GATT in 1995.

why_wrong.0: The IMF oversees the international monetary system and lends to countries in balance of payments difficulty.
why_wrong.1: The World Bank lends for long-term development projects.
why_wrong.3: UNDP works on human development and poverty reduction. All four are international bodies, so their functions must be learnt separately.

why_correct: The balance of trade is the difference between a country's visible exports and visible imports, that is trade in goods alone. If imports exceed exports the balance is unfavourable.

why_wrong.1: Population against resources is a matter of carrying capacity, not trade.
why_wrong.2: Total foreign investment received is a capital account item.
why_wrong.3: Government income against expenditure is the budget deficit or surplus. Note that the balance of payments is wider than the balance of trade, since it includes services, income and capital flows as well.

why_correct: Al-Qanun al-Mas'udi is Alberuni's great work on astronomy, dedicated to Sultan Mas'ud of Ghazni. It draws on Greek and Indian astronomy alike.

why_wrong.1: Kitab al-Manazir, the Book of Optics, was written by Ibn al-Haytham, a different scholar.
why_wrong.2: The Book on Astronomy is not the title of any work of his.
why_wrong.3: Alberuni's India, properly Tarikh al-Hind, is his famous account of Indian society, religion and science. His best known book, but not the astronomical one.

why_correct: Marco Polo, passing along the Indian coast in the late thirteenth century, described the king of Gujarat among the rulers he encountered, along with the region's trade and piracy.

why_wrong.0: Kumaragupta was a Gupta emperor of the fifth century, some eight hundred years before Marco Polo.
why_wrong.2: Srigupta founded the Gupta dynasty in the third century.
why_wrong.3: Rajyavardhana was Harsha's elder brother, in the seventh century. All three wrong options are far too early, so the dates alone settle the question.

why_correct: Muhammad bin Tughluq appointed Ibn Battuta qazi, or judge, of Delhi. The Moroccan traveller stayed several years and later served as envoy to China.

why_wrong.0: Ghiyasuddin Tughluq founded the dynasty and died in 1325, before Ibn Battuta arrived.
why_wrong.1: Firoz Shah Tughlaq succeeded Muhammad bin Tughluq, by which time Ibn Battuta had left India.
why_wrong.3: Abu Bakr Shah ruled briefly and much later. Ibn Battuta's Rihla is a major source for the period precisely because he served inside the administration.

why_correct: Francois Bernier, the French physician who spent years at Aurangzeb's court, is regarded as the first European to visit Kashmir. He accompanied the emperor there and described the valley in his Travels in the Mogul Empire.

why_wrong.1: Marco Polo travelled along the Indian coast and through Central Asia but did not reach Kashmir.
why_wrong.2: Vasco da Gama landed at Calicut in 1498, on the far southern coast.
why_wrong.3: Niccolo Conti was a fifteenth-century Venetian who described Vijayanagara in the south.

why_correct: Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, the French jeweller who made six voyages to the East, described the magnificence of Shah Jahan's court and famously reported on the Peacock Throne and the great diamonds.

why_wrong.0: Babur founded the empire in 1526 and died in 1530, long before Tavernier's time.
why_wrong.1: Humayun ruled in the mid sixteenth century.
why_wrong.3: Aurangzeb was on the throne during part of Tavernier's later visits, but the court he is famous for describing in its splendour is Shah Jahan's.

why_correct: Niccolao Manucci's account is Storia do Mogor, a long and vivid history of the Mughals based on nearly sixty years spent in India as a soldier and physician.

why_wrong.0: A Passage to India is E. M. Forster's novel of 1924.
why_wrong.2: The Wonder That Was India is A. L. Basham's modern history, published in 1954.
why_wrong.3: The Voyage to India is not the title of his work. Manucci's value is that he wrote from long residence rather than a brief visit.

why_correct: Manucci was Venetian and wrote Storia do Mogor chiefly in Italian, though the manuscript mixes in Portuguese and French, reflecting the many languages he used in India.

why_wrong.0: Spanish was not his language.
why_wrong.1: Portuguese appears in the manuscript, since it was the common European language of trade in the East, but it is not the main one.
why_wrong.2: French also appears, and the first published version was in French, which is why this is a fair guess. The author himself was Italian.

why_correct: Karaikkal Ammaiyar is the female Bhakti saint named in the Tirumurai, the Tamil Shaiva canon. She is one of the sixty-three Nayanars and among the earliest of them.

why_wrong.0: Kanni Pannayar is not a recognised saint of this canon.
why_wrong.2: Tilakavatiyar was the sister of the saint Appar, remembered for bringing him back to Shaivism, but she is not the figure named here.
why_wrong.3: Iyarpagai Nacciyar is not among the Nayanars. Karaikkal Ammaiyar is remarkable for asking to be freed from her beauty so that she could worship as a devotee.

why_correct: Guru Nanak was born in 1469 at Talwandi, in what is now Pakistan. The village was renamed Nankana Sahib in his honour and is a major place of Sikh pilgrimage.

why_wrong.0: Vehari is a town in Punjab, Pakistan, with no such association.
why_wrong.2: Gojra is another Punjabi town unconnected with his birth.
why_wrong.3: Kamalia is likewise unconnected. The name to remember is Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib.

why_correct: Mirabai's devotional poems are addressed to Lord Krishna, whom she regarded as her husband. A Rajput princess, she abandoned rank and family for that devotion, and her padas are still sung.

why_wrong.0: Durga is not the object of her devotion, though she is worshipped widely in the Bhakti period.
why_wrong.1: Lakshmi is not the deity she addresses.
why_wrong.2: Saraswati is not either. Mirabai belongs to the Vaishnava saguna tradition, which worships God with form and attributes.

why_correct: Baba Farid, or Fariduddin Ganjshakar, was a leading Chishti Sufi of the thirteenth century in Punjab and did much to spread Sufism in India. Some of his verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib.

why_wrong.0: Abu Bakr was the first caliph of Islam and never came to India.
why_wrong.1: Muhammad Iqbal was a twentieth-century poet and philosopher, far too late.
why_wrong.3: Al-Bukhari was a ninth-century compiler of hadith in Central Asia. Only one of the four is an Indian Sufi, which settles the question.

why_correct: Alauddin Hussain Shah, who ruled Bengal from 1494 to 1519, is called the Akbar of Bengal for his tolerance, his patronage of Bengali literature and the prosperity of his reign.

why_wrong.0: Sayyed Hussain is not the name by which this ruler is known.
why_wrong.1: Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah founded the independent sultanate of Bengal in the fourteenth century and first united the region.
why_wrong.3: Jalaluddin Muhammad Shah was a fifteenth-century sultan of Bengal, a convert and a patron of building, but not the one so called. Chaitanya lived during Hussain Shah's reign, which is part of why it is remembered as a golden age.

why_correct: Magellan sailed under commission from the Spanish Crown, funded by King Charles I, to find a westward route to the Spice Islands. His expedition made the first circumnavigation of the globe, though he died on the way.

why_wrong.0: The British Crown sponsored other voyages but not this one.
why_wrong.2: The French Crown was not involved.
why_wrong.3: Magellan was himself Portuguese, which makes this the natural wrong answer, but Portugal refused to back him and he took his plan to Spain instead.

why_correct: Nelson Mandela became South Africa's first black President in 1994, after the first elections held under universal franchise. He had spent twenty-seven years in prison under apartheid.

why_wrong.0: F. W. de Klerk was the last President under apartheid, who released Mandela and shared the Nobel Peace Prize with him.
why_wrong.2: Jomo Kenyatta was the first President of Kenya.
why_wrong.3: Kwame Nkrumah led Ghana to independence and was its first leader. All three are real figures of the same history, so the country must be matched carefully.

why_correct: The Jim Crow laws, enacted across the southern United States from the 1870s and in force until the Civil Rights Act of 1964, required Black and White Americans to be kept apart in schools, railway carriages, buses, waiting rooms, restaurants and even drinking fountains, and they stripped Black citizens of the vote through literacy tests, poll taxes and grandfather clauses. Their purpose was segregation and the maintenance of White supremacy. The name itself comes from a mocking stage caricature of a Black man, which tells you the spirit in which the laws were made.

why_wrong.0: The laws did the opposite of promoting the cause of Black Americans. They were passed in the decades after Reconstruction precisely to undo the political and civil gains Black Americans had just won.
why_wrong.1: Ending racial discrimination was the work of the movement that fought these laws, of Rosa Parks, Martin Luther King and the Montgomery boycott, and it was achieved by the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which dismantled Jim Crow.
why_wrong.2: This is the separate but equal formula upheld by the Supreme Court in Plessy versus Ferguson in 1896, the very words the laws hid behind. The separation was real and the equality was not: Black schools, carriages and hospitals were deliberately starved of funds. In Brown versus Board of Education in 1954 the Court held that separate is inherently unequal and overturned the doctrine. This was the printed key, and it has been corrected, because to leave it standing would be to teach that segregation promoted equality.

why_correct: The Holocaust was carried out during the Second World War, between 1941 and 1945, when the Nazi regime systematically murdered around six million Jews along with Roma, disabled people and others.

why_wrong.0: The First World War ended in 1918, well before the Nazis came to power in 1933.
why_wrong.2: The Soviet-Japanese conflict was a separate theatre of the same war in the Far East.
why_wrong.3: The Battle of Sedan belongs to the Franco-Prussian War of 1870, though a second battle of that name was fought in 1940.

why_correct: The World Bank was established in 1944 at the Bretton Woods Conference, alongside the International Monetary Fund. It began operations in 1946.

why_wrong.1: 1945 is the year the United Nations was founded and the war ended.
why_wrong.2: 1946 is when the Bank actually began lending, so it is a fair guess. Established and began operations are two years apart here.
why_wrong.3: 1950 is well after both. Bretton Woods in 1944 is the anchor date for the whole post-war financial system.

why_correct: Sir Thomas Roe was the first English ambassador to India, sent by James I to the court of Jahangir from 1615 to 1619. He secured trading rights for the East India Company.

why_wrong.0: William Norris was sent much later, in 1699, by a rival English company.
why_wrong.2: James Fraser was an eighteenth-century traveller and scholar.
why_wrong.3: William Hawkins reached Jahangir's court in 1609, before Roe, but he came as a Company representative rather than as an accredited royal ambassador. That distinction is what the question turns on.

why_correct: Pitt's India Act of 1784 was introduced by William Pitt the Younger, then Prime Minister. It created the Board of Control, giving the British government authority over the East India Company's political affairs.

why_wrong.0: William Jones was a judge and orientalist who founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal.
why_wrong.2: Warren Hastings was Governor-General in India at the time, not a British Prime Minister, and he was later impeached.
why_wrong.3: William Pitt the Elder was his father, Prime Minister a generation earlier during the Seven Years War. Father and son are the trap here, and the Act belongs to the son.

why_correct: After 1929 the imperial powers turned inward and taxed imports to shield their own producers, Britain through the Import Duties Act of 1932 and the Ottawa agreements with the dominions. Protectionism is the word for that new policy, and it is the change in attitude the question is after.

why_wrong.0: This is the same shift seen from the other side, and it is true that Britain gave up free trade after 1929. What the question wants named is the policy that took its place, and that policy is protectionism.
why_wrong.2: Decolonisation did not follow immediately. India became independent in 1947 and most African colonies only in the 1950s and 1960s, two decades and more after the Depression.
why_wrong.3: The Reserve Bank of India was set up under the RBI Act of 1934 and began work in 1935, on the recommendation of the Hilton Young Commission of 1926. It was planned well before the Depression, not caused by it.

why_correct: Statements one and three are true. The Ilbert Bill of 1883 would have allowed Indian judges to try Europeans, which increased their powers and removed a racial distinction in the judicial service.

why_wrong.1: Statement two contradicts statement one, and it was powers being increased that caused the outcry.
why_wrong.2: Statement four is false. The British community in India protested furiously and forced the bill to be watered down, which taught Indians the value of organised agitation.
why_wrong.3: This reverses the truth entirely. The episode is often called a lesson in agitation that fed directly into the founding of the Congress in 1885.

why_correct: Of these four, Lord Elgin came first. Elgin served as Viceroy in the 1860s, followed by Curzon from 1899, Wavell from 1943 and Mountbatten in 1947, who was the last.

why_wrong.0: Lord Wavell was Viceroy from 1943 to 1947, during the war and the negotiations that followed.
why_wrong.1: Lord Mountbatten was the last Viceroy, overseeing the transfer of power in 1947, so he is the latest of the four.
why_wrong.3: Lord Curzon was Viceroy from 1899 to 1905 and is remembered for the partition of Bengal. Placing the four in order gives Elgin, Curzon, Wavell, Mountbatten.

why_correct: Both statements are true and the reason does explain the assertion. The Treaty of Versailles imposed crushing reparations, territorial losses and the war guilt clause, and the resentment that followed was exactly what Hitler exploited to build support.

why_wrong.1: The reason is not merely true alongside the assertion; it is the cause of it. In assertion-reason questions the more precise correct option is the answer.
why_wrong.2: Both statements are correct, so this fails at once.
why_wrong.3: The assertion is correct. The link between Versailles and the rise of Nazism is one of the best established explanations in modern history.

why_correct: The passage says civil servants from all the presidencies trained at Fort William College before taking up their postings, so its aim was to prepare British civil servants for administrative work in India, chiefly by teaching them Indian languages.

why_wrong.1: The passage speaks of civil servants, not Indian leaders, and Indians were not being trained to govern.
why_wrong.2: Merchants are not mentioned, and the College trained administrators rather than traders.
why_wrong.3: The local population is not mentioned either. Answer a case-based question from the passage itself rather than from wider knowledge.

why_correct: Locke held that substance is the unknown substratum in which the primary qualities inhere. He called it a something, he knew not what, since we perceive qualities and never the thing that bears them.

why_wrong.0: Plato's reality is the world of Forms, which is quite a different account.
why_wrong.2: Descartes defined substance as that which needs nothing else to exist, and admitted thinking and extended substance, but the substratum of primary qualities is Locke's formulation.
why_wrong.3: Leibniz held that substances are monads, simple and windowless, with no material substratum at all.

why_correct: For Kant, causality is one of the twelve categories of the understanding, an a priori form the mind itself brings to experience rather than something it reads off from the world. We do not find the causal connection in what we observe; we supply it, and that is why the causal law can be both necessary and universal. This was Kant's answer to Hume, who he said had woken him from his dogmatic slumber.

why_wrong.0: Locke holds that the mind begins as a blank slate and that every idea, causality included, comes from experience. That is the opposite of treating it as a form the intellect already possesses.
why_wrong.1: Hume is the tempting answer because he is the philosopher most associated with the problem of causation, and this was the printed key. But his view is that we observe only constant conjunction and that the idea of necessary connection is a habit of expectation in the mind, a psychological association rather than a form of the intellect. Question 6 on this same paper keys Hume correctly for that view.
why_wrong.2: Ewing is a modern writer whose survey of the theories of causation appears in this chapter, so his name is familiar from the same pages. But the doctrine that causality is an a priori form of the understanding is Kant's; Ewing discusses it rather than originating it.

why_correct: Shankara is regarded as the first systematic preacher of Advaita Vedanta. In a short life in the eighth century he wrote commentaries on the Upanishads, the Gita and the Brahma Sutra, and founded four monasteries across India.

why_wrong.1: Ramanuja founded Vishishtadvaita, or qualified non-dualism, in the eleventh century.
why_wrong.2: Gaudapada was Shankara's teacher's teacher and wrote the Mandukya Karika, so he prepared the ground. But it was Shankara who built the system and preached it across the country.
why_wrong.3: Vacaspati Mishra was a later commentator on Shankara's work, founder of the Bhamati school.

why_correct: Maya has two functions: avarana, which conceals the true nature of Brahman, and vikshepa, which projects the appearance of the world in its place. Together they explain why the one reality appears as many.

why_wrong.0: Brahman is what is concealed, not the concealer.
why_wrong.1: Jiva is the individual soul, itself a product of Brahman appearing under maya.
why_wrong.2: Jagat is the world, which is what maya projects. The rope-and-snake illustration captures both functions: the rope is hidden and the snake is thrown up in its place.

why_correct: Shankara's system is Kevaladvaitavada, absolute or unqualified non-dualism. Brahman alone is real, the world of appearances is maya, and the individual self is not merely similar to Brahman but identical with it. The prefix kevala, meaning only or absolute, is what marks it off from the other Vedanta schools.

why_wrong.1: Vishishtadvaitavada, qualified non-dualism, is Ramanuja's. Brahman is real and one, but the souls and matter are equally real and form its body, so the unity is a qualified one. This was the printed key.
why_wrong.2: Dvaitadvaitavada, dualistic non-dualism, is Nimbarka's, on which the soul is both different from and non-different from Brahman.
why_wrong.3: Dvaitavada, dualism, is Madhva's, on which Brahman and the individual soul are eternally and completely distinct. It is the furthest of the four from Shankara.

why_correct: Hume argued that we never observe a necessary connection between cause and effect, only their constant conjunction. The sense of necessity is a habit of expectation formed in the mind, so the relation is psychological rather than logical.

why_wrong.1: Ewing was a twentieth-century philosopher who discussed such theories rather than originating this one.
why_wrong.2: Kant answered Hume by making causality an a priori category of the understanding, which restores its necessity rather than reducing it to habit.
why_wrong.3: Russell went further still and argued that mature science can dispense with the notion of cause altogether.

why_correct: Advaita accepts the reality of Brahman alone. Brahman is real, the world is appearance, and the individual soul is not different from Brahman, which is the whole doctrine in one line.

why_wrong.1: The jiva, or individual soul, is ultimately identical with Brahman rather than a separate reality.
why_wrong.2: The jagat, or world, is vyavaharika, real for practical purposes but not ultimately real.
why_wrong.3: There is a definite answer, so none of these is wrong. Advaita means not two, and that is what the doctrine asserts.

why_correct: Kant's ethics is deontological, judging an act by the duty behind it rather than by its results. His test is the categorical imperative: act only on a maxim you can will to become a universal law.

why_wrong.0: Teleological ethics judges by consequences, which is utilitarianism and precisely what Kant rejected.
why_wrong.2: Kant does not combine the two. For him an act done for the sake of good results, rather than from duty, has no moral worth at all.
why_wrong.3: There is a correct answer here. The word deon means duty, which fixes the term.

why_correct: The family is the smallest unit of society. It is the first group a person belongs to and the one in which the basic habits, language and values are learnt.

why_wrong.1: A school is a secondary institution, entered later and left behind.
why_wrong.2: A place of worship is a voluntary association.
why_wrong.3: A university is a specialised institution of higher learning. The family is universal, found in every society, which the others are not.

why_correct: MacIver defined society as a web of social relationships. The image is exact: society is not the people themselves but the network of relations among them.

why_wrong.1: Gisbert defined society as a group working together for common ends.
why_wrong.2: Ginsberg defined it as a collection of individuals united by certain relations.
why_wrong.3: Mackenzie also wrote on the subject. All four are sociologists offering definitions, so the exact wording must be matched to its author.

why_correct: The unchecked exploitation of nature, through deforestation, over-extraction of resources, pollution of air and water and the burning of fossil fuels, has produced what is called the environmental crisis: global warming, loss of biodiversity, shrinking water supplies and degraded land. It is the term the chapter uses, and it names the whole of the damage rather than one part of it.

why_wrong.0: An individual crisis is a crisis in a single person's life. It is not what follows from a country exploiting its natural resources, and nothing in the chapter connects the two. This was the printed key.
why_wrong.2: There is a real moral dimension here, and the chapter does argue that our treatment of nature is an ethical failure and that we owe a duty to future generations. But the problem countries are described as facing is the environmental crisis itself; the moral question is why it arose, not what it is.
why_wrong.3: Loss of habitat is genuinely one part of the damage, for wildlife and for displaced people alike. It is too narrow, though: environmental crisis is the wider term that includes it along with pollution, climate change and resource depletion.

why_correct: Ecology concerns the mutual interdependence of organisms with one another and with their surroundings. Animals, trees and plants form a single web in which each depends on the others.

why_wrong.1: Environmental ethics asks what our moral duties towards nature are, which is a question of value rather than a description of relationships.
why_wrong.2: Deep ecology is a particular philosophical movement holding that all living things have intrinsic worth regardless of human use.
why_wrong.3: Shallow ecology values nature for human benefit. Both deep and shallow ecology are ethical positions, whereas ecology itself describes how the web actually works.

why_correct: In the strict sociological sense an institution is an established set of norms and procedures for meeting a social need, so marriage is an institution. Institutions are rules, not bodies of people.

why_wrong.0: The family is an association or group, that is people organised together. Marriage is the institution through which families are formed, which is exactly the distinction being drawn.
why_wrong.1: A school is likewise an association, while education is the institution.
why_wrong.2: The state is an association too, while government is the institution through which it acts.

why_correct: Educational sociology is the application of sociological principles to education, using what is known about society to shape aims, curriculum and method.

why_wrong.0: Sociology of education studies education as a social institution, looking at it from outside. The direction of application is opposite, and that is the distinction.
why_wrong.2: Social foundation of education is a broader descriptive phrase rather than this technical term.
why_wrong.3: Social science of education is not an established term at all.

why_correct: The family educates informally, through imitation, affection and the routine of daily life. There is no syllabus, no timetable and no trained teacher, yet the influence is the deepest a child receives.

why_wrong.0: Formal education needs a curriculum and an institution, which the family has not.
why_wrong.2: Deliberate is wrong because most family learning is unplanned. Parents teach some things on purpose, but that is not what characterises the agency.
why_wrong.3: Regular suggests a timetable. Family influence is constant rather than scheduled.

why_correct: The school gives formal education: planned, deliberate, organised by a curriculum and delivered by trained teachers within a fixed timetable.

why_wrong.1: Informal education is what the home and the playground give, without any plan.
why_wrong.2: Highly standardised describes one feature of schooling rather than naming the category.
why_wrong.3: Traditional describes a style of teaching, not the type of agency. The category asked for is formal, and the other options describe qualities within it.

why_correct: A social class is a group of people similar in certain respects, above all in income, occupation and education, who share a broadly similar position and way of life.

why_wrong.0: Social order is the general arrangement of a society that keeps it stable.
why_wrong.2: Social hierarchy is the ranking of classes one above another, so it describes the arrangement rather than the group.
why_wrong.3: A social system is the whole set of interrelated institutions. Class is distinguished from caste by being open: a person can move between classes but is born into a caste.

why_correct: Advaita's theory of liberation rests mainly on the Upanishads, whose great sayings such as Tat tvam asi, that thou art, assert the identity of the individual soul with Brahman.

why_wrong.0: The Vedas in their earlier ritual portions deal with sacrifice and the fruits of action rather than with liberation.
why_wrong.2: The Gita is one of the three foundational texts Shankara commented on, so it is not baseless, but the doctrine of identity comes from the Upanishads.
why_wrong.3: The Brahma Sutra is the third of those texts and systematises Upanishadic teaching, again resting on it rather than replacing it.

why_correct: Liberation in Advaita Vedanta is moksha, the realisation that the self is Brahman and the consequent release from the cycle of birth and death. It comes through knowledge rather than through works.

why_wrong.0: Nirvana is the Buddhist term, the extinction of craving and suffering.
why_wrong.1: Apavarga is the term used in the Nyaya and Vaisheshika schools.
why_wrong.3: There is a proper term, so none of these is wrong. Each tradition has its own word, and matching word to school is what the question tests.

why_correct: India's present system of primary education draws mainly on Gandhi's philosophy, with its emphasis on the mother tongue, free and compulsory schooling, learning through a productive craft and education for character.

why_wrong.0: Tagore's Santiniketan model, teaching in the open air in communion with nature, has influenced particular schools rather than the national system.
why_wrong.1: Vivekananda's man-making education shaped ideals more than institutional arrangements.
why_wrong.3: Sri Aurobindo's integral education is practised at Pondicherry and in a few schools. Gandhi's Basic Education, or Nai Talim, was adopted as national policy after independence.

why_correct: The centre of education at Pondicherry grew under Sri Aurobindo, who settled there in 1910 and founded his ashram, with the Mother carrying the work forward into the Sri Aurobindo International Centre of Education.

why_wrong.0: Gandhi founded ashrams at Sabarmati and Sevagram and the scheme of Basic Education.
why_wrong.2: Tagore founded Visva-Bharati at Santiniketan in Bengal.
why_wrong.3: Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission. Each of the four is associated with one place, and Pondicherry is Aurobindo's.

why_correct: Vivekananda included religion, philosophy, the Upanishads and the Puranas in order to develop the child spiritually. For him education was the manifestation of the perfection already within, and that perfection is spiritual.

why_wrong.1: Intellectual development mattered to him, but these particular subjects were chosen for their spiritual content.
why_wrong.2: Propagating Indian culture was a result he welcomed rather than the purpose of including them.
why_wrong.3: Complete development of personality is a broader aim he certainly held, and it is the most tempting distractor. But the question asks what these specific subjects were included to achieve, and that is spiritual growth.

why_correct: Vivekananda's philosophy came chiefly from Vedanta, which he interpreted as Practical Vedanta: the divinity within every person, and service to humanity as service to God.

why_wrong.0: He respected Buddhism and spoke of the Buddha with reverence, but his own position was Vedantic.
why_wrong.2: Sankhya is a dualist school, quite unlike his non-dualism.
why_wrong.3: Plato's idealism is Western and had no direct part in forming his thought. His teacher Ramakrishna is the other great influence on him.

why_correct: Gandhi combined all three. He is a naturalist in trusting the child's natural growth, an idealist in making truth and non-violence the aims of education, and a pragmatist in teaching through a productive craft and learning by doing.

why_wrong.0: Naturalist alone captures only his trust in nature and free growth.
why_wrong.1: Idealist alone captures only his moral and spiritual aims.
why_wrong.3: Pragmatist alone captures only his craft-centred method. Each is true in part, which is exactly why the combined option is the answer.

why_correct: Philosophy comes from the Greek philos, meaning love, and sophia, meaning wisdom or knowledge, so it literally means love of wisdom. The word is credited to Pythagoras.

why_wrong.1: Criticism is one activity of philosophy but not what the word means.
why_wrong.2: A particular method is not the literal meaning either; philosophy uses several methods.
why_wrong.3: There is a correct answer, so none of these is wrong. The literal sense matters: a philosopher is one who loves and seeks wisdom rather than one who possesses it.

why_correct: A bipolar world means power concentrated in two opposing military blocs, the Western alliance led by the United States and the Eastern bloc led by the Soviet Union. Most other states were drawn towards one pole or the other.

why_wrong.1: The division of Germany was a consequence and a symbol of bipolarity, not the meaning of the term.
why_wrong.2: NATO and the UN were not rivals. NATO's rival was the Warsaw Pact, and the UN included both blocs.
why_wrong.3: The two superpowers were not confined to Europe. Their rivalry was worldwide, from Korea and Vietnam to Cuba and Afghanistan, which is precisely what made the world bipolar rather than the continent.

why_correct: The dissolution of the Soviet Union in December 1991 ended the Cold War, leaving the United States as the sole superpower and the world unipolar.

why_wrong.0: The Korean War of 1950 to 1953 was an early episode of the Cold War, not its end.
why_wrong.1: The Vietnam War ended in 1975, with the Cold War continuing for another sixteen years.
why_wrong.3: NATO was formed in 1949, at the beginning of the confrontation. The fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 is the other event commonly cited, but the Soviet collapse is the formal end.

why_correct: The Bandung Conference of 1955 brought together twenty-nine Asian and African states and is regarded as the precursor of the Non-Aligned Movement, which was formally founded at Belgrade in 1961.

why_wrong.0: NATO was formed in 1949 as a Western military alliance, the opposite of non-alignment.
why_wrong.1: The Warsaw Pact was formed in 1955 as the Soviet bloc's answer to NATO, in the same year but for the opposite purpose.
why_wrong.3: The European Union grew from the European Economic Community, an entirely separate development.

why_correct: Ronald Reagan was President of the United States in the 1980s and a leader of one of the two blocs, so he could not be a founder of a movement defined by refusing to join either. The founders were Nehru, Tito, Nasser, Sukarno and Nkrumah.

why_wrong.0: Nehru of India was among the founders and gave the movement much of its philosophy.
why_wrong.1: Tito of Yugoslavia hosted the first summit at Belgrade in 1961.
why_wrong.2: Nasser of Egypt was the third of the central figures. All three belong to the 1950s and 1960s, while Reagan belongs to the 1980s and to the opposite camp.

why_correct: The General Assembly may discuss and make recommendations on any matter within the scope of the Charter. All member states sit in it with one vote each, which makes it the most representative organ.

why_wrong.0: The Security Council deals specifically with international peace and security, and its scope is narrower even though its powers are stronger.
why_wrong.2: The Secretariat is the administrative arm, headed by the Secretary-General.
why_wrong.3: The International Court of Justice settles legal disputes between states and gives advisory opinions.

why_correct: The Security Council has five permanent members: China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States. Each holds the power of veto.

why_wrong.0: 10 is the number of non-permanent members, elected for two-year terms.
why_wrong.1: 12 is not a figure used in the Council's composition.
why_wrong.3: 15 is the total membership, that is 5 permanent plus 10 non-permanent. All three wrong options are real numbers from the same body, so the question is which one it asks for.

why_correct: The International Court of Justice sits at the Peace Palace in The Hague, in the Netherlands. It is the only principal organ of the UN not based in New York.

why_wrong.0: Geneva houses the UN Office at Geneva, the WHO and the ILO.
why_wrong.1: New York is the UN headquarters, where the other principal organs meet.
why_wrong.3: Paris is the headquarters of UNESCO.

why_correct: UNICEF, the United Nations Children's Fund, is the agency for children's welfare. It works on child health, nutrition, education and protection, and was set up in 1946 for children affected by the war.

why_wrong.0: The WHO deals with public health generally, for people of all ages.
why_wrong.1: UNESCO deals with education, science and culture.
why_wrong.3: The ILO deals with labour standards, including the abolition of child labour, which is a real overlap but a different mandate.

why_correct: Human security shifts the focus from the state to the individual, holding that people should be secure from hunger, disease, poverty and violence, not merely that borders should be defended.

why_wrong.0: Military strength alone is the traditional conception of security, which human security was framed to broaden.
why_wrong.1: Protecting borders is again the traditional state-centred view.
why_wrong.3: Nuclear deterrence is a traditional security instrument. The whole point of the concept is that a state can be militarily secure while its people are not.

why_correct: Climate change is a non-traditional security threat: it endangers lives and livelihoods without any armed attack, crosses borders freely, and cannot be met by military means. Epidemics, terrorism and human trafficking belong to the same category.

why_wrong.0: Border invasion is the classic traditional threat, one state attacking another.
why_wrong.1: Nuclear war is traditional too, involving state armed force.
why_wrong.3: A military coup is an internal use of armed force, still within the traditional frame. The test is whether the threat comes from military force between or within states.

why_correct: Global warming is an environmental security threat. It endangers food supplies, coastlines and water resources without any use of force, and no country can meet it alone.

why_wrong.0: Traditional threats involve military force between states.
why_wrong.2: Military security concerns armies and armed attack.
why_wrong.3: Nuclear security concerns weapons and their proliferation. Rising seas may drown low-lying island states entirely, which is a threat to national survival by wholly non-military means.

why_correct: Terrorism deliberately targets civilians to create fear and force political change, so it threatens both lives and the stability of governments. Its victims are chosen precisely because they are defenceless.

why_wrong.0: Terrorism may prompt cooperation against it, but that is a response rather than what makes it a challenge.
why_wrong.2: It undermines democracy rather than promoting it, by driving states towards emergency powers.
why_wrong.3: It raises international tensions rather than reducing them.

why_correct: Linguistic reorganisation was an immediate challenge after independence. Agitation, notably Potti Sriramulu's fast unto death, led to Andhra Pradesh in 1953 and then to the States Reorganisation Act of 1956.

why_wrong.0: Cyber security is a twenty-first-century concern.
why_wrong.2: Space exploration began for India with the founding of INCOSPAR in 1962 and ISRO in 1969.
why_wrong.3: Artificial intelligence is a recent challenge altogether. The three challenges of nation-building in 1947 were territorial integration, refugee rehabilitation and the reorganisation of states.

why_correct: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, as Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, integrated over five hundred princely states into the Indian Union, using persuasion, the instrument of accession and, in a few cases, force. He is called the Iron Man of India.

why_wrong.0: Nehru was Prime Minister and led foreign policy, leaving integration largely to Patel.
why_wrong.1: Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constitution.
why_wrong.3: Rajendra Prasad presided over the Constituent Assembly and became the first President. V. P. Menon worked closely with Patel as the civil servant who drafted the accession scheme.

why_correct: NATO was formed in 1949 as a Western military alliance and had nothing to do with India's nation-building. It is an external event, not an internal challenge.

why_wrong.0: Refugee rehabilitation was an immense challenge after Partition displaced millions.
why_wrong.1: National integration was a challenge, holding together a country of many languages, religions and regions.
why_wrong.2: Reorganisation of states was the third great task, settled by the Act of 1956. The three genuine challenges are exactly the ones this question lists alongside the odd one out.

why_correct: A political party is an organised group of people sharing a broad programme who seek to capture political power through elections. Seeking power itself, rather than merely influencing it, is what defines a party.

why_wrong.0: A pressure group seeks to influence those in power without contesting elections itself. That is exactly the distinction being tested.
why_wrong.2: A social movement seeks change in society and may or may not enter politics.
why_wrong.3: A government department is part of the administration, not a competitor for power.

why_correct: The Indian National Congress dominated the first two decades after independence, winning the elections of 1952, 1957 and 1962 comfortably. Political scientists call this the era of one-party dominance.

why_wrong.0: The Bharatiya Jana Sangh, founded in 1951, was a small opposition party in this period.
why_wrong.1: The Communist Party of India was the main opposition but never came close to power at the centre, though it formed a government in Kerala in 1957.
why_wrong.3: The Swatantra Party was founded only in 1959. Dominance here came through free elections, which distinguishes it from a one-party state.

why_correct: A multi-party system is one in which several parties compete for power, and governments are often formed by coalition. India has such a system, with national and state parties alike.

why_wrong.0: A single party describes a one-party system, as in China.
why_wrong.2: Rule by military leaders is a military dictatorship, in which parties are usually banned.
why_wrong.3: Without elections there is no party competition at all.

why_correct: Judicial review is the power of the courts to examine whether laws conform to the Constitution. It belongs to the judiciary and is quite separate from the work of political parties.

why_wrong.0: Political recruitment is a party function, bringing people into politics and selecting candidates.
why_wrong.1: Interest articulation is a party function too, gathering demands and voicing them.
why_wrong.3: Political education is another, informing citizens and shaping opinion. Three of the four are textbook party functions, so the judicial one stands out.

why_correct: India's foreign policy rests on constitutional values, including the promotion of international peace under Article 51, together with the national interest in security and development.

why_wrong.0: Colonial interests are what India's foreign policy was framed against, having emerged from colonial rule itself.
why_wrong.2: Military alliances were deliberately avoided under non-alignment.
why_wrong.3: Expansionism has never been an Indian objective. Article 51 is a Directive Principle, and it expressly directs the state to promote international peace and security.

why_correct: Non-alignment has been the cornerstone of India's foreign policy since independence: refusing to join either Cold War bloc while retaining freedom to judge each issue on its merits. Nehru was its principal architect.

why_wrong.0: Colonialism is what India fought to end, and it supported anti-colonial movements elsewhere.
why_wrong.2: Isolationism means withdrawing from world affairs, which India never did. Non-alignment is active engagement without alliance, and confusing the two is the common error here.
why_wrong.3: Imperialism has never been an Indian policy.

why_correct: The Panchsheel Agreement was signed in 1954 between India and China, in the agreement on trade with Tibet. Nehru and Zhou Enlai gave it the slogan Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai.

why_wrong.0: India and Pakistan signed the Indus Waters Treaty in 1960 and the Simla Agreement in 1972.
why_wrong.2: No such agreement was made with the United States.
why_wrong.3: India and the USSR signed a treaty of peace and friendship in 1971. The 1962 war with China showed how little the Panchsheel principles had secured.

why_correct: The five principles are mutual respect for territorial integrity and sovereignty, mutual non-aggression, non-interference in each other's internal affairs, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence. A military alliance is the opposite of all of them.

why_wrong.0: Mutual respect for territorial integrity is the first principle.
why_wrong.1: Mutual non-aggression is the second.
why_wrong.3: Peaceful coexistence is the fifth and the best known. An alliance against common enemies would contradict both non-aggression and non-alignment.

why_correct: India supported anti-colonial struggles in Asia and Africa because it believed every people has the right to self-determination and freedom, a conviction drawn from its own experience of colonial rule.

why_wrong.0: Imperialism is the domination India opposed.
why_wrong.1: Colonialism is what those struggles were against.
why_wrong.3: Military expansion was never the aim. India's opposition to apartheid in South Africa, raised at the UN from 1946, is the clearest example of this commitment.

why_correct: India's contemporary foreign policy pursues global cooperation together with strategic autonomy, engaging widely with many partners while keeping freedom of decision. It is non-alignment adapted to a world that is no longer bipolar.

why_wrong.0: Territorial expansion is no part of Indian policy.
why_wrong.2: India joins groupings such as BRICS and the Quad but avoids binding military blocs.
why_wrong.3: Political isolation is the opposite of the extensive engagement India now pursues.

why_correct: Goodwill is an intangible asset. It has real value and can be bought and sold with the business, but it has no physical existence, being the reputation and earning capacity built up over time.

why_wrong.0: A tangible asset can be touched, such as machinery or a building.
why_wrong.1: A fictitious asset has no value at all and is only an unwritten-off expense, such as preliminary expenses. Goodwill is often confused with these, but goodwill is genuinely valuable.
why_wrong.3: A current asset is expected to be converted into cash within a year, which goodwill is not.

why_correct: A partnership needs a minimum of two partners, since it is by definition a relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them.

why_wrong.0: One person alone is a sole proprietorship, and no agreement is possible with oneself.
why_wrong.2: Three is above the minimum, though many firms have more.
why_wrong.3: Four is likewise above the minimum. The pair to remember is a minimum of 2 and a maximum of 50.

why_correct: Interest on capital is an appropriation of profit, that is a distribution of profit already earned, so it is debited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account. It is allowed only if there is profit, unless the deed says otherwise.

why_wrong.0: A charge against profit must be paid whether or not there is profit, as rent to a partner is. Interest on capital is not treated that way.
why_wrong.2: It is not an ordinary expense, since it is paid to the owners rather than to an outsider.
why_wrong.3: It is not a liability but a way of dividing profit among the partners.

why_correct: The maximum number of partners is 50, prescribed by the Companies Rules made under the Companies Act 2013. Beyond that the association must be registered as a company.

why_wrong.0: 20 was the old limit under the Companies Act 1956, and 10 for banking. It is out of date, which is what makes it the common wrong answer.
why_wrong.2: 100 is not the limit for a partnership firm.
why_wrong.3: There is a limit, so no limit is wrong. A private company, by contrast, may have up to 200 members.

why_correct: Debentures are issued by companies as an acknowledgement of debt, carrying a fixed rate of interest. They form part of a company's borrowed capital.

why_wrong.0: Partnership firms cannot issue debentures; they borrow by ordinary loan.
why_wrong.2: Banks may issue debentures, but as companies, so this is too narrow. The word only is what makes it wrong.
why_wrong.3: Individuals cannot issue debentures.

why_correct: A share represents ownership in the company. A shareholder owns a part of it, shares in its profits as dividend and has a vote in its affairs.

why_wrong.0: A loan to the company is represented by a debenture, whose holder is a creditor rather than an owner. Share against debenture is the key distinction in this chapter.
why_wrong.2: A share is not an expense of the company.
why_wrong.3: Share capital does appear on the liabilities side, because the company owes it to its owners, but a share itself represents ownership rather than a liability of the shareholder.

why_correct: The excess over face value is credited to the Securities Premium Account. It is a capital receipt and can be used only for the purposes the Companies Act permits, such as issuing bonus shares or writing off preliminary expenses.

why_wrong.0: Share Capital is credited only with the face value of the shares.
why_wrong.1: A general reserve is built out of profits, whereas the premium is a capital receipt and must be kept separate.
why_wrong.3: The cash account is debited with the whole amount received, not credited.

why_correct: The Cash Flow Statement is prepared according to Accounting Standard 3, which classifies flows into operating, investing and financing activities.

why_wrong.0: AS-1 deals with the disclosure of accounting policies.
why_wrong.2: AS-10 deals with property, plant and equipment.
why_wrong.3: AS-26 deals with intangible assets. Only one of the four concerns cash flows, and it is worth memorising the number.

why_correct: The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities. It measures short-term liquidity, and the ideal is generally taken as 2 to 1.

why_wrong.1: Inverting the ratio would make a strong position look weak, since a higher figure would then mean less ability to pay.
why_wrong.2: Sales over assets is the asset turnover ratio, a measure of efficiency.
why_wrong.3: Profit over capital is a return ratio, a measure of profitability. The name tells the order: current assets first.

why_correct: Dissolution means the closing down of the firm. Its assets are realised, its liabilities are paid, and the partnership itself comes to an end.

why_wrong.0: Admission of a partner is a reconstitution: the old firm ends but the business continues.
why_wrong.1: Retirement is likewise a reconstitution rather than a closure.
why_wrong.3: Purchase of assets is an ordinary transaction. Note the difference between dissolution of partnership, which is reconstitution, and dissolution of firm, which is closure.

why_correct: Reserve capital is that part of uncalled capital which a company resolves, by special resolution, to call up only in the event of winding up. It is created by the company's own resolution.

why_wrong.0: Shareholders act through the company in general meeting, so the resolution is the operative act rather than the shareholders individually.
why_wrong.1: Directors cannot create it, since it needs a special resolution of the members.
why_wrong.3: Creditors have no such power, though reserve capital exists precisely to protect them at winding up. Note it is quite different from capital reserve, which is created out of capital profits.

why_correct: Cash received from customers arises from the main revenue-producing activity of the business, so it is an operating activity under AS-3.

why_wrong.0: Financing activities concern the raising and repayment of capital and borrowings.
why_wrong.1: Investing activities concern the purchase and sale of long-term assets and investments.
why_wrong.3: This is very much a cash activity. Ask what produced the cash: trading, funding, or buying and selling fixed assets.

why_correct: The Balance Sheet is a statement of assets and liabilities at one particular date, so it shows the financial position at a moment in time. It is a snapshot rather than a record of a period.

why_wrong.0: A period is what the Profit and Loss Account covers, showing performance over the year.
why_wrong.2: A month is a period too, and the same objection applies.
why_wrong.3: A year is again a period. The distinction to hold is that the Profit and Loss Account is for a period ended, the Balance Sheet as at a date.

why_correct: The Revaluation Account is prepared whenever the firm is reconstituted, that is on the admission, retirement or death of a partner, to record the increase or decrease in the value of assets and liabilities before the change.

why_wrong.0: Purchase of goods is an ordinary trading transaction.
why_wrong.2: Sale of shares does not arise in a partnership firm.
why_wrong.3: The Trial Balance is a check on the ledger and calls for no revaluation. The purpose is to make sure the gain or loss on old values goes to the old partners, in whose time it arose.

why_correct: The debt-equity ratio compares long-term debt with shareholders' funds. It measures solvency, that is how far the business is financed by borrowing rather than by its owners.

why_wrong.0: Sales and profit give profitability ratios such as the net profit ratio.
why_wrong.1: Assets and liabilities together are shown by the balance sheet, but this ratio takes only particular parts of each.
why_wrong.3: Cash and bank concern immediate liquidity. The ideal debt-equity ratio is generally taken as 2 to 1.

why_correct: A person invited to buy shares is an investor, and the invitation is made through a prospectus. Once shares are allotted the investor becomes a shareholder and a member of the company.

why_wrong.0: A debenture holder has lent money to the company and is a creditor, not an invited buyer of shares.
why_wrong.2: A promoter is one who conceives and forms the company, acting before the invitation is issued.
why_wrong.3: A director manages the company after it exists.

why_correct: Authorised capital, also called nominal or registered capital, is the maximum amount of share capital stated in the Memorandum of Association. The company cannot issue more than this without altering the Memorandum.

why_wrong.0: Capital issued to the public is issued capital, which may be less than authorised.
why_wrong.1: Capital called up is called-up capital, which may be less than issued.
why_wrong.3: Capital received is paid-up capital, the last and smallest of the series. The order runs authorised, issued, subscribed, called-up, paid-up, each no larger than the one before.

why_correct: Share capital appears on the liabilities side, under Equity and Liabilities, because the company is a separate legal person and owes that capital to its shareholders.

why_wrong.0: The asset side shows what the company owns, not what it owes to its owners.
why_wrong.2: The Trading Account deals with buying and selling goods.
why_wrong.3: The Profit and Loss Account deals with income and expenses of the period. This follows from the business entity concept, the same principle that puts a proprietor's capital on the liabilities side.

why_correct: Debenture holders have lent money to the company, so they are its creditors. They receive interest whether or not there is profit, and are repaid before shareholders at winding up.

why_wrong.0: Owners are the shareholders, who receive dividend out of profit.
why_wrong.2: Partners belong to a partnership firm, not a company.
why_wrong.3: Directors manage the company and need not hold debentures at all. Interest is a charge against profit; dividend is an appropriation of it.

why_correct: The Profit and Loss Appropriation Account is prepared by a partnership firm to show how the net profit is divided: interest on capital, salary to partners, transfers to reserve and the final share of each partner.

why_wrong.0: A sole trader has no one to appropriate profit among, so the whole profit simply goes to capital.
why_wrong.2: Government accounts are kept on quite different principles.
why_wrong.3: Customers have no interest in the firm's internal division of profit. Companies prepare a similar statement, but in the partnership syllabus this account is the partnership's own.

why_correct: Interest on drawings is charged to the partner for money taken out during the year, so it is a gain to the firm. It is credited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account.

why_wrong.1: Interest on capital is the expense-like item, paid by the firm to the partner. Interest on drawings runs the other way, which is the pair being tested.
why_wrong.2: It is not an asset but an item of income.
why_wrong.3: It is not a liability, since the firm owes nothing here; the partner owes the firm.

why_correct: On retirement the retiring partner's share of goodwill is paid for by the partners who continue, since it is they who gain that share. The adjustment is made in their gaining ratio.

why_wrong.0: Old partners includes the retiring partner, who is being compensated rather than charged.
why_wrong.2: New partners do not arise on a retirement; that happens on admission.
why_wrong.3: Creditors are outsiders and have no part in goodwill. On admission the new partner pays; on retirement the continuing partners pay.

why_correct: Issuing shares raises long-term funds and changes the size and composition of the company's capital, so it is a financing activity under AS-3.

why_wrong.0: Operating activities are the main revenue-producing ones, such as selling goods.
why_wrong.1: Investing activities are the purchase and sale of long-term assets.
why_wrong.3: It brings in cash, so it is certainly a cash activity. Financing covers both raising capital and repaying it, including dividends and loan repayments.

why_correct: The inventory turnover ratio shows how many times stock is sold and replaced in a year, so it measures the efficiency with which stock is used. A high ratio generally means stock is moving briskly.

why_wrong.0: Liquidity is measured by the current and quick ratios.
why_wrong.1: Profitability is measured by the gross and net profit ratios.
why_wrong.3: Solvency is measured by the debt-equity and proprietary ratios. Turnover ratios are the activity or efficiency group.

why_correct: A company may issue shares at par, at a premium, or at a discount so far as the law allows. Under the Companies Act 2013 a discount issue is permitted only in narrow cases such as sweat equity, which is what the qualification in the option covers.
