why_wrong.0: Premium is one of the three, so naming it alone is incomplete.
why_wrong.1: Discount is permitted only subject to legal provisions, and it is still one of the three.
why_wrong.2: Par is the third. Since each is possible, all of these is the answer, and the phrase subject to legal provisions is what makes the discount option acceptable.

why_correct: Management is both an art and a science. It is a science in having a systematic body of principles built on observation, and an art in that applying those principles to a particular situation calls for personal skill and judgement.

why_wrong.0: Art only ignores the tested body of knowledge that management rests on.
why_wrong.1: Science only ignores the practice and creativity that using it well demands. No two managers apply the same principle identically.
why_wrong.3: It is certainly both. Management is often called an inexact science, because its principles are flexible rather than rigid like those of physics.

why_correct: F. W. Taylor is the father of scientific management. He advocated replacing rule of thumb with science, and gave techniques such as time study, motion study and differential piece wage.

why_wrong.0: Henri Fayol is the father of general or administrative management, and gave the fourteen principles. Taylor and Fayol are the pair this chapter always contrasts: Taylor worked upward from the shop floor, Fayol downward from the top.
why_wrong.2: Peter Drucker is the father of modern management and gave management by objectives.
why_wrong.3: Elton Mayo led the Hawthorne experiments and founded the human relations approach.

why_correct: Planning is deciding in advance what to do and how to do it, and it begins with setting objectives. It is the primary function, because every other function follows from the objectives set.

why_wrong.0: Organising arranges resources to carry out the plan already made.
why_wrong.2: Staffing fills the posts that organising has created.
why_wrong.3: Controlling checks performance against the standards that planning laid down, so it comes last rather than first.

why_correct: Organising identifies the work to be done, groups it into jobs and departments, and assigns duties along with the authority needed to perform them. It creates the structure of relationships.

why_wrong.0: Setting goals belongs to planning.
why_wrong.2: Recruiting belongs to staffing, which fills the posts organising has defined.
why_wrong.3: Measuring performance belongs to controlling.

why_correct: Staffing is the management of people: estimating manpower needs, recruiting, selecting, placing, training and appraising. Recruitment and selection are its central steps.

why_wrong.0: Financial planning is a finance function, not a staffing one.
why_wrong.2: Advertising is a marketing function, though recruitment advertising is one small overlap.
why_wrong.3: Production is an operations function. Staffing is often called the human resource function, and it puts the right person in the right job.

why_correct: Motivation is one of the four elements of directing, along with supervision, communication and leadership. Directing is the function concerned with getting people to work.

why_wrong.0: Planning decides what is to be done, before any people are led.
why_wrong.1: Organising creates the structure within which they work.
why_wrong.3: Controlling checks what they achieved afterwards. Directing is the only function performed directly on and through people.

why_correct: Controlling compares actual performance with the planned standards, finds the deviations and takes corrective action. It is what closes the loop back to planning.

why_wrong.0: Planning sets the standards that controlling later measures against, so the two are linked but distinct.
why_wrong.1: Organising arranges the resources.
why_wrong.2: Directing guides people while the work is being done. Planning and controlling are often called the twin functions, since neither is of use without the other.

why_correct: Unity of command is one of Henri Fayol's fourteen principles: an employee should receive orders from one superior only, so that responsibility is clear and conflict is avoided.

why_wrong.0: Taylor's functional foremanship actually contradicts this, giving a worker eight bosses. That direct clash is why the question is asked.
why_wrong.2: Elton Mayo worked on human relations, not on structural principles.
why_wrong.3: Peter Drucker gave management by objectives. Do not confuse unity of command, one boss per employee, with unity of direction, one head and one plan per group of activities.

why_correct: Span of management, or span of control, is the number of subordinates a manager can effectively supervise. A narrow span gives a tall structure with many levels; a wide span gives a flat one.

why_wrong.0: The number of departments is a matter of departmentation, not span.
why_wrong.2: The number of managers follows from the span rather than defining it.
why_wrong.3: Customers have nothing to do with internal structure.

why_correct: Decentralisation is the systematic dispersal of decision-making authority to the lower levels of the organisation. It relieves top management and develops managers lower down.

why_wrong.0: Concentration of authority at the top is centralisation, the opposite.
why_wrong.2: Authority is not eliminated but spread out; someone still decides.
why_wrong.3: Central control only is again centralisation. Note that decentralisation is an extension of delegation, made a policy throughout the organisation.

why_correct: Planning begins with setting objectives, because everything that follows depends on knowing what is to be achieved. Objectives should be clear and stated for every department.

why_wrong.0: Selecting an alternative comes much later, after alternatives have been developed and evaluated.
why_wrong.2: Implementation is the last step, once the plan is settled.
why_wrong.3: Follow-up action comes after implementation, to see whether the plan is working.

why_correct: Recruitment is the process of searching for prospective employees and encouraging them to apply. It is a positive process, aiming to build up a large pool of candidates.

why_wrong.0: Selecting candidates is selection, which is a negative process because it rejects the unsuitable. Recruitment and selection are the pair being tested.
why_wrong.1: Appointing is placement, which comes after selection.
why_wrong.3: Training comes after appointment.

why_correct: The labour market is a market for human effort, not for funds, so it is not a financial market. Financial markets deal in the transfer of money from those who have surplus to those who need it.

why_wrong.0: The money market deals in short-term funds, up to one year.
why_wrong.1: The capital market deals in medium and long-term funds.
why_wrong.3: The stock market is part of the capital market, dealing in shares and debentures.

why_correct: SEBI is the Securities and Exchange Board of India, set up in 1988 and given statutory powers in 1992. It regulates the securities market and protects investors.

why_wrong.1: State is wrong; SEBI is a national body.
why_wrong.2: It is a board, not a bank, and it does no banking business.
why_wrong.3: Stock is narrower than securities, which cover shares, debentures, bonds and derivatives alike.

why_correct: The primary market deals in new securities, issued for the first time, so the money goes directly to the company. It is also called the new issue market.

why_wrong.0: Old or existing securities are traded in the secondary market, where the money passes between investors rather than to the company. That is the distinction being tested.
why_wrong.2: Foreign securities are not a separate market of this classification.
why_wrong.3: Government securities may be issued in the primary market, but so may company securities, so the word only makes this wrong.

why_correct: The marketing mix has four elements, the four Ps: product, price, place and promotion. They are the controllable variables a firm combines to serve its target market.

why_wrong.0: 3 Ps leaves one of the four out, and no standard version of the mix has only three.
why_wrong.2: 5 Ps and beyond, adding people, process and physical evidence, belong to the extended mix for services. For the basic mix in this syllabus the answer is four.
why_wrong.3: 6 Ps is not a standard formulation either.

why_correct: Recruitment is a staffing function, not a marketing one. Marketing functions concern getting the product to the customer and include branding, packaging, transport, storage, pricing and promotion.

why_wrong.0: Branding gives the product an identity and is a marketing function.
why_wrong.1: Packaging protects the product and helps sell it.
why_wrong.3: Transportation creates place utility and is one of the physical supply functions of marketing.

why_correct: Advertising is one of the four tools of promotion, along with personal selling, sales promotion and public relations. Promotion is about communicating with the customer.

why_wrong.0: Product concerns what is offered, including quality, design and branding.
why_wrong.1: Price concerns what the customer pays and how it is set.
why_wrong.3: Place concerns distribution, that is channels and physical movement. Advertising informs and persuades, which is squarely a promotion activity.

why_correct: The Consumer Protection Act exists to protect the interests of consumers, giving them rights and a machinery of district, state and national commissions to enforce them.

why_wrong.0: Producers are the party the Act regulates rather than protects.
why_wrong.2: Taxation is not its subject.
why_wrong.3: Export promotion is dealt with by trade policy. The Act of 2019 replaced the earlier Act of 1986 and added a central regulatory authority.

why_correct: The Right to Safety protects a consumer against goods and services that are hazardous to life and property. It is why standards such as ISI and AGMARK exist.

why_wrong.0: The Right to Information entitles the consumer to know the quality, quantity, price and date of expiry.
why_wrong.2: The Right to Choose entitles the consumer to a range of goods at competitive prices.
why_wrong.3: The Right to Seek Redressal entitles the consumer to compensation after harm has occurred, whereas safety is about preventing it.

why_correct: Delegation is the downward entrustment of authority together with the responsibility for carrying out the assigned work. Its three elements are authority, responsibility and accountability.

why_wrong.0: Responsibility alone would leave the subordinate unable to act, since no one can perform a duty without the power to make the necessary decisions.
why_wrong.2: Accountability cannot be transferred at all. This is the important point in the chapter: a manager who delegates remains answerable to their own superior for the result.
why_wrong.3: Ownership is not transferred by delegation; the manager delegating still holds the post.

why_correct: Top level management, that is the board of directors and chief executives, frames the policies and overall objectives of the organisation and is answerable to the owners.

why_wrong.0: Lower level management supervises workers and carries out day-to-day operations.
why_wrong.1: Middle level management interprets top-level policies and passes them down as departmental plans.
why_wrong.3: Supervisory level is another name for the lower level. The three levels differ in the time horizon of their decisions, and policy is the longest.

why_correct: On-the-job training teaches the employee at the actual workplace while doing the real work. It is cheap and directly relevant, and includes coaching, job rotation and internship.

why_wrong.0: Vestibule training uses a duplicate workplace away from the real one, so the trainee is not on the job.
why_wrong.1: Apprenticeship training combines instruction with work over a long period under a master. It is a specific programme rather than the general term the question asks for.
why_wrong.3: Internship links a school or college with a firm, and it is one method within on-the-job training rather than the category itself.

why_correct: A trademark is a brand or part of a brand given legal protection, so it identifies the product as that of a particular seller and distinguishes it from others.

why_wrong.0: A trademark does not reduce cost; registering and defending one costs money.
why_wrong.2: It does not affect production, though a strong mark may raise demand.
why_wrong.3: It has nothing to do with hiring. Its whole purpose is identification and the exclusive right that goes with it.

why_correct: Motivation is the process of stimulating people to act willingly towards the organisation's goals. Willingly is the key word: a person can be ordered to work, but not ordered to want to.

why_wrong.0: Planning decides what is to be done.
why_wrong.1: Organising arranges the resources to do it.
why_wrong.3: Staffing puts people into the posts. Motivation is one of the elements of directing, and Maslow's hierarchy of needs is its best-known theory.

why_correct: Cost accounting ascertains the cost of each product, process or department and then works to control it, by comparing actual costs against standards and investigating the differences.

why_wrong.0: Recording financial transactions is the work of financial accounting, which reports to outsiders.
why_wrong.2: The balance sheet is a financial accounting statement, showing position to shareholders and lenders.
why_wrong.3: Auditing is an independent examination of accounts already prepared, carried out by someone outside the accounting function.

why_correct: A fixed cost stays the same in total whatever the level of output, within a relevant range. Rent and insurance are the standard examples, payable whether the factory runs or stands idle.

why_wrong.0: Variable cost rises and falls in direct proportion to output.
why_wrong.2: Semi-variable cost has both a fixed and a variable part, as a telephone bill does with its rental and its call charges.
why_wrong.3: Direct cost is a classification by traceability rather than by behaviour, so it answers a different question. A cost can be both direct and fixed.

why_correct: Raw materials used in production can be traced directly to the finished product, so they are direct material cost. They form part of prime cost.

why_wrong.0: Office stationery is consumed by the office generally and is an administrative overhead.
why_wrong.2: Office rent serves the whole business and cannot be traced to any unit of output.
why_wrong.3: Advertising is a selling overhead. The test is traceability: if you cannot say which unit of output it belongs to, it is indirect.

why_correct: Overheads are indirect costs, that is costs which cannot be traced to a particular unit of output. They are grouped as factory, administration, and selling and distribution overheads and are apportioned rather than traced.

why_wrong.0: Direct costs are precisely the ones that can be traced, and they make up prime cost.
why_wrong.2: Selling price is what the customer pays, not a cost at all.
why_wrong.3: Profit is the difference between selling price and cost.

why_correct: Prime cost is direct material plus direct labour plus direct expenses. It is the first total in the cost sheet, and everything in it is directly traceable to the product.

why_wrong.1: Factory overheads are added after prime cost to give works cost, so they are the next stage rather than part of this one.
why_wrong.2: Selling expenses come at the very end of the cost sheet, after production is complete.
why_wrong.3: Administrative expenses are added to works cost to give cost of production. The cost sheet builds up in that order: prime, works, production, total.

why_correct: Factory rent is fixed. It is payable in full whether output is high, low or nil, so its total does not change with the level of production.

why_wrong.0: A variable cost would rise and fall with output, which rent does not.
why_wrong.2: Rent cannot be traced to any one unit of output, so it is indirect rather than direct.
why_wrong.3: It is a factory cost, incurred in production, not a selling cost incurred after it. Note that fixed cost per unit does fall as output rises, even though the total stays the same.

why_correct: A variable cost changes in direct proportion to the level of production. Double the output and the raw material cost doubles, which is what makes it variable.

why_wrong.0: Fixed cost stays constant in total regardless of output.
why_wrong.2: Sunk cost is a past cost that cannot now be recovered, and it is irrelevant to future decisions.
why_wrong.3: Historical cost is the actual cost incurred in the past, a basis of valuation rather than a pattern of behaviour.

why_correct: GST is Goods and Services Tax, a single indirect tax on the supply of both goods and services that replaced a whole set of central and state levies.

why_wrong.1: General Sales Tax is not the expansion, and sales tax was one of the taxes GST subsumed.
why_wrong.2: Government Service Tax is invented. Service tax existed separately before GST and was absorbed into it.
why_wrong.3: Gross Sales Tax is not a real tax. The name matters because it shows the reform's point: goods and services taxed together under one law.

why_correct: GST came into force on 1 July 2017, launched at a midnight session of Parliament. It replaced excise duty, service tax, VAT and several other taxes at once.

why_wrong.0: 1 April 2016 is before even the Constitution amendment that made GST possible.
why_wrong.2: 1 January 2018 is after the launch, by which time GST was already running.
why_wrong.3: 1 April 2019 is much later. The dates to keep in order are the 101st Constitution Amendment in 2016 and the tax itself in 2017.

why_correct: Income tax is a direct tax, levied on a person's income and borne by that same person. The burden cannot be shifted to anyone else.

why_wrong.1: An indirect tax is one whose burden is passed on, as GST is passed to the consumer.
why_wrong.2: Service tax was an indirect tax and has been subsumed into GST.
why_wrong.3: Excise duty is indirect, levied on manufacture and recovered in the price. The test for a direct tax is whether the person who pays it is the person who bears it.

why_correct: GST is an indirect tax. The seller collects it and pays it to the government, but it is included in the price and finally borne by the consumer.

why_wrong.0: A direct tax is borne by the person who pays it in, which GST is not.
why_wrong.2: Wealth tax was a direct tax on net wealth, abolished in 2015.
why_wrong.3: Property tax is a direct tax levied by local bodies on the owner of property.

why_correct: In an indirect tax the burden is shifted along the chain of supply until it reaches the final consumer, who pays it in the price and has no one further to pass it to.

why_wrong.0: The government receives the tax and does not bear it.
why_wrong.1: The producer pays the tax at its stage but recovers it in the price charged to the next buyer, so the burden does not rest there. Impact and incidence fall on different people, and that is the whole idea.
why_wrong.3: Employees bear income tax on their salaries, which is a direct tax and a separate matter.

why_correct: Income tax is levied on a person's income from salary, house property, business, capital gains and other sources. It is administered by the Income Tax Department.

why_wrong.0: GST is levied on the supply of goods and services, that is on a transaction.
why_wrong.1: Customs duty is levied on goods crossing the border.
why_wrong.3: Excise duty was levied on the manufacture of goods. All three wrong options tax a transaction; only income tax taxes a person.

why_correct: Factory electricity is consumed in the works while goods are being made, so it is a production or factory overhead. It is added to prime cost to arrive at works cost.

why_wrong.1: Sales commission is paid for securing orders, so it is a selling overhead.
why_wrong.2: Advertisement is likewise a selling overhead, incurred after the goods exist.
why_wrong.3: Office rent is an administrative overhead. The three overhead groups follow the stages of the business: making, administering, and selling.

why_correct: Selling and distribution cost is incurred after production, to secure orders and deliver the goods. It covers advertising, salesmen's salaries, packing for despatch and carriage outward.

why_wrong.0: Prime cost is the direct cost of production, at the start of the cost sheet.
why_wrong.1: Production cost is incurred while the goods are being made.
why_wrong.3: Direct cost classifies by traceability rather than by stage, and most selling costs are indirect anyway.

why_correct: The primary objective of taxation is to raise revenue for the government, so that it can provide defence, administration, infrastructure and welfare. Redistribution and the discouragement of harmful consumption are secondary aims.

why_wrong.0: No individual benefits personally from tax revenue; it is spent on the community.
why_wrong.2: Increasing losses is not an objective of any policy.
why_wrong.3: Reducing production is not the aim, though a tax may deliberately discourage particular goods such as tobacco.

why_correct: A cost sheet is a statement showing the build-up of cost element by element, from prime cost through works cost and cost of production to total cost. Its purpose is to determine the total cost of production and the cost per unit.

why_wrong.0: Profit can be shown on a cost sheet if selling price is included, but calculating profit alone is not its purpose, and the word only makes this too narrow.
why_wrong.2: The balance sheet is a financial statement, prepared separately.
why_wrong.3: Auditing is an independent examination of accounts, not a use of the cost sheet.

why_correct: Administrative expenses are the costs of running the office and directing the business generally: office salaries, office rent, printing, stationery and legal charges.

why_wrong.0: Direct expenses are traceable to the product and form part of prime cost.
why_wrong.2: Selling expenses are incurred to obtain orders and deliver goods.
why_wrong.3: Production expenses are incurred in the factory while the goods are made. Office management is what separates this group from the other two.

why_correct: Income tax is paid directly by the taxpayer to the government, whether by deduction at source or by self-assessment. There is no intermediary collecting it in a price.

why_wrong.0: GST is collected by the seller from the buyer and then remitted.
why_wrong.1: Customs duty is paid by the importer and recovered in the price of the goods.
why_wrong.3: Sales tax likewise reached the government through the seller, and it has been replaced by GST.

why_correct: Cost control makes each element of cost visible, so that waste and inefficiency can be identified and unnecessary expenses cut without harming quality or output.

why_wrong.0: Reducing wastage is the aim, not increasing it.
why_wrong.2: Reducing sales is no part of it; better cost information usually supports pricing that helps sales.
why_wrong.3: Cost control depends on accounting rather than avoiding it.

why_correct: Excise duty is an indirect tax levied on the manufacture of goods. The manufacturer pays it but includes it in the price, so the consumer finally bears it. Most excise has now been subsumed into GST.

why_wrong.0: A direct tax cannot be shifted, and excise plainly is.
why_wrong.2: Wealth tax was a direct tax on net wealth, abolished in 2015.
why_wrong.3: Income tax is direct, levied on a person's income.

why_correct: Sales commission is paid to secure orders, so it is a selling expense, charged after the goods are ready. It appears in the selling and distribution section of the cost sheet.

why_wrong.0: Factory wages are a direct labour cost, part of prime cost.
why_wrong.2: Raw material cost is direct material, also part of prime cost.
why_wrong.3: Machine depreciation is a factory overhead, incurred in production. Only sales commission arises after the goods exist.

why_correct: Cost accounting tells management what each product, process or department actually costs, which supports decisions on pricing, on whether to make or buy, and on which lines to continue or drop.

why_wrong.1: Increasing taxes is not an objective, and better records may in fact reduce tax legitimately by establishing true profit.
why_wrong.2: Reducing production is not an aim of any accounting system.
why_wrong.3: Cost accounting supplements the financial records that audits examine rather than avoiding them.

why_correct: Tax revenue funds public welfare and development: defence, roads, schools, hospitals and welfare schemes. It is spent on the community rather than returned to any individual payer.

why_wrong.0: No official's personal income is a legitimate use of tax money.
why_wrong.2: Private companies are funded by their owners and lenders, though the state may support industry through policy.
why_wrong.3: Business profits are not what tax revenue is for. The absence of any direct return to the individual payer is part of the very definition of a tax.

why_correct: Income tax is a direct tax, since it is levied on and borne by the same person. India's other direct taxes include corporation tax and capital gains tax.

why_wrong.0: GST is indirect, its burden shifting to the consumer.
why_wrong.1: Customs duty is indirect, passed into the price of imported goods.
why_wrong.3: Excise duty is indirect too. Of the four, only income tax is levied on a person rather than on a transaction.

why_correct: Banking and insurance are services, so they belong to the tertiary sector. This sector does not produce goods but supports production and distribution, and it now contributes the largest share of India's GDP.

why_wrong.0: The primary sector draws directly on nature, through farming, fishing, forestry and mining.
why_wrong.1: The secondary sector manufactures goods from raw materials.
why_wrong.3: Agriculture is part of the primary sector, so this names the same wrong sector twice over.

why_correct: GDP is Gross Domestic Product, the money value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a year, whoever produces them.

why_wrong.1: General is not the word; gross means before deducting depreciation.
why_wrong.2: Gross Development Plan is invented.
why_wrong.3: Global would contradict domestic. The contrast to hold is GDP by territory against GNP by nationality.

why_correct: The Reserve Bank of India has the sole right to issue currency notes, except the one rupee note, which is issued by the Ministry of Finance. It is the country's central bank.

why_wrong.0: The State Bank of India is the largest commercial bank but has no note-issuing power.
why_wrong.2: NABARD refinances rural and agricultural credit.
why_wrong.3: SEBI regulates the securities market. Note issue is a monopoly of the central bank everywhere.

why_correct: The central problem is scarcity: resources are limited while wants are unlimited, so choices must be made about what to produce, how, and for whom.

why_wrong.0: Inflation is a particular macroeconomic problem, serious but not universal.
why_wrong.1: Unemployment is likewise a specific problem arising from how the economy is run.
why_wrong.3: Poverty is a consequence of how scarce resources are distributed. All three are problems within economics; scarcity is the reason economics exists.

why_correct: National income is the total income earned by the normal residents of a country in a year, whether within the country or abroad. Formally it is net national product at factor cost.

why_wrong.0: Government income is only one part, coming largely from taxes.
why_wrong.1: Income earned by foreign companies in India is part of domestic product but is excluded from national income, since those earners are not residents.
why_wrong.3: Tax revenue is a transfer from citizens to the state rather than newly earned income.

why_correct: Income tax is a direct tax: it is levied on a person's income and borne by that same person, so the burden cannot be shifted.

why_wrong.0: GST is indirect, passed on to the consumer in the price.
why_wrong.1: Excise duty is indirect, levied on manufacture and recovered in the price.
why_wrong.3: Customs duty is indirect, levied on goods crossing the border.

why_correct: By the law of demand, other things being equal, quantity demanded falls when price rises. That inverse relationship is why the demand curve slopes downward.

why_wrong.0: Demand rising with price describes the exceptions, Giffen and Veblen goods, not the general law.
why_wrong.2: Demand does change; a constant quantity would mean perfectly inelastic demand, which is a special case.
why_wrong.3: Nothing doubles automatically. How much demand changes is a question of elasticity, which varies from good to good.

why_correct: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, which means each rupee buys less than before. It is measured by index numbers such as the Consumer Price Index.

why_wrong.0: A fall in prices is deflation, the opposite condition.
why_wrong.2: An increase in exports affects the balance of trade.
why_wrong.3: An increase in imports likewise concerns trade. The word general matters: a rise in the price of one commodity is not inflation.

why_correct: The RBI is called the banker's bank because commercial banks keep deposits with it, borrow from it in difficulty, and clear their mutual claims through it. It is also the lender of last resort.

why_wrong.0: The State Bank of India is a commercial bank, even though it is government-owned and the largest.
why_wrong.1: Punjab National Bank is also a commercial bank.
why_wrong.3: ICICI is a private commercial bank. All three of the wrong options are banks that themselves bank with the RBI.

why_correct: Fiscal policy is the government's policy on its own expenditure, taxation and borrowing. It is announced mainly through the annual Budget.

why_wrong.0: Money supply is the subject of monetary policy, run by the RBI. Fiscal against monetary is the distinction this question tests: fiscal is the government's money, monetary is the central bank's control of credit.
why_wrong.2: Foreign trade is governed by trade policy.
why_wrong.3: Agriculture has its own sectoral policies.

why_correct: GDP is the value of all final goods and services produced within a country's territory in a year, regardless of who produces them.

why_wrong.0: NNP is net national product, that is GNP after deducting depreciation.
why_wrong.2: GNP counts what a country's nationals produce anywhere in the world, so it uses nationality rather than territory.
why_wrong.3: Personal income is what households actually receive, after corporate savings and taxes are taken out.

why_correct: Tax revenue is a revenue receipt, because it neither creates a liability for the government nor reduces its assets. It is a regular and recurring source of income.

why_wrong.0: Borrowings create a liability, so they are a capital receipt.
why_wrong.1: Recovery of loans reduces the government's assets, making it a capital receipt.
why_wrong.3: Sale of assets also reduces assets and so is capital. The test is simple: does the receipt create a liability or reduce an asset? If neither, it is revenue.

why_correct: The Balance of Payments is a systematic record of all economic transactions between the residents of a country and the rest of the world during a year, covering both the current and the capital account.

why_wrong.0: Internal transactions are recorded in national income accounts, not here.
why_wrong.2: Government expenses appear in the Budget.
why_wrong.3: Bank transactions alone are far narrower than the whole external account.

why_correct: Devaluation lowers the external value of the currency, so foreigners pay less of their own money for the same goods. Exports therefore become cheaper abroad and more competitive.

why_wrong.0: Imports become dearer, not cheaper, so they usually fall.
why_wrong.1: Exports increase rather than decrease, which is the whole purpose of devaluing.
why_wrong.3: Production of export goods usually rises in response. Devaluation is used to correct a deficit in the balance of payments, by encouraging exports and discouraging imports together.

why_correct: Monopoly is a market with a single seller and no close substitutes, so the seller is a price maker. Entry of rivals is blocked.

why_wrong.0: Perfect competition has very many sellers of an identical product, each a price taker.
why_wrong.2: Oligopoly has a few large sellers, each watching the others.
why_wrong.3: Monopolistic competition has many sellers of differentiated products, as in soaps or restaurants. The four are best remembered by the number of sellers.

why_correct: The expenditure method is one of the three ways of measuring national income, adding consumption, investment, government spending and net exports. The other two are the income and product methods.

why_wrong.0: Inflation is measured by price index numbers.
why_wrong.2: Poverty is measured against a poverty line based on calorie or consumption norms.
why_wrong.3: Population is counted by the census. All three methods of national income must give the same total, which is a useful check.

why_correct: GST is an indirect tax on the supply of goods and services. The seller collects it and remits it, but the consumer bears it in the price.

why_wrong.0: A direct tax is borne by the person who pays it in, which GST is not.
why_wrong.2: Wealth tax was a direct tax on net wealth, abolished in 2015.
why_wrong.3: Income tax is a direct tax on income.

why_correct: The repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities. Raising it makes borrowing costlier and tightens credit in the economy.

why_wrong.0: The rate banks charge customers is the lending rate, based on the repo but not the same thing.
why_wrong.2: Government borrowing from the RBI is a different arrangement altogether.
why_wrong.3: The rate paid on public deposits is the deposit rate. The companion to remember is the reverse repo, at which the RBI borrows from banks.

why_correct: Borrowings are a capital receipt because they create a liability for the government, which must be repaid with interest.

why_wrong.0: Income tax creates no liability and reduces no asset, so it is revenue.
why_wrong.1: GST is likewise a revenue receipt.
why_wrong.3: Fees collected are revenue receipts too. Only borrowing adds to what the government owes.

why_correct: Human capital formation is the process of adding to people's productive capacity through education, training, health care and skills. It treats spending on people as an investment rather than consumption.

why_wrong.0: Building factories is physical capital formation.
why_wrong.2: Roads are infrastructure, again physical capital.
why_wrong.3: Machinery is physical capital too. The distinction is whether the investment is embodied in people or in things.

why_correct: The current account of the Balance of Payments records exports and imports of goods and services, together with income and current transfers. It deals with flows that do not create claims.

why_wrong.0: Foreign loans belong to the capital account, since they create a claim.
why_wrong.1: Foreign investment is also a capital account item.
why_wrong.3: Government borrowing is capital account too. The dividing line is whether the transaction alters assets and liabilities: if it does, it is capital account.

why_correct: Open market operations are the RBI's purchase and sale of government securities in the open market, used to expand or contract the money supply. They are a quantitative instrument of monetary policy.

why_wrong.0: Commercial banks trade in securities but do not conduct monetary policy.
why_wrong.2: SEBI regulates the securities market rather than using it as a policy tool.
why_wrong.3: NABARD refinances rural credit. The other quantitative instruments are the bank rate and the reserve ratios.

why_correct: Intermediate goods are excluded from GDP because their value is already contained in the price of the final goods they go into. Counting both would inflate the total, which is the double counting problem.

why_wrong.0: Including them twice is exactly the error the exclusion prevents.
why_wrong.2: Adding them separately would overstate the total for the same reason.
why_wrong.3: There is no connection with exports. The alternative solution is the value added method, which counts only what each stage adds.

why_correct: Deficit financing means the government spends more than it receives, meeting the gap by borrowing or by creating new money. It can stimulate a slack economy but risks inflation.

why_wrong.0: A cut in taxes may cause a deficit but is not itself deficit financing.
why_wrong.2: Exports concern the external account rather than the budget.
why_wrong.3: Imports likewise concern trade. The deficit here is between government revenue and expenditure, not between exports and imports.

why_correct: India's liberalisation began in 1991, under the New Economic Policy introduced during a severe balance of payments crisis. Licensing was dismantled and the economy opened to trade and foreign investment.

why_wrong.0: Some cautious loosening began in the 1980s, but the decisive reform came in 1991.
why_wrong.1: 1985 saw further partial steps under Rajiv Gandhi, again short of the full reform.
why_wrong.3: By 2000 liberalisation was nearly a decade old. The three strands of 1991 are worth naming together: liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation.

why_correct: Hugo de Vries proposed mutation theory from his work on the evening primrose, holding that evolution proceeds by sudden, large, random changes he called saltation, rather than by slow accumulation.

why_wrong.0: Recombination reshuffles existing genes during meiosis and produces variation, but not new alleles.
why_wrong.1: Adaptation is the outcome of selection, not a source of variation.
why_wrong.3: Gene flow is the movement of alleles between populations. The contrast de Vries drew was with Darwin's small, gradual, directional variations.

why_correct: Penguin and dolphin flippers look alike and do the same job but have different embryonic origins, one a bird wing and the other a mammal forelimb. Similar function from different origin makes them analogous, an example of convergent evolution.

why_wrong.0: Homologous organs share a common origin but may differ in function, as a whale's flipper and a human arm do. That is the reverse case.
why_wrong.2: Vestigial organs are reduced remnants with no present function, such as the human appendix.
why_wrong.3: Atavism is the reappearance of an ancestral character, such as a human born with a tail.

why_correct: Palaeontology is the study of fossils, the preserved remains or traces of past life. Fossils provide the direct evidence for evolution and for the sequence of life through geological time.

why_wrong.0: Embryology studies the development of the embryo, which gives indirect evidence of evolution.
why_wrong.1: Herpetology is the study of reptiles and amphibians.
why_wrong.3: Phylogeny is the evolutionary history of a group, which palaeontology helps to reconstruct but is not itself.

why_correct: DNA fingerprinting uses satellite DNA, in particular variable number tandem repeats, because the number of repeats differs greatly between individuals while remaining the same in every cell of one person.

why_wrong.0: Exons are the coding regions and are highly conserved, so they vary too little between individuals to be useful.
why_wrong.1: Introns are non-coding and do vary, but the specific repetitive sequences used are the satellite regions.
why_wrong.3: Ribosomal RNA is highly conserved across species, which makes it useful for tracing evolutionary relationships but useless for telling two people apart.

why_correct: The lac z gene codes for beta-galactosidase, the enzyme that hydrolyses lactose into glucose and galactose. It is the first of the three structural genes in the operon.

why_wrong.0: lac y codes for permease, which lets lactose into the cell.
why_wrong.2: lac a codes for transacetylase.
why_wrong.3: lac i is the regulatory gene, coding for the repressor protein. It is not a structural gene at all, which is the distinction the question is testing.

why_correct: Transcription is the copying of genetic information from the template strand of DNA into a strand of RNA, carried out by RNA polymerase.

why_wrong.0: Replication copies DNA into DNA, doubling the genetic material before cell division.
why_wrong.1: Translation converts the message in mRNA into a sequence of amino acids at the ribosome.
why_wrong.3: Reverse transcription makes DNA from an RNA template, as retroviruses such as HIV do. Note the direction in each case: this question asks for DNA to RNA.

why_correct: The purines are adenine and guanine, both double-ring bases. The pyrimidines, with a single ring, are cytosine and thymine in DNA.

why_wrong.0: Cytosine is a pyrimidine, not a purine.
why_wrong.1: Both cytosine and thymine are pyrimidines, so this names the other class entirely.
why_wrong.3: Guanine is right but uracil is a pyrimidine and belongs to RNA rather than DNA. A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, which is what keeps the double helix a constant width.

why_correct: A karyotype of 44 autosomes with XXY, giving 47 chromosomes in all, is Klinefelter's syndrome. The individual is male with an extra X, and shows some female characteristics with sterility.

why_wrong.0: Turner's syndrome is 44 plus XO, with 45 chromosomes. The individual is female and sterile, and it is a monosomy rather than a trisomy.
why_wrong.2: Down's syndrome is trisomy of chromosome 21, an autosomal condition.
why_wrong.3: Edward's syndrome is trisomy 18, also autosomal. Turner and Klinefelter are the sex-chromosome pair, and counting the X's tells them apart.

why_correct: Down's syndrome is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21, so the person has three of them and 47 chromosomes in all. It was first described by Langdon Down.

why_wrong.0: Trisomy 13 is Patau's syndrome.
why_wrong.1: Trisomy 18 is Edward's syndrome.
why_wrong.3: Trisomy 22 is a separate and much rarer condition. The three autosomal trisomies worth knowing are 21, 18 and 13, in that order of frequency.

why_correct: Sutton and Boveri proposed the chromosomal theory of inheritance in 1902, noting that chromosomes behave in meiosis exactly as Mendel's factors must, and so concluding that the factors are carried on chromosomes.

why_wrong.0: Mendel gave the laws of inheritance in 1866, before chromosomes were understood at all.
why_wrong.1: Morgan proved the theory experimentally with Drosophila and discovered linkage, but he confirmed it rather than proposing it.
why_wrong.3: Watson and Crick gave the double helix structure of DNA in 1953, half a century later.

why_correct: Human skin colour is controlled by several genes acting together, each adding a small amount of pigment, so the result is a continuous range rather than distinct types. That is polygenic inheritance.

why_wrong.0: Multiple allelism means one gene with more than two alleles, as in ABO blood groups. One gene, several forms, which is a different idea.
why_wrong.2: Incomplete dominance gives an intermediate phenotype from a single gene pair, as in pink four o'clock flowers.
why_wrong.3: Pleiotropy is one gene affecting several traits, which is the reverse of this.

why_correct: Haemophilia is X-linked recessive, so it appears mostly in males, who have only one X. A female carrier passes it to half her sons, which is why it ran through European royal families.

why_wrong.0: Thalassemia is autosomal recessive, not sex-linked.
why_wrong.1: Down's syndrome is a chromosomal disorder, not a single-gene one, and it is not inherited in this way.
why_wrong.3: Sickle cell anaemia is autosomal recessive, on chromosome 11. Only haemophilia and colour blindness among the common examples are X-linked.

why_correct: The anther is the microsporangium of a flower, where microspore mother cells divide by meiosis to produce pollen grains, the male gametophytes.

why_wrong.0: The ovule is the megasporangium, producing the female gametophyte.
why_wrong.2: The filament merely supports the anther and produces nothing.
why_wrong.3: The pollen grain is the microspore, that is the product of the microsporangium rather than the sporangium itself.

why_correct: Double fertilisation is unique to angiosperms. One male gamete fuses with the egg to form the zygote, and the other fuses with two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm.

why_wrong.0: Bryophytes have a single fertilisation and no seeds at all.
why_wrong.1: Pteridophytes likewise have single fertilisation and reproduce by spores.
why_wrong.2: Gymnosperms have a single fertilisation, and their endosperm is haploid and formed before fertilisation. That contrast is what makes double fertilisation the defining angiosperm feature.

why_correct: Apomixis is the formation of seeds without fertilisation, so the offspring are genetically identical to the parent. It is valuable in agriculture because hybrid vigour can then be preserved across generations.

why_wrong.0: Parthenocarpy is fruit without fertilisation, and such fruits are seedless. Seed against fruit is exactly what separates these two.
why_wrong.1: Polyembryony is more than one embryo in a single seed, as in citrus.
why_wrong.3: Budding is a form of asexual reproduction in animals such as Hydra and in yeast.

why_correct: Parthenocarpy is the development of fruit without fertilisation, giving seedless fruit such as banana and some grapes. It can be induced with growth hormones.

why_wrong.0: Apomixis produces seeds without fertilisation, which is the paired term and the opposite way round.
why_wrong.2: Polyembryony is several embryos in one seed.
why_wrong.3: Outbreeding is crossing between unrelated individuals, a breeding practice rather than a developmental process.

why_correct: After fertilisation in the fallopian tube the zygote divides repeatedly to form the morula, which travels down to the uterus. There it develops a fluid filled cavity and becomes the blastocyst, with an inner cell mass and an outer trophoblast. It is the trophoblast that attaches to and invades the uterine lining, and NCERT puts it plainly: the blastocyst becomes embedded in the endometrium. Implantation is therefore a blastocyst stage event.

why_wrong.0: The zygote is a single cell and is still in the fallopian tube. It has not even reached the uterus, let alone attached to it.
why_wrong.1: The morula is genuinely the stage that arrives in the uterus, which is why this option is tempting and why it was the printed key. But it floats free in the uterine cavity; it must first cavitate into a blastocyst, because it is the trophoblast of the blastocyst that does the attaching.
why_wrong.3: The gastrula comes after implantation, not before. Gastrulation, the formation of the three germ layers, takes place in an embryo that is already embedded in the endometrium.

why_correct: In blood group AB both the A and the B alleles are fully expressed, so both antigens appear on the red cells. Neither masks the other, which is co-dominance.

why_wrong.0: Incomplete dominance would give a blend, some intermediate antigen between A and B, and no such thing exists. This is the distinction the question turns on.
why_wrong.2: Pleiotropy is one gene affecting several traits.
why_wrong.3: Polygenic inheritance involves several genes acting on one trait, whereas blood group is governed by a single gene with three alleles.

why_correct: A pleiotropic gene produces several apparently unrelated phenotypic effects. Phenylketonuria is the standard example, causing mental retardation, reduced hair and skin pigmentation together.

why_wrong.0: Polygenic describes many genes acting on one trait, which is the reverse relationship.
why_wrong.1: An epistatic gene masks the expression of a different gene.
why_wrong.3: A codominant gene pair expresses both alleles equally, as in AB blood group. Pleiotropy is one gene to many traits; polygeny is many genes to one trait.

why_correct: The interstitial cells of Leydig, lying between the seminiferous tubules, secrete testosterone under the influence of luteinising hormone.

why_wrong.0: Sertoli cells lie inside the tubules and nourish the developing sperm. They respond to FSH and secrete inhibin, not testosterone.
why_wrong.2: Spermatogonia are the germ cells that divide to form sperm.
why_wrong.3: Primary spermatocytes are a later stage of those germ cells. Leydig for hormone, Sertoli for nursing, and the two are the classic pair to keep straight.

why_correct: A sharp surge of luteinising hormone at about the middle of the cycle ruptures the Graafian follicle and releases the ovum. The remains of the follicle then become the corpus luteum.

why_wrong.0: Rising oestrogen from the growing follicle is what triggers the LH surge, so it is the cause of the cause rather than the immediate trigger.
why_wrong.1: Progesterone is secreted after ovulation by the corpus luteum, to maintain the endometrium.
why_wrong.3: FSH stimulates follicles to grow in the first half of the cycle but does not itself release the ovum.

why_correct: The signals for parturition come from both the fully developed foetus and the placenta, forming the foetal ejection reflex. This triggers oxytocin release from the maternal pituitary, which causes uterine contractions.

why_wrong.0: The placenta contributes, but it is only half the source.
why_wrong.1: The foetus contributes too, and again only half. When two options are each partly right and a third combines them, the combination is usually the answer.
why_wrong.3: The maternal pituitary releases the oxytocin that drives labour, but it acts in response to the signals rather than originating them.

why_correct: Amniocentesis withdraws amniotic fluid to examine foetal cells for chromosomal and genetic abnormalities, such as Down's syndrome. It is legally restricted in India to prevent its misuse for sex determination.

why_wrong.0: Foetal age is estimated by ultrasound.
why_wrong.2: The heartbeat is monitored by ultrasound or a foetal stethoscope.
why_wrong.3: Weight is estimated by ultrasound measurements. All three wrong options are things ultrasound does, whereas amniocentesis examines cells.

why_correct: Industrial melanism is directional selection. Soot darkened the tree trunks, so the dark moths were better camouflaged and the population shifted steadily towards one extreme of the range.

why_wrong.1: Disruptive selection favours both extremes and eliminates the middle, splitting the population in two.
why_wrong.2: Stabilising selection favours the average and removes both extremes, which is the opposite of what happened here.
why_wrong.3: Artificial selection is carried out deliberately by humans. Soot was a human product, but no one was choosing which moths survived, so the selection was natural.

why_correct: Hershey and Chase used radioactive phosphorus-32 to label DNA and sulphur-35 to label protein. Only the phosphorus entered the bacteria, proving DNA is the genetic material.

why_wrong.0: Carbon and nitrogen occur in both DNA and protein, so labelling them could not have separated the two.
why_wrong.2: Hydrogen and carbon are likewise present in both.
why_wrong.3: Phosphorus is right, but nitrogen occurs in protein as well as DNA. The experiment works precisely because phosphorus is in DNA but not protein, and sulphur is in protein but not DNA.

why_correct: Nylon-6,6 is made by condensation polymerisation of adipic acid with hexamethylenediamine, a small molecule of water being eliminated at each linkage.

why_wrong.0: Teflon is made by addition polymerisation of tetrafluoroethene, with nothing eliminated.
why_wrong.1: Polyacrylonitrile is an addition polymer of acrylonitrile.
why_wrong.3: Low density polyethene is an addition polymer of ethene. The test is whether a small molecule is lost during polymerisation, and only nylon loses one.

why_correct: DNA contains adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine. Uracil takes the place of thymine in RNA, so it is the base absent from DNA.

why_wrong.1: Adenine is present in DNA and pairs with thymine.
why_wrong.2: Thymine is the base characteristic of DNA, and the one uracil replaces in RNA.
why_wrong.3: Guanine is present in DNA and pairs with cytosine. The single swap to remember is thymine in DNA, uracil in RNA.

why_correct: At the isoelectric point glycine exists as a zwitterion, with the amino group protonated and the carboxyl group deprotonated. The molecule carries both charges and is electrically neutral overall.

why_wrong.0: The fully un-ionised form does not exist in appreciable amount in aqueous solution, since the proton transfers internally.
why_wrong.1: The anionic form dominates in alkaline solution, above the isoelectric point.
why_wrong.2: The cationic form dominates in acidic solution, below the isoelectric point. The isoelectric point is precisely where the two charges balance.

why_correct: XeF4 is square planar, with two lone pairs on xenon lying above and below the plane. The symmetry cancels every bond dipole, so the net dipole moment is zero.

why_wrong.0: XeF6 is distorted octahedral because of its lone pair, so it has a small but non-zero dipole moment.
why_wrong.1: XeO3 is pyramidal with one lone pair, and the dipoles do not cancel.
why_wrong.3: XeOF2 is T-shaped and contains two different bonded atoms, so it cannot be symmetrical. Symmetry is what makes a dipole moment vanish, and only the square planar shape here has it.

why_correct: Oxygen has the lowest electron affinity of these four, at about 141 kJ per mole against sulphur's 200. Its atom is so small that the incoming electron meets strong repulsion from the electrons already crowded there.

why_wrong.0: Tellurium is the largest and its electron affinity is lower than sulphur's, but still higher than oxygen's.
why_wrong.1: Selenium sits between sulphur and tellurium.
why_wrong.2: Sulphur has the highest electron affinity in the group, which is the surprise the question is testing. The expected trend of decrease down the group holds from sulphur onward; oxygen is the exception at the top.

why_correct: The Gattermann reaction converts a diazonium salt to an aryl halide using copper powder with the corresponding halogen acid, here HCl with Cu.

why_wrong.0: Cuprous chloride with HCl is the Sandmeyer reaction, the closely related alternative. Sandmeyer uses the copper salt, Gattermann uses copper metal, and that is the whole difference.
why_wrong.1: Chlorine with iron is direct halogenation of the ring, not a diazonium reaction.
why_wrong.3: Potassium chloride with HCl supplies no copper and would not bring about the substitution.

why_correct: Both nitrogen dioxide and hydrogen peroxide can act either way, because the central element is in an intermediate oxidation state and so can be raised or lowered.

why_wrong.0: In sulphur trioxide the sulphur is already at its maximum, plus six, so it can only be reduced.
why_wrong.1: In carbon dioxide the carbon is at its maximum, plus four, so it acts only as an oxidant.
why_wrong.3: In dinitrogen pentoxide nitrogen is at its maximum, plus five, and ozone is a powerful oxidant only. The general rule is that an element in an intermediate state can go either way.

why_correct: Pyrosulphuric acid, H2S2O7, has two sulphur atoms joined through an ordinary oxygen bridge, with no oxygen-oxygen bond. It is the acid present in oleum.

why_wrong.0: Hydrogen peroxide is the simplest peroxo compound of all, with a direct O-O bond.
why_wrong.1: Caro's acid, H2SO5, contains one peroxo linkage.
why_wrong.3: Marshall's acid, H2S2O8, contains a peroxo linkage joining its two sulphur-bearing halves. Counting the oxygens against the expected valency is the quickest way to spot the peroxo group.

why_correct: Fog is tiny droplets of liquid water dispersed in air, so it is a liquid in a gas. That kind of colloid is called an aerosol.

why_wrong.0: Solid in gas describes smoke and dust.
why_wrong.2: Gas in gas is not a colloid at all, since gases mix at the molecular level to form a true solution.
why_wrong.3: Gas in liquid describes foam, such as whipped cream or soap lather.

why_correct: Novolac is a phenol-formaldehyde resin, made with an excess of phenol under acidic conditions. Heating it with a hardener gives the cross-linked thermoset bakelite.

why_wrong.1: Isoprene is the monomer of natural rubber.
why_wrong.2: Neoprene is the polymer of chloroprene, a synthetic rubber.
why_wrong.3: Chloroprene is that monomer. Neoprene and chloroprene are polymer and monomer of the same pair, and neither is a phenolic resin.

why_correct: Orlon, also called acrilan, is polyacrylonitrile, made by addition polymerisation of acrylonitrile. It is used as a substitute for wool.

why_wrong.1: Teflon is polytetrafluoroethene, whose monomer is tetrafluoroethene.
why_wrong.2: Dacron is a polyester of ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid.
why_wrong.3: Nylon is a polyamide from a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid. Learning each trade name with its monomer is what these questions test.

why_correct: Glucose is an aldose and fructose a ketose, and the aldehyde group is the one thing they do not share. Bromine water is mildly acidic and a mild oxidising agent, so it oxidises the aldehyde group of glucose to gluconic acid and is itself decolourised, while fructose, having no aldehyde group and no acid to isomerise it, does not react. The colour either goes or it stays, and that tells the two sugars apart.

why_wrong.1: Chlorine in potassium hydroxide is both alkaline and a vigorous oxidant. It attacks both sugars, so it distinguishes nothing.
why_wrong.2: Tollens' reagent is alkaline, and in alkali fructose rearranges to glucose through the enediol intermediate, the Lobry de Bruyn van Ekenstein rearrangement. So fructose gives the silver mirror too, and the test cannot separate them. This was the printed key.
why_wrong.3: Fehling's solution is alkaline for the same reason and fails for the same reason: both sugars give the red precipitate of copper(I) oxide. Any test carried out in alkali is disqualified here.

why_correct: The iodoform test needs either a methyl ketone grouping or an alcohol carrying a methyl group and a hydrogen on the carbon bearing the hydroxyl, since the alkaline iodine first oxidises that alcohol to the methyl ketone. Propan-2-ol has exactly that arrangement: it is oxidised to acetone, the three hydrogens of one methyl group are then replaced by iodine and the carbon chain is cleaved by the alkali, giving the yellow precipitate of iodoform.

why_wrong.0: 2-Methylpropan-2-ol is a tertiary alcohol. The carbon bearing the hydroxyl group has no hydrogen on it at all, so it cannot be oxidised to a ketone, and without a methyl ketone there is no iodoform. This was the printed key.
why_wrong.2: Propan-1-ol is a primary alcohol and oxidises to propanal and then propanoic acid, neither of which is a methyl ketone. Note that ethanol does give iodoform, because oxidising it produces acetaldehyde, which has the methyl group next to the carbonyl. Ethanol is the exception that makes this option tempting.
why_wrong.3: Methanol has a single carbon, so there is no methyl group attached to a carbonyl or carbinol carbon for the reaction to work on. It is the one alcohol that cannot possibly give the test.

why_correct: Ammonia does not obey Henry's law because it reacts with water rather than merely dissolving in it, forming ammonium and hydroxide ions. The law applies only to gases that dissolve without reacting.

why_wrong.0: Oxygen dissolves physically in water and follows the law well.
why_wrong.2: Hydrogen is only sparingly soluble and follows the law closely.
why_wrong.3: Nitrogen likewise dissolves without reacting. The conditions for the law are moderate pressure, moderate temperature and no chemical reaction, and ammonia fails the last.

why_correct: The institution has ruled for ozonation. The connection the question is reaching for is the treatment of water: in a water works, coagulation, in which alum is added so that fine suspended particles clump into a floc heavy enough to settle, is one stage of purification and ozonation, in which ozone is used to disinfect, is another. Of the four processes listed, ozonation is the one carried out alongside coagulation.

why_wrong.0: Peptization is the most tempting option, because it is the process taught next to coagulation in every account of colloids. But it is coagulation's exact reverse: peptization breaks a fresh precipitate back up into a colloidal sol by adding a suitable electrolyte, whereas coagulation destroys a sol into a precipitate.
why_wrong.1: Sublimation is a solid passing straight into vapour without melting. It is a change of state of a pure substance and has nothing to do with colloids or with the clumping of dispersed particles.
why_wrong.2: Condensation does have a colloid connection, since condensation methods are one of the two ways of preparing a sol, as when hydrogen sulphide is passed into a solution of arsenious oxide. But that is the making of a colloid, which is the opposite of coagulating one.

why_correct: Depression of freezing point depends on the number of particles, so on the van't Hoff factor times the molality. Magnesium chloride gives three ions per formula unit, the most of these, so its solution freezes lowest.

why_wrong.0: Sucrose is a non-electrolyte and gives one particle, so its factor is 1.
why_wrong.1: Potassium chloride gives two ions, so its factor is 2, which is more than sucrose but less than magnesium chloride.
why_wrong.3: Glucose is also a non-electrolyte with a factor of 1. All four are 1 molal, so only the number of particles distinguishes them.

why_correct: Sulphur dioxide bleaches by reduction, in the presence of moisture, and the bleaching is temporary. The coloured substance is reduced rather than destroyed, and slowly reoxidises in air so the colour returns.

why_wrong.0: Chlorine bleaches by oxidation, and its action is permanent.
why_wrong.2: Hydrogen peroxide also bleaches by oxidation, and permanently.
why_wrong.3: Ozone bleaches by oxidation too. Sulphur dioxide is the only common reducing bleach, and reduction is exactly why its effect does not last.

why_correct: Acid strength in the oxoacids of chlorine rises with the oxidation state of chlorine, because more oxygen atoms spread the negative charge of the anion and stabilise it. Perchloric acid, with chlorine at plus seven, is the strongest.

why_wrong.1: Chloric acid has chlorine at plus five and is strong but weaker than perchloric.
why_wrong.2: Hypochlorous acid has chlorine at plus one and is the weakest of the four.
why_wrong.3: Chlorous acid has chlorine at plus three. The order runs HOCl, HClO2, HClO3, HClO4, increasing with the number of oxygens.

why_correct: R-MgX is the Grignard reagent, an alkyl or aryl magnesium halide prepared in dry ether. The carbon bonded to magnesium is strongly nucleophilic, which makes it one of the most useful reagents in organic synthesis.

why_wrong.1: Nessler's reagent is an alkaline solution of potassium tetraiodomercurate, used to test for ammonia.
why_wrong.2: Tollens' reagent is ammoniacal silver nitrate, used to test for aldehydes.
why_wrong.3: Collins reagent is a chromium trioxide-pyridine complex, used to oxidise primary alcohols to aldehydes.

why_correct: Catalytic hydrogenation of an aldehyde over palladium adds hydrogen across the carbon-oxygen double bond, giving a primary alcohol, RCH2OH.

why_wrong.0: ROH has lost a carbon atom, and reduction does not shorten the chain.
why_wrong.1: RCHOH is not a complete formula, since that carbon would have only three bonds.
why_wrong.3: RCH3OH shows five bonds to the same carbon, which is impossible. Count the bonds on the carbon and only one option is chemically valid.

why_correct: Dry chlorine passed over heated phosphorus gives phosphorus trichloride, a fuming liquid. With excess chlorine the product would be phosphorus pentachloride instead.

why_wrong.0: P2Cl2 is not a stable known chloride of phosphorus.
why_wrong.1: P2Cl5 is not a recognised formula either; the pentachloride is PCl5.
why_wrong.2: P2Cl gives phosphorus an impossible valency. Phosphorus forms PCl3 and PCl5, and which one you get depends on how much chlorine is present.

why_correct: An outer configuration of ns2 np1 means three valence electrons, which places the element in Group 13, the boron family.

why_wrong.1: Group 17, the halogens, have ns2 np5, that is seven valence electrons.
why_wrong.2: Group 15 has ns2 np3, five valence electrons.
why_wrong.3: Group 18, the noble gases, have ns2 np6, a full octet. Count the valence electrons and add ten for the p-block: two plus one gives three, and three plus ten is thirteen.

why_correct: Boiling point falls as the carbon chain shortens, because the molecule is smaller and the van der Waals forces between molecules are weaker, so less energy is needed to separate them.

why_wrong.0: Boiling point rises with a longer chain, not a shorter one.
why_wrong.2: It does not stay constant, and the difference is large: methanol boils at 65 degrees and butanol at 118.
why_wrong.3: There is a clear trend, so none of the above is wrong. Hydrogen bonding raises the boiling points of all alcohols, but chain length still governs the trend within the series.

why_correct: Add the atomic masses: carbon 12.01 plus four chlorines at 35.45 each, that is 141.8, giving about 153.8 grams per mole.

why_wrong.1: 15.38 is the right digits with the decimal point moved. Chlorine alone is 35.45, so the total must exceed that several times over.
why_wrong.2: 150.41 uses 34.6 for chlorine, which is not its atomic mass.
why_wrong.3: 1.53 is lighter than a carbon atom, which is impossible for a five-atom molecule.

why_correct: The Sandmeyer reaction converts an aryl diazonium salt into an aryl halide, using cuprous chloride, bromide or cyanide. It is the standard route to aryl halides that cannot be made by direct substitution.

why_wrong.0: Alkyl halides are made from alcohols with hydrogen halides or phosphorus halides, not by this route.
why_wrong.1: Alcohols are not the product; the diazonium group is replaced by halogen.
why_wrong.3: Aryl nitrates are not formed. Diazonium salts come from aromatic amines, so the product must be aromatic, which rules out both alkyl options at once.

why_correct: A is 2, 4 and 6, so it has 3 elements, and B is 2, 3, 5 and 7, so it has 4. A relation is any subset of the Cartesian product, which has 12 elements, so there are 2 to the power 12 relations.

why_wrong.0: 2 to the 9 would need the product to have 9 elements, which would mean 3 times 3. B has four primes below 8, not three, because 2 is prime.
why_wrong.2: Subtracting 1 would exclude the empty relation, but the empty set is a perfectly good relation.
why_wrong.3: This makes the same subtraction error on the right power. The count of relations is 2 raised to the product of the two sizes, with nothing removed.

why_correct: If one line is perpendicular to another, the second is perpendicular to the first, so the relation is symmetric. That is the only one of the three properties it has.

why_wrong.0: An equivalence relation must be reflexive, symmetric and transitive, and this relation fails two of the three.
why_wrong.1: It is not reflexive, since no line is perpendicular to itself.
why_wrong.3: It is not transitive: if L1 is perpendicular to L2 and L2 to L3, then L1 is parallel to L3, not perpendicular to it.

why_correct: The inverse image of 37 is the set of x with x squared plus 1 equal to 37. So x squared is 36 and x is plus or minus 6.

why_wrong.0: Plus or minus 4 would give 17, not 37.
why_wrong.2: Plus or minus 8 would give 65.
why_wrong.3: Plus or minus 2 would give 5. Subtract the 1 first and then take the square root, and check by substituting back.

why_correct: Doubling gives g of f equal to 4x squared minus 10x plus 4, so f squared plus f minus 2 equals that. Trying f as 2x minus 3 gives f squared as 4x squared minus 12x plus 9, and adding f gives exactly 4x squared minus 10x plus 6, which matches.

why_wrong.1: 2x plus 3 gives 4x squared plus 14x plus 6, whose middle term has the wrong sign.
why_wrong.2: A quadratic f would make g of f a quartic, but the right-hand side is only quadratic.
why_wrong.3: The same objection applies: composing a quadratic with a quadratic gives degree four. Comparing degrees first rules out both quadratic options at once.

why_correct: The principal value of cos inverse of minus 1 is pi, and of sin inverse of 1 is pi over 2. Subtracting gives pi over 2.

why_wrong.0: Minus 3 pi over 2 reverses the subtraction and misreads a principal value.
why_wrong.1: 3 pi over 2 would come from adding rather than subtracting.
why_wrong.2: Pi is the value of the first term alone, with the second not subtracted. Remember the principal ranges: 0 to pi for cos inverse, and minus pi over 2 to pi over 2 for sin inverse.

why_correct: When the three inverse tangents add to pi, the standard identity gives x plus y plus z equal to xyz. It follows from the addition formula for the tangent of a sum.

why_wrong.1: 2xyz is not the identity, and it fails on the simple case x, y and z all equal to root 3, where each angle is pi over 3.
why_wrong.2: 0 is the result when the three inverse tangents sum to zero, not to pi.
why_wrong.3: 1 does not follow from anything here. Test any candidate with x, y and z all root 3: the sum is 3 root 3 and so is the product.

why_correct: A symmetric matrix equals its own transpose, so the entry in row 1 column 2 must equal the entry in row 2 column 1. That gives x equal to y.

why_wrong.0: x plus y equal to 1 is satisfied by x as 0 and y as 1, which is not symmetric.
why_wrong.1: xy equal to 1 is satisfied by x as 2 and y as one half, again not symmetric.
why_wrong.2: x minus y equal to 1 forces x and y to differ, which is the opposite of symmetry. The diagonal entries never enter the condition.

why_correct: Adding the second row to the first turns every entry of the first row into x plus y plus z, so that row becomes a multiple of the third row of ones. A determinant with two proportional rows is zero.

why_wrong.1: 1 would require the rows to be independent in a very particular way, which they are not.
why_wrong.2: This expression appears in other determinant identities but not here.
why_wrong.3: x plus y plus z is the common factor that comes out of the combined row, but what remains is a determinant with two identical rows, which is zero.

why_correct: The system is triangular, so its determinant is the product of the diagonal entries, K plus 1 times K minus 1 times K plus 2. A unique solution needs that product to be non-zero, which rules out K equal to minus 1, 1 and minus 2, leaving 0.

why_wrong.1: K equal to 1 makes the second diagonal entry zero, so the determinant vanishes.
why_wrong.2: K equal to minus 1 makes the first entry zero.
why_wrong.3: K equal to minus 2 makes the third entry zero. Each of the three wrong options is precisely a value that kills one diagonal entry.

why_correct: For a matrix of order n, the determinant of the adjoint is the determinant raised to the power n minus 1. Here n is 3, so it is 7 squared, that is 49.

why_wrong.0: 7 would be the answer if the power were 1, that is for a 2 by 2 matrix.
why_wrong.2: 7 cubed uses the order itself rather than one less than the order.
why_wrong.3: 7 to the fourth is further still. The rule comes from A times adj A equalling the determinant times the identity.

why_correct: As x tends to 0, sin ax over x tends to a, so sin squared ax over x squared tends to a squared. Continuity requires that limit to equal the value 1, so a squared is 1 and a is plus or minus 1.

why_wrong.0: Minus 1 works, but so does plus 1, so giving only one of them is incomplete.
why_wrong.1: Plus 1 works too, and the same objection applies. When a condition involves a square, always check both roots.
why_wrong.3: One half would give a limit of one quarter, not 1.

why_correct: Near zero, 1 minus cos px behaves like p squared x squared over 2 and x sin x behaves like x squared, so the limit is p squared over 2. Setting that equal to one half gives p squared equal to 1, so p is plus or minus 1.

why_wrong.0: 2 would give a limit of 2, four times too large.
why_wrong.1: Minus 2 gives the same limit as 2, since the answer depends on p squared, and it is likewise too large.
why_wrong.3: There is a correct option. Note that both signs of p work, because cosine is an even function.

why_correct: At x equal to 2 the numerator is 2 times f of 2 minus 2 times f of 2, which is zero, so this is a zero over zero limit. Rewrite the numerator by adding and subtracting 2 times f of 2: it becomes f of 2 times x minus 2, minus 2 times the quantity f of x minus f of 2. Dividing by x minus 2 gives f of 2, minus 2 times the difference quotient of f at 2, and letting x tend to 2 gives f of 2 minus twice f dashed of 2, that is 4 minus 8, which is minus 4.

why_wrong.0: 2 is half of f of 2 and arises from no step in the derivation. A useful check for all of these: the function f of x equal to 4x minus 4 satisfies both conditions given, and substituting it makes the whole quotient exactly minus 4 for every x other than 2.
why_wrong.1: Minus 2 has the right sign but the wrong size. It is what f of 2 over 2 minus f dashed of 2 would give, so check the factor 2 on each term.
why_wrong.2: 4 is f of 2 standing alone, which is what remains if the minus twice f dashed of 2 term is dropped, or if the subtraction is done the wrong way round as 8 minus 4. This was the printed key, and the concrete function f of x equal to 4x minus 4 settles the sign beyond argument.

why_correct: Take logarithms: log y equals x log x. Differentiating gives one over y times dy by dx equal to log x plus 1, so the derivative is x to the x times 1 plus log x.

why_wrong.0: The sign inside the bracket is wrong. Differentiating x log x by the product rule gives log x plus 1, both terms positive.
why_wrong.1: This keeps only the log x term and drops the 1 that comes from differentiating x itself.
why_wrong.2: x to the power x plus 1 is not what logarithmic differentiation produces; the factor outside stays x to the x. The power rule cannot be used here because the exponent is not constant.

why_correct: Divide dy by dx by dz by dx. Differentiating sin of x degrees brings out the degree-to-radian factor, and differentiating log to base 10 of x gives log base 10 of e divided by x. Dividing one by the other gives x degrees times cos x degrees over log base 10 of e.

why_wrong.1: This drops the degree conversion in the numerator, leaving plain x where the angle measure is needed.
why_wrong.2: This makes both errors at once, using plain x and the natural log of 10.
why_wrong.3: This keeps the degree factor but uses log e of 10 instead of log 10 of e, and the two are reciprocals of each other.

why_correct: The denominator factorises as 1 plus x times 1 plus x squared, and expanding y as a series gives 1 minus x plus x to the fourth and higher terms. The coefficient of x squared is zero, so the second derivative at 0 is zero.

why_wrong.1: 1 would need a coefficient of one half for x squared in the expansion.
why_wrong.2: Minus 1 would need a coefficient of minus one half.
why_wrong.3: 2 would need a coefficient of 1. Multiplying numerator and denominator by 1 minus x turns the denominator into 1 minus x to the fourth, which makes the series easy to read off.

why_correct: Area is pi r squared, so the rate of change of area is 2 pi r times the rate of change of radius. With r equal to 2 and the rate 1 over pi, that is 2 times pi times 2 times 1 over pi, which is 4.

why_wrong.0: 2 would come from forgetting the factor of 2 in the derivative of r squared.
why_wrong.2: 6 does not follow from any correct step here.
why_wrong.3: 8 comes from using a radius of 4, or from doubling once too often. The pi cancels neatly, which is a sign the arithmetic is on track.

why_correct: Implicit differentiation gives the tangent slope as b squared x over a squared y, which at the given point simplifies to b over a sin theta. The normal slope is the negative reciprocal, that is minus a sin theta over b.

why_wrong.0: This is positive and has b over a, so it is neither the tangent slope nor its negative reciprocal.
why_wrong.1: This has the right sign but keeps b over a, which is the tangent's ratio rather than the normal's.
why_wrong.2: This has the right ratio but the wrong sign. The normal slope must be the negative reciprocal of the tangent slope, so both the sign and the inversion must change.

why_correct: On xy equal to 1 the tangent slope is minus 1 over x squared, which is always negative, so the normal slope is x squared, always positive. The line's slope is minus a over b, and for that to be positive a and b must have opposite signs.

why_wrong.0: Both positive makes minus a over b negative, which would be a tangent direction rather than a normal one.
why_wrong.1: Both negative gives the same negative slope, for the same reason.
why_wrong.3: c not equal to zero says nothing about the slope, and the condition here is entirely about direction. Note that a negative with b positive would work too, but it is not among the options.

why_correct: The slopes are 1 over 2y for the parabola and minus y over x for the hyperbola. Setting their product to minus 1 gives x equal to one half, and since x cubed equals k squared at the intersection, k squared is one eighth.

why_wrong.0: One half is the value of x at the intersection, not of k squared. The final cubing step is still needed.
why_wrong.1: One quarter is x squared rather than x cubed.
why_wrong.2: One sixth does not arise from any step here. Curves cut at right angles when the product of their slopes at the common point is minus 1.

why_correct: With a fixed sum, the product is greatest when the two numbers are equal. So x and y are each 12 and the maximum product is 144.

why_wrong.0: 80 comes from 4 and 20, which sum correctly but are far apart.
why_wrong.1: 128 comes from 8 and 16, closer together but still not equal.
why_wrong.2: 140 comes from 10 and 14, closer still. The pattern is clear: the nearer the two numbers are to each other, the larger the product, with the maximum at equality.

why_correct: The probability of A and B is P of B given A times P of A, that is 0.60 times 0.40, which is 0.24. Dividing that by P of A given B, which is 0.75, gives P of B as 0.32.

why_wrong.0: 0.24 is the probability of A and B, which is the intermediate step rather than the answer.
why_wrong.2: 0.48 would come from dividing by 0.5 somewhere.
why_wrong.3: 0.52 does not arise from any correct step. Work out the intersection first from one conditional, then divide by the other.

why_correct: By De Morgan's law, the union of the complements is the complement of the intersection. So the answer is 1 minus 5 over 13, which is 8 over 13.

why_wrong.0: 4 over 13 does not arise from subtracting from 1.
why_wrong.1: 6 over 13 would follow from a total of 11 over 13.
why_wrong.2: 7 over 13 would follow from subtracting from 12 over 13. Recognising the De Morgan pairing turns this into a one-line subtraction.
